title: SpaceX’s AI business is beating expectations
snippet: SpaceX hit profitability in the third quarter, with net income of $4.4 billion. AI was the engine.
fullText:
SpaceX’s data centers and Grok agents were more profitable than investors expected in the third quarter of the year, as the company leaves its roots as a space company behind to focus on artificial intelligence, which now makes up 52% of its income.

CEO Elon Musk’s deep tech conglomerate reported $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to its regulatory filing.

That number was driven by growth in all segments, but especially its renamed “Super Intelligence” business line, which generated $7.5 billion in revenue from the recently acquired Cursor coding tool, Grok bot, and most importantly, the company’s burgeoning neocloud business, which now boasts 1.7 GW of compute. The AI business generated $431 million in profit, which would have been higher without $1.2 billion in one-time stock-based compensation expenses related to the Cursor acquisition.

The top-line revenue number was also boosted by about $1 billion in income related to the recovery of Bitcoin prices and unspecified related-party income that might be attributed to a SpaceX investment in another company.

The growing revenue is balanced against total capital expenditures of $19.6 billion, as SpaceX continues to build out a second data center project, Colossus II, and increase investment in Starship, the heavy-lift rocket it sees as vital to deploying a new generation of Starlink satellites and developing orbital data centers. CFO Bret Johnsen said the company would spend $35 billion to $40 billion on new capital investments in the fourth quarter.

During a livestreamed discussion of the results with investors, Musk said he was spending four days a week in Memphis, Tennessee, the site of Colossus II, working to bring the data center online.

“People are starting to realize [that] the constraint on deployment of super intelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips,” Musk argued, saying that he had tasked a team of SpaceX engineers to solve that problem. “This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League. It’s not fair, but the net result is being able to deploy power cooling infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than any anyone else.”

In one example, Musk noted that manufacturers of turbines to power data centers are facing 12- to 18-month delays in obtaining the metals that blades and vanes required for those machines. Now, SpaceX is using the metal casting capabilities developed for SpaceX to make those components and obtain turbines more quickly.

Musk also said that the next test flight of the Starship rocket, expected in November, would see SpaceX attempt to recover both the first-stage booster and the second stage. Recovering both segments of the vehicle would be a “massive technology milestone,” Musk said, but the true milestone will be reflying both stages.

SpaceX also saw growth in subscribers to its Starlink space internet network, reaching 13.6 million consumers, with Musk predicting that the growth of AI agents would lead to more demand for connectivity.

Despite those capital expenditures, the company’s revenue boost was substantial enough to push it back into profitability. SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion, a turnaround from the $1 billion loss in the same quarter last year. It will still have some catching up to do if it wants to remain profitable for the year, however. In the first nine months of the year, SpaceX still had a net income loss of $413 million.

Musk took a particularly bullish stance on the company’s Super Intelligence business segment, predicting that SpaceX’s annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 will be “somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion.”

More concretely, Johnsen forecast total revenue for the first quarter of 2027 in the range of $33 billion to $37 billion.

This is a developing story. TechCrunch will update.

title: Google restricts every free AI Pro trial from Pixel & more compared to paid subscribers
snippet: Google hands out extended free trials to its AI Pro subscription frequently with new smartphone purchases and more, but trial users end up getting less access compared to paid subscribers in what is a bit of a misleading situation. more…
fullText:
Google hands out extended free trials to its AI Pro subscription frequently with new smartphone purchases and more, but trial users end up getting less access compared to paid subscribers in what is a bit of a misleading situation.

Free trials are a pretty standard practice across the industry when it comes to subscriptions, and the general understanding is that you’re getting full access to the same subscription you are later set to pay for unless there’s an upfront stipulation about restrictions.

And that’s where things are getting a bit messy with Google’s AI Pro subscription.

Google One AI Pro is a $19.99/month subscription that delivers access to expanded Gemini usage limits, 5TB of storage across Google products, and bundles in other subscriptions such as Google Home Premium, Health Premium, and YouTube Premium Lite. Earlier this year, we called AI Pro “one of the best deals in tech today.”

	

But the rollout of Gemini 4 Argon to Google’s Antigravity development tool put a spotlight on a restriction on AI Pro’s free trials. Put simply, they’re limited compared to paid subscribers, and it’s not something Google made abundantly clear.

There are two specific downsides with a Google One AI Pro trial compared to an actively paid subscription. As mentioned, Antigravity on AI Pro trials leaves out Gemini 4 Argon. Google has a page that specifically puts a trial account in a completely different bucket compared to a paid AI Pro plan, and it treats the trial as a free user with expanded usage limits rather than a full user as @evowizz was one of the first to point out.

The other restriction is YouTube Premium Lite, which is not available for Google One AI Pro trial users until they start paying.

In Google’s defense, this is technically spelled out on support documents. The YouTube Premium Lite restriction, for example, is clearly spelled out as Google says that the “benefit is unavailable until trials of Google AI Pro conclude and you convert to a paid subscription.” But, as far as we can see, this is not disclosed as clearly at the time of sign-up or alongside advertising of the AI Pro trials.

Another loss here is the lack of Google One’s 10% cashback (store credit) perk in the Google Store, which is lacking in free trials. That one is certainly easier to see the reasoning behind, though.

The Google Store touts the Pixel 11’s AI Pro trial as delivering “expanded usage limits in Gemini, access to Gemini in Google apps, and 5 TB of cloud storage,” as well as Health Premium. Nowhere does Google promise the YouTube perks, but the wording around Gemini also lacks any hint at the restriction found in Antigravity. Pages including offer details also lack any mention of this.

As mentioned, Google hands out free, extended trials to AI Pro all over the place. Just a few active examples include:

6 months free with the purchase of a Pixel 11

12 months free with the purchase of a Googlebook

6 months free for select Verizon customers

12 months free with Chromebook Plus or 3 months with any other Chromebook

6 months free with the purchase of a Galaxy Z Fold 8

And that’s just a few examples – you can absolutely find more.

	

Google explicitly lists all of these trials at their full monthly value (i.e. $119 value for Pixel’s 6-month trial) despite the restricted access that trial users see.

While Google has not addressed the somewhat misleading nature of the AI Pro trial restrictions, one Googler responded to the other headache that exists here – you can’t just press a button to start paying for AI Pro if you’re on a trial. You either have to wait for the trial to end, or reach out to Google for help converting your account. 

What do you think of the situation?

The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Americans have a privacy problem, and that shouldn’t surprise anyone. Between the unprecedented backlash around Flock cameras and, more quietly, data brokers selling off our identities, individual privacy is center stage right now. I would go as far as to make it the inaugural Security Bite ‘Theme of the Year.’

Yet despite all of that, a new survey from data removal service Incogni found that 45% of the 1,517 U.S. adults polled say they aren’t concerned about their online privacy. That wasn’t even the best part of this survey though…

Among people who said they have nothing to hide, 58% would refuse to hand a stranger their unlocked phone for any amount of money, 39% cover the camera on their phone or laptop, and nearly half wouldn’t hand over their text messages to the government or “Big Tech,” even for three months of their income.

I asked Ron Zayas, founder and CEO of Ironwall by Incogni, what’s actually going on here, and he basically replied that privacy only feels abstract until it isn’t.

“We take privacy for granted, until it means that someone will read our messages, charge us more, put us in danger or disclose intimate details about us,” he told me. “But the reality is, all of that is privacy.” He also thinks companies lean on that gap on purpose, pointing out that if a privacy policy actually said “download this app and we will go through your contacts, suck in your photos, analyze your habits and share those details with anyone willing to pay us,” most of us would pause. Instead, they open with “we value your privacy” and bury the rest in legalese.

The survey also found that 65% of respondents have no idea how many websites they’re registered on, and honestly, I’m not sure I could tell you mine either. We’ve all spent the last decade or so creating accounts for things we used once and forgot about, and every one of them is still holding onto something. You can’t protect data you don’t remember giving away, right?

So I asked Zayas where someone on an iPhone or Mac should start if they want to cut that down without going full underground, and his answer was more Apple-friendly than I was expecting. “Apple has some pretty good safety protocols, much better than Google in my opinion, and makes them far easier to access,” he said. “Turn off as much of ad personalization, location sharing and contact sharing as you can. It only takes a moment.” He also recommends treating your phone number like you would a credit card number. Allowing an app to have access to your contacts will also give it your own.

Zayas put it well when he said that believing you have to “go full bunker in Montana” to have any privacy is a fallacy companies push to make people feel helpless, and I agree with him. If you live in California, the CCPA and Delete Act let you force a good chunk of your data off the market for free. For everyone else, a few minutes to clean things up in Privacy & Security can go a long way. The survey honestly put it better by saying, most of us already act like our privacy matters, so we might as well stop saying it doesn’t.

title: Google has joined Amazon in attacking Nvidia’s stronghold with AI app developers
snippet: Google has joined Amazon in releasing a developer tool that makes it easy for PyTorch users to move their apps off Nvidia GPUs.
fullText:
On Tuesday, Google announced that TorchTPU, its long-awaited version of PyTorch, is now available as an open source project. With this, Google joins Amazon in trying to break Nvidia’s stranglehold on the AI industry, where most AI apps are written by default to run on Nvidia’s chips, or GPUs.

PyTorch is the popular open source toolkit that AI app developers and startups use to build, train, and run AI models. It is, by some accounts, used by 85% of the AI apps. PyTorch was originally developed by Meta (then Facebook) in 2016, long before the world had an inkling that LLMs would change the world. At the time, Nvidia’s GPUs were already the standard hardware for AI research, so many of PyTorch’s features were built to work specifically with them. In 2022, Meta turned PyTorch over to the Linux Foundation, a nonprofit that manages many important open source projects.

Google’s version, TorchTPU, lets AI apps run on Google’s AI chips, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). It also makes it easy to move existing PyTorch apps to TPUs and, therefore, to Google Cloud. Developers can do this with a simple configuration change and no rewriting of their apps.

Amazon made a similar announcement Monday, when it released its own version of PyTorch, called TorchNeuron. TorchNeuron allows AI apps to be ported to Amazon’s homegrown AI chip, Trainium, and to AWS with no rewriting. Amazon also said it’s going even further in its effort to loosen Nvidia’s hold on PyTorch. It is submitting code to the main PyTorch project that decouples various features from Nvidia’s chips, making it more open to any hardware by default.

Google may be one-upping Amazon in a few ways, however. It says it worked directly with Meta, Hugging Face, Inferact (maker of vLLM), RadixArk (maker of SGLang), and others to ensure that TorchTPU’s features and code libraries work well with these popular AI development tools, just as the original PyTorch does.

Plus the search giant has launched a dedicated tool, the TPU agent suite, to help developers move their apps to Google’s chips and cloud and fix errors along the way. It even updated its popular LiteRT tool, which runs AI on phones, laptops, and embedded devices, to work better with PyTorch AI apps.

None of this means AI app developers will automatically ditch Nvidia’s hardware en masse just because they can now easily move to alternative chips and clouds. But Amazon and Google are clearly working to end Nvidia’s advantage.

Emma Roth

 

is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

OpenAI disclosed a pair of safety incidents that involved AI agents weakening their safety monitoring systems during internal coding tasks. In one incident, OpenAI says its GPT-6 Astra agent disabled its safety monitor when copying reference code — and then lied about it.

“The reference didn’t configure a monitor, and Astra decided that was reason to remove the monitoring integration from the user’s code,” Marcus Williams, an AI safety researcher at OpenAI, writes on X. “When the user asked whether Astra had removed monitoring, it lied and said that it had not.”

A separate incident occurred after a GPT-6.1 Sol agent suppressed automatic security alerts to OpenAI’s security team on Slack. In this case, the AI agent carried over an earlier instruction not to send any Slack messages to OpenAI’s team, using that to justify turning off the alerts.

These incidents add to security concerns surrounding AI agents, some of which have circumvented their testing environment’s restrictions to hack outside companies. “In addition to making it harder for models to disable monitoring, we are looking to understand why models might seek to do so in the first place,” OpenAI says. “We are also developing evaluations to test whether models might have a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring in particular and exhibit motivated reasoning in order to do so.”

title: Mach9 raises $34M after pivoting to AI CAD software
snippet: The startup initially set out to build better, faster, and cheaper surveying hardware in 2021.
fullText:
When Alex Baikovitz co-founded Mach9 Robotics in 2021, his goal was to build a better, faster, and cheaper way for civil engineers to do visual inspections. The company aimed to cut through red tape and modernize the slow, outdated processes that bog down construction in the United States.

Within a few years, Mach9 Robotics had built that hardware, but the effort led Baikovitz to a realization: hardware wasn’t the bottleneck.

“We saw how tedious it was for civil engineering organizations to take data from these amazing laser scanners and image data capture systems and turn that into a usable survey,” he told TechCrunch in an interview, referring to a detailed map of a site that engineers use for design work. “The real pain was in their workflows,” he said, and “how to turn all the endless amounts of data that they’re able to collect into . . .information that people can use to make the best design and asset management decisions across the board.”

So Baikovitz dropped “Robotics” from the company’s name and pivoted to developing AI-powered computer-aided design (CAD) software instead. The bet paid off, as Mach9 has racked up nearly 100 customers for the private beta of its software, and they’ve used it on more than 2,500 projects to date.

That momentum helped Mach9 unlock new funding. On Wednesday, the startup announced a $34 million Series A funding round co-led by First Round Capital and Bessemer Venture Partners. Also throwing in were Prudence, an early-stage, New York-based firm that focuses on investing in AI software use cases for construction and real estate, and Quiet Capital, a VC firm already on the cap table.

Mach9 is one of a number of startups racing to modernize the planning-to-building pipeline for construction and infrastructure. In August, a startup called CivilGrid raised $26 million to grow what it calls the “Google Maps for the underground.” Meanwhile, Blueprints AI, which uses AI to produce code-compliant, permit-ready architectural blueprints in just a few minutes, was among the top 200 companies in the Startup Battlefield competition at last week’s TechCrunch Disrupt.

Baikovitz said Mach9 is focused on disrupting CAD software because it’s one of the slowest and most labor-intensive pieces of that overall pipeline.

“It takes months to be able to deliver a project, and about a week per mile for someone to do manually in the legacy incumbent software that’s built by the Autodesk and Bentley Systems of the world,” he said.

Mach9 says its software automates a lot of that work, making the process 10 times faster and dramatically reducing costs. This allows customers doing surveying and civil engineering work to “expand their own capacity and take on more types of work, bigger projects, and expand the reach of how reality-capture data can influence major infrastructure decisions,” Baikovitz said.

Baikovitz said Mach9 developed and trained its own in-house AI models to reach the centimeter-accurate level that construction and infrastructure work requires.

“That’s not something that a lot of off-the-shelf models are able to do or deliver at in any capacity,” he said. “A big part of what our development process has looked like since 2024 has been, how do we build the industry leading models that can turn imagery or these multimodal image and laser scan data sets into survey grade like geometry, like tracing out the curbs, the pavement striping, all of this exactly how our customers want it to be at the accuracies that the industry demands.”

Mach9’s AI CAD system takes the survey data and creates a first draft of a plan, which engineers can then refine. The startup is “giving them all of the tools to draw, remove, adjust vertices, assess the quality of the AI-generated model, so that they can put effectively their name behind the deliverable that they’re producing, because there is a lot of liability in this particular industry, and it requires licensed professionals that know what they’re looking at,” Baikovitz said.

As for the funding, Baikovitz said his startup will split it between improving the product, hiring industry experts, and scaling “all parts of our organization to keep up with where the market is taking us.”

In retrospect, Baikovitz said he’s thankful that he initially went down the hardware path. It gave his startup something to pitch to potential customers, and it was largely those customers who told him they didn’t need better devices to capture data.

“I’m not interested in getting this cheaper, lower-cost hardware,” he remembers one VP telling him. But better software could “improve our efficiency in delivering these big statewide transportation mapping initiatives,” he said. He added that such projects help make states that Mach9 has worked with, like Texas, “much more like safe [and] effective.”

title: OpenAI acquires startup Orchestra Bio⁠ to beef up its biotech business
snippet: OpenAI says it's adding Orchestra's team and technology to work on Rosalind, its AI model for life sciences research, and to its related Rosalind Workbench tool, a harness that aims to help researchers plan experiments and analyze results.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

1:35 PM PDT · October 20, 2026

Image Credits:FotografiaBasica (opens in a new window) / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

OpenAI on Tuesday acquired a four-year-old AI biotech software startup called Orchestra Bio, the company announced on its website. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the startup had reportedly raised around $20 million as of 2025 from backers like Andreessen Horowitz, Atria, and 8VC.

Orchestra creates AI agents that help biotech companies manage the minutiae of drug-discovery operations, from tracking finances to resolving scheduling issues with clinical trials.

OpenAI says it’s adding Orchestra’s team and technology to work on Rosalind, its AI model for life sciences research, and to its related Rosalind Workbench tool, a harness that aims to help researchers plan experiments and analyze results. OpenAI has already won some big names as customers for Rosalind, including, it says, Moderna⁠ and Novo Nordisk⁠.

The acquisition is a classic example of how the biggest AI labs (namely OpenAI and Anthropic) are building ever more software for the biggest industries, like pharma. In the startup world, there is an ongoing fear that at any moment, the labs will launch new features and become competitors. In this case, Orchestra is getting absorbed, rather than stomped out.

snippet: Google has begun emailing Gemini AI Plus members to inform them when their Gemini subscription will no longer include access to the advanced models – just Flash. more…
fullText:
Google has begun emailing Gemini AI Plus members to inform them when their Gemini subscription will no longer include access to the advanced models – just Flash.

A change in Gemini’s subscription model was announced earlier this month. It came right before Google’s new Argon model went live and became the new high-performance offer in Gemini. The company made it clear that Gemini 4 Argon would be included for AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers, but it also said AI Plus members would lose access to AI Pro entirely.

According to one user on Reddit, Google has begun emailing AI Plus subscribers to let them know Gemini Pro models would be excluded from the AI Plus tier starting on November 13. The email lists Flash-Lite and Flash as the only two options after that date.

We wanted to let you know about changes to the models that you can access with your Google AI Plus plan.

Starting on ﻿1﻿3﻿ ﻿N﻿o﻿v﻿e﻿m﻿b﻿e﻿r﻿ ﻿2﻿0﻿2﻿6﻿, the ability to select Pro models in both the Gemini app and AI Mode in Google Search will only be available to Google AI Pro subscribers and above. You’ll still have access to our latest Flash-Lite model and Flash, built for speed and intelligence. Your previous chats using the Pro model can be continued with a different model.

To learn more about these changes, you can visit our Help Centre article for additional details. You can manage or cancel your subscription at any time.

Thank you for being a Google AI Plus subscriber.

– The Google One team

A couple of others report getting the same email, which puts a pin on exactly when the Gemini AI Plus plan changes.

	

The $4.99/month option will give users access to just two models, while the $19.99/month tier gains access to Argon, leaving a bigger gap between the two. Google is still keeping the free plan around, which leaves everyone with access to Flash-lite.

Of course, these subscriptions tie into Google Workspace for cloud storage and other perks, like YouTube Premium. Still, the $4.99/month plan seemed like a good deal for those who wanted access to more capable models for more than just passive chats.

title: Data Centers Are Burning Fossil Fuels. It’s Destroying Big Tech’s Climate Goals
snippet: In his new book, Paris Marx explores how global anti-data center movements are fighting Big Tech’s power over us.
fullText:
From Ashburn, Virginia, to South Dublin, Ireland, the data centers that journalist Paris Marx visited all looked remarkably similar: large industrial facilities with loud air-conditioning units running to keep racks upon racks of servers cool. But it was the security measures around the data centers that struck Marx more than anything. 

Tall fences. Security cameras everywhere. Locks on every door that required one of the few full-time employees to unlock with a badge. And in one memorable instance, standing on an Irish public curb outside a cluster of Microsoft-owned centers, there was an eerie feeling of being watched by men on lawn mowers, trimming grass that clearly didn’t need to be cut.

“It was just really staggering to me that it was at that level that it was so hard to move through these spaces,” Marx told me.

			

More from CNET

The intense security should give you an idea of just how serious Big Tech is about its data centers. These facilities are the key to the artificial intelligence programs at OpenAI, Meta, Google, Amazon and elsewhere, creating vast amounts of compute and sucking up equally staggering amounts of electricity and water. 

There is no stronger metaphor for the manifestation of Big Tech’s power than the increasing sprawl of data centers. Amazon, Microsoft and Google alone control 59% of hyperscale data center capacity. In his new book available now, Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires, Marx, host of the Tech Won’t Save Us podcast, highlights how global data center protests are one of many ways that communities are pushing back against Big Tech’s power over us.

Hyperscale demands

Data centers existed long before generative AI; we called them server farms, and they’re what keep us online. But in this AI era, we have hyperscale data centers.

Before, a large data center might require around 50 megawatts of power to keep everything running. Now, hyperscale data centers can require triple that amount of power. Newer ones, like Meta’s Louisiana data center, may require 4,500 megawatts (4.5 gigawatts) — staggering demand that officials say is four times more than all of the electricity used in New Orleans on its hottest day in 2025. It’s more than the two gigawatts the Hoover Dam produces.

Hyperscale data centers are also housing more advanced tech. Chips like GPUs are key to creating compute, and newer chips built for AI data centers can run hotter. That makes it even harder to cool facilities, so in addition to air conditioning, facilities are using water systems to avoid servers overheating. It’s an additional environmental toll. A hyperscale center can suck up 1 million to 5 million gallons of water every day, equivalent to a town of more than 10,000 residents, according to a 2025 estimate.

So how do you keep these facilities running? The process to get approved and connected to a town’s electrical grid can take years. So tech companies have started building their own power plants right next to data centers for the sole purpose of keeping them on — perfect for burning massive amounts of fossil fuels, the main contributor to the climate crisis.

Hyperscale impacts

In the 2010s, Amazon, Microsoft, Google and many others pledged some version of becoming carbon neutral (or negative) in the next few decades — meaning they would offset the emissions they created with at least as much emission-reducing actions. 

Sustainability reports from that time show that, overall, tech companies were measurably decreasing their environmental footprint. “And then ChatGPT comes along, and all of a sudden, that’s out the window,” Marx told me.

Tech leaders have been candid about allowing generative AI to override their climate goals. Google reported a 50% increase in its greenhouse gas emissions in 2024 to support its generative AI. Microsoft’s pledge to be carbon negative by 2030 “was before the explosion in artificial intelligence,” Brad Smith, the company’s president, told Bloomberg in 2023, saying the carbon goal was “five times as far away as it was in 2020” because of AI. 

Modern data centers and their power plants burn fossil fuels for power, requiring gas turbines, huge tanks of diesel fuel kept on-site in case of a power outage or good old-fashioned coal. This has devastating environmental and health consequences, both immediately for local communities and in the long term for the entire world. 

Communities that neighbor data centers have reported brown or unsafe drinking water, unending noise, and in one lawsuit against Elon Musk’s xAI centers in Memphis, extreme health risks; Memphis residents “are feeling it in their lungs because of the fossil fuels that are being burned,” Marx said.

Tennessee state representative Justin Pearson speaks at a rally in opposition to Elon Musk’s data center in Memphis on April 25, 2025.

Brandon Dill for The Washington Post via Getty Images

And as decades of climate research prove, burning additional fossil fuels is only going to exacerbate the effects of climate change. That’ll lead to even more extreme weather, health risks and natural disasters. As Marx put it in his book, “The world will suffer through the worsening natural disasters fueled by the quest for computation by some of the most powerful people on the planet.”

With data centers and their fossil fuels, we’re fundamentally reshaping the planet for AI. So anti-data center movements are asking: Is it worth it?

“How much computation do we really need here?” Marx asked in our conversation. “How many resources are we willing to dedicate to this vision of the future? And is this technology really delivering in such a way that expending all those resources is justified?”

The answer — for many data center neighbors in Memphis, Oregon, Chile, Ireland and thousands of other communities across the globe — is an unflinching no.

title: Yelp’s AI Assistant Can Call a Restaurant and Join the Waitlist for You
snippet: The updated agent also can tell you if it’s going to rain and maybe you shouldn’t book that outdoor table.
fullText:
Hate calling restaurants to check wait times? Yelp is rolling out a new AI-powered tool to handle just that, along with other tools as the platform deepens its employment of agentic artificial intelligence.

“This release is another step forward as we transform Yelp with AI, with updates across every category on Yelp, from booking a table at a restaurant to hiring a pro for a home project,” Akhil Kuduvalli Ramesh, Yelp’s chief product officer, said in a statement. 

Yelp expands its AI offerings

Just months after launching an updated AI assistant, Yelp Assistant, that can book reservations for you, Yelp is expanding its AI integrations with a new AI agent. Check for Me will call restaurants on your behalf to check wait times in real time and text you with updates within a few minutes. As personal and shopping assistants become more widely used, new reports show the hardships faced by both businesses and customers: Businesses must contend with an influx of calls and emails from bots, while human customers must compete with AI agents to make reservations.    

			

More from CNET

Yelp Assistant now works with OpenTable, allowing you access to thousands of restaurants across the US. You can simply ask the assistant for recommendations on “dog-friendly coffee shops” and booking help.

You can also use Yelp Waitlist to get in line before you arrive. After you join the line, Yelp Assistant will send you status updates, such as when your table becomes available. 

Check for Me will call restaurants on your behalf to check wait times in real time and text you with updates within a few minutes.Yelp

Yelp Assistant gets personal

Yelp is further expanding its Assistant capabilities while also adding more personalization. 

A new feature, Keep Me Posted, lets you tailor your reminders based on your personal schedule. With the feature, you can have Yelp Assistant send you weekend date night ideas every Thursday or dog-friendly hikes once a month. These personal AI agents that execute tasks on your behalf are becoming increasingly popular. Meta Muse and OpenAI Dots recently hit the market, and Google is continuously incorporating agentic AI into its booking and planning services. 

Yelp Assistant’s personalization will also apply to conversations by referencing past chats and your Yelp review history. For instance, if you’ve recently chatted on Yelp for vegan restaurants near you, the Assistant will ask if you’re interested in more vegan options. 

For further personalization, the app can now reference local weather forecasts when you make reservations, so you don’t book an outdoor patio on a night it’s supposed to pour. And a new feature, My Lists, lets you save, rank and promote your favorite local businesses, and then Yelp will give you more tailored recommendations based on your lists. 

Yelp initially debuted its AI Assistant in 2024, but these new integrations and features show how Yelp is evolving as AI tools become more adept at actually doing things, not just telling you things.

title: Amazon launches two Bee AI recorders to remember everything you say
snippet: Just over a year after acquiring the AI company, Bee, Amazon has officially unveiled two of its first AI wearables, so you never forget what was said. more…
fullText:
Just over a year after acquiring the AI company, Bee, Amazon has officially unveiled two of its first AI wearables, so you never forget what was said.

Amazon announced two models: the Bee Frontier and the Bee Eclipse. Both can be considered wearables, with one taking on a bracelet form factor that works just fine clipped to a shirt. The Eclipse is a magnetic version of the always-listening device for use with Qi2 or MagSafe-equipped phones.

The Frontier is not dissimilar to the first preview Bee introduced before it was purchased by Amazon. At the time, the company had seemingly high hopes for being a genuine cornerstone of people’s lives to make their lives easier.

Amazon says both models are designed with “privacy principles” in mind, noting that a visible LED indicates when the Bee Frontier or Eclipse is listening. That’s what they do, after all. Both are designed to stay active and compile your ideas, thoughts, and even nonsense into reminders or notes, based on what Bee’s AI model decides you might need.

	

All of that can be found in the companion app, whether on mobile or desktop. Users can connect their Google Account to let it access emails and calendar information. That feeds into the selling idea that Bee becomes your personal assistant so you don’t miss out on a thing.

As for hardware, the Bee Frontier wearable is IP67 and rated for seven days of battery. The magnetic Eclipse model is able to power through a longer workload with up to 21 days of battery on a charge.

Of course, Amazon also added Alexa+ and Amazon.com integration into how the Bee wearables operate. The devices will be able to surface products based on your anticipated needs. That’s fun.

The Bee Frontier is available now for $74.99, while the Bee Eclipse will goi on sale “soon” starting at $99.99.

title: Apple is right about the wild west of AI, and the growing backlash
snippet: Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak didn’t hold back when he described the most ambitious figures in the AI race as the “lunatic fringe” of Silicon Valley. The piece suggested that the iPhone maker is hoping to position itself as being on the right side of a growing AI backlash. Given the pace of development, trying to predict the future of AI is a risky business, but I do think Apple is absolutely right about the dangers … more…
fullText:
Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak didn’t hold back when he described the most ambitious figures in the AI race as the “lunatic fringe” of Silicon Valley. The piece suggested that the iPhone maker is hoping to position itself as being on the right side of a growing AI backlash.

Given the pace of development, trying to predict the future of AI is a risky business, but I do think Apple is absolutely right about the dangers …

The piece cites the familiar refrain that Apple’s slow pace when it comes to AI features could see the company being left behind.

Virtually [all other tech giants] have flung themselves into the AI arms race, pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into training ever more intelligent thinking machines. While Apple trains its own models, it is nowhere near the technology’s frontier, leaving the company vulnerable to being left behind if super-smart AI transforms industry and society in the coming years.

Joswiak counters that the company is focused on launching AI features that will perform useful tasks for ordinary people, and that Apple’s privacy focus will become increasingly valuable in the context of an AI backlash against a “lunatic fringe” of unconstrained acceleration of a technology we can barely control today.

Lunacy is certainly a good word to describe a world in which AI companies fear that their work may destroy humanity, but they are even more afraid that one of their competitors will beat them to it.

AI is the first technological development that has ever threatened such a wide variety of jobs, with a huge number of positions likely to be eliminated in fields as diverse as truck driving, marketing, and software development. Academics have even expressed concern that future generations will no longer become mathematicians or scientific researchers over fears that those roles will be made redundant by AI.

For example, math professor Giordano Scarciotti recently said that when AI models are solving in days problems academics have worked on for years, the results could be devastating because it will seem pointless to future generations to even attempt this type of work.

I explore a potentially devastating consequence of AI’s growing capabilities: what happens when the next generation of talented students no longer sees a reason to become mathematicians? The implications could extend far beyond mathematics and affect the future of scientific progress itself.

	

He argues that when today’s students see no future in academic research, this may leave AI models technically solving scientific problems, but with no one left to understand the implications and to apply the findings in meaningful ways. Similar effects are likely to occur in software development, where there are fewer and fewer humans able to understand the code being generated by increasingly advanced AI models.

The nightmare scenario here is that AI takes on ever more tasks as once-expert human beings become sidelined and marginalized because there’s no point in future generations attempting to compete. And if you think that’s baseless paranoia, I highly recommend listening to the podcast series Suspicious Minds: AI and the Apocalypse.

Quite how much power Apple has to fight back against such a dystopian future is questionable, but it could certainly be argued that at least the company is not applying its vast resources to accelerating the effect. Here’s hoping that the AI backlash grows sufficiently rapidly and loudly that politicians are forced to take steps to bring the current wild west of AI under some form of control.

The technology also removes mid-game "just-in-time" shader compilation, reducing stuttering and CPU spikes. Microsoft's Advanced Shader Delivery works by offloading shader compilation for different hardware combinations to the cloud. fullText:
Tom Warren

 

is a senior correspondent and author of Notepad, who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years.

Nvidia is rolling out a new GPU driver today (621.01) that enables Microsoft’s new Advanced Shader Delivery technology to speed up game launches. The technology also removes mid-game “just-in-time” shader compilation, reducing stuttering and CPU spikes.

Microsoft’s Advanced Shader Delivery works by offloading shader compilation for different hardware combinations to the cloud. “Using DirectX 12, Windows 11, and the Microsoft Agility SDK, developers capture shaders into a State Object Database (SODB), allowing Microsoft’s cloud network to precompile shaders for hundreds of thousands of hardware and driver combinations,” explains Nvidia’s Andrew Burnes.

Gears of War: E-Day and Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 now both support Advanced Shader Delivery, as long as you download the games via the Xbox PC app. “This system is storefront-agnostic, meaning you benefit even when playing games purchased on Steam, as long as the Xbox PC app is installed on your PC,” says Burnes.

Advanced Shader Delivery will let you skip the annoying shader compilation screen in Call of Duty, and it should improve the overall performance of supported games. “With a near-100 percent cache hit rate, it eliminates mid-game ‘just-in-time’ shader compilation, wiping out CPU spikes and frame stutters in titles like Gears of War: E-Day, and Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

You can download Nvidia’s latest 621.01 update here, and Advanced Shader Delivery is also supported on AMD GPUs with Adrenalin 26.6.1 or higher and Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 series with driver version 2026.08.3 or higher.

title: Meta says it has fixed an issue that let its Ray-Ban smart glasses record on their own
snippet: As privacy complaints continue to dominate the conversation around Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, the company is now fixing an issue that was letting the glasses record on their own without the user prompting the recording. more…
fullText:
As privacy complaints continue to dominate the conversation around Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, the company is now fixing an issue that was letting the glasses record on their own without the user prompting the recording.

A number of Ray-Ban Meta users on Reddit note that, recently, their glasses have been invoking Meta AI and, in turn, voice recording, without prompts. The “Hey Meta” wake word was not used and, for some, not even enabled. One user says this happened across three separate pairs of glasses. 

The glasses still alert users to the recordings by lighting up the LED on the inner frame of the glasses, but it’s obviously a bit concerning to randomly have the glasses start recording on their own, even if it is audio only. 

Speaking to Android Authority, Meta confirmed that the issue has been “resolved.”

	

This issue has been resolved. People can manage, review and delete voice logs of their interactions with Meta AI via settings at any time.

The cause isn’t mentioned, but it comes at a time where Meta’s smart glasses are under continual scrutiny for privacy. Meta, in trying to correct its course, has made adjustments to its glasses including rolling out a mandatory update that disables the camera on its glasses if someone tampers with the LED privacy light.

title: SpaceX alum’s aviation startup, Reliable Robotics, lands $115M, topping $1B valuation
snippet: Reliable Robotics extended its Series D round with $115 million in equity and $25 million in debt.
fullText:
Reliable Robotics has been working for nearly a decade to commercialize autonomous flying technology that can be installed on existing aircraft. Now, with a $115 million funding boost, the Mountain View, California-based startup has a longer runway as it pushes to get its autonomous flight system certified by the Federal Aviation Administration — a critical milestone that co-founder and CEO Robert Rose said the startup is inching toward.

The financing is an extension of its Series D round and includes $90 million in equity funding led by Nimble Partners and $25 million in debt from Silicon Valley Bank. The Series D round, which now totals $275 million, has pushed the startup’s valuation beyond the $1 billion mark. Other investors include Gideon Strategic Partners, RockCreek, Geek Ventures, Gold Hill Capital, Sparkwave Capital, and others. Reliable has raised $380 million to date.

“We continue to make steady progress and deliver evidence to the FAA and every day, we inch closer and closer,” said Rose, a former director of flight software at SpaceX who has also had stints at Tesla and Google. Reliable co-founder and CTO Juerg Frefel is also a SpaceX veteran who spent nearly a decade there as an engineer.

And in aviation — one of the most regulated industries in the world — moving toward certification of new technology is progress.

Reliable Robotics is working to gain FAA certification on four fronts, all of which are linked to its goal of autonomous flight.

Its first product, called continuous autopilot engagement, handles the engine startup, taxiing, takeoff, and landing for the pilot, who remains in the aircraft and interacts with the autonomous flight system through a touchscreen. Rose expects to receive certification for this critical first system in 18 to 24 months.

The second certification, which Rose says is at least three years away, removes the pilot from the cockpit and moves them to a ground-control station. 

Reliable is also working toward certification of a collision-avoidance radar, which the company has developed in-house after failing to attract legacy suppliers to take on the project. Most conventional radar systems use an antenna that moves to scan the surrounding airspace. Reliable has developed a solid-state radar that has no moving parts and scans the sky at a longer range and at much higher resolution, according to Rose. It’s also easier to maintain because there are no moving parts and it costs less, he added.

“This is of great interest to operators these days, given the collisions that we’ve had recently in commercial aviation,” he said, adding that the radar also works on the ground to prevent collisions with other aircraft or infrastructure. Rose expects the solid-state radar to be certified by the end of 2027.

The final certification is for its airline, called Reliable Airlines, which will be the first airline certified to use the autonomous flying technology. The airline is based in Albuquerque and uses six Cessna Caravans — workhorses of the aviation industry — to fly cargo six days a week. (The FAA certifies equipment, but the agency also must certify the airline operations under a separate set of regulations.)

While the certification process is lengthy, Nimble Partners founder John Burbank said the benefits will be broad and significant.

“It’s a much bigger effort and much bigger opportunity than to just build one plane,” Burbank said, noting that Reliable is building a system that can be adopted by any airframe. “They had a really big vision nine years ago, and saw this as something needed and essential. Once they get the first one approved, then everyone will realize this is going to be the path for the industry, just as we’re seeing the path for the auto industry being autonomous.”

fullText:
Spotify announced Wednesday the launch of its next-generation, fully native in-car app, built directly on Google’s Android Automotive operating system. The standalone app, which is launching today in select Audi models, runs directly on the vehicle’s infotainment hardware — eliminating the need for phone tethering, Bluetooth connections, or aux cables.

It’s the clearest sign yet that Spotify is ready to move beyond Apple CarPlay and Android, popular phone projection systems that currently dominate the way most people consume media in their cars. And with 34 percent of Spotify’s monthly active users and 77 percent of Premium subscribers streaming music in their cars, the platform they use to listen has never been more important.

Spotify’s new native app will launch with several Audi models, including the electric A6 e-tron and Q6 e-tron, as well as the gas-powered A5, Q5, and A6. Jonathan Tarlton, Spotify’s automotive business development lead, said the app, which has been in development for a little more than a year, is about delivering a more inviting experience to users — and specifically one that’s completely controlled by Spotify.

1/7

Spotify’s standard Android Automotive app operated as a “headless” integration, meaning that Spotify supplied the underlying backend data, playlists, and music catalog, but Google’s templates dictated how the interface was drawn and structured onscreen. The new Audi application is “headful,” allowing Spotify to draw and render its own native UI directly on the vehicle’s screens from scratch.

“We’re drawing all the pixels,” Tarlton said in an interview. “We own the user experience. So we’re not in a template or a framework. It’s 100 percent Spotify.”

To be sure, Spotify isn’t turning its back on Apple CarPlay and Android Auto; the company is still “heavily invested” in phone projection, Tarlton assured us. That said, the native Spotify app is being set up to compete directly with phone mirroring. Apple CarPlay and Android Auto remain the default way many people listen to music or podcasts in their vehicles: Drivers get in, connect their phones automatically, and tap into their familiar mobile interface. A native Spotify app could encourage people to listen through the car’s own operating system instead of projecting their phones — a scenario that Tarlton says he welcomes.

“We’re drawing all the pixels. We own the user experience. So we’re not in a template or a framework. It’s 100 percent Spotify.”

— Jonathan Tarlton, head of automotive business development at Spotify

“We want to give users choice,” he said. “We want to be wherever they are and we want to make sure that they’re accessing Spotify in the way they want to access it, whether they’re locked into the iOS ecosystem … or Android on the phone as well.”

People may love their CarPlay, but the experience is not without its tradeoffs. Wireless connection, in particular, can be spotty depending on your vehicle. Tarlton said the new app is aimed at reducing some of those headaches, like “a cold start in the morning,” he said. “You’re not having to wait to boot. You’re not having to wait for a screen to load. You’re not having to plug your phone in.”

There are other benefits to using the native Spotify app over a projected one from your phone. Passengers can scan a QR code displayed on the screen to join a wireless “Spotify Jam” session and add songs directly to the queue from their smartphones. On vehicles with a dedicated secondary passenger display, front passengers can browse, view lyrics, and watch video content without disturbing the driver. And while the vehicle is parked or charging, those motion graphics, like video podcasts and lyrics, move to the central display so everyone can enjoy.

With these features in particular, Spotify feels like it’s doing its part in helping to bring car passengers together again, Tarlton said. Often today you’ll find parents rocking out to their favorite hits in the front while kids are wearing their headphones in the back. The new app aims to correct that dynamic. “I’m excited that we can bring joy to the cabin again,” he said. “It’s not just technology.”

The rollout of the new Spotify app will focus in particular on cars with Android-based operating systems, he said. In that way, Spotifty can avoid having to build separate, bespoke applications for every individual automaker. Rather, the company can use a standard Android Automotive APK that it can then distribute through multiple app stores, whether it’s the Google Play Store or proprietary automaker stores like the Audi Application Store.

“Our number one goal was to prevent fragmentation, not just for our sake, but for the sake of the whole industry,” Tarlton said, “because we believe in having an open and fair place for apps to play — and the car is such a great place for that.”

Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

Andrew J. Hawkins

Spotify announced Wednesday the launch of its next-generation, fully native in-car app, built directly on Google’s Android Automotive operating system. The standalone app, which is launching today in select Audi models, runs directly on the vehicle’s infotainment hardware — eliminating the need for phone tethering, Bluetooth connections, or aux cables.

It’s the clearest sign yet that Spotify is ready to move beyond Apple CarPlay and Android, popular phone projection systems that currently dominate the way most people consume media in their cars. And with 34 percent of Spotify’s monthly active users and 77 percent of Premium subscribers streaming music in their cars, the platform they use to listen has never been more important.

title: Galaxy S26 Ultra is one of the ‘best inventions of 2026’ thanks to its Privacy Display
snippet: A new 2026 roundup has the Galaxy S26 Ultra included in a list of best inventions for the year, all thanks to what it doesn’t display. more…
fullText:
A new 2026 roundup has the Galaxy S26 Ultra included in a list of best inventions for the year, all thanks to what it doesn’t display.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra split in a slightly different direction. Instead of a display panel treatment with an anti-gflare coating, Samsung decided to pack an entirely different feature into the panel itself.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display allows users to block certain aspects of the screen from nearby onlookers, effectively circumventing the privacy screen protector so many users opt for.

According to Time‘s “best inventions of 2026” collection, the Galaxy S26 Ultra gets its plaudits for not the phone’s performance necessarily, but the Privacy Display. The listing quotes Samsung’s SVP of Mobile Product Management, who points to its flexible nature.

	

It’s undoubtedly a cool piece of display tech. The Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display not only blocks side-angle viewing, but it can do so in isolated portions of the screen to block PIN codes or notifications that drop from the top shade in Android.

It has some drawbacks, though, as we’ve pointed out before. It can be a little inconsistent in certain lighting conditions, and sometimes screen elements can look off. But it’s cool, and a nice addition to a phone that sits at a price range we now consider more affordable than what we’re probably getting here soon.

Time‘s piece goes on to list a couple of other familiar devices, like a lengthy segment on the iPhone Duo, propping it up rather highly. Another product we’re happy to see is the Clicks Power Keyboard.

AS for whether the Galaxy S27 Pro or Ultra will get a Privacy Display, rumors suggest it could happen. Time will tell as Samsung plans to launch the devices early next year.

title: Apple strikes deal with AI startup that lets musicians rework recorded music

fullText:
The EU’s List of Acquisitions website was updated today with details of a deal struck in June between Apple and Samplab, a Swiss startup that described itself as offering “music production for the age of AI.” Here are the details.

Apple’s string of AI deals continues

Last week, the List of Acquisitions section of the EU’s DMA website was updated with details on Apple’s move to acqui-hire Huxe, a startup founded by former NotebookLM engineers that specialized in generating personalized audio briefings and podcast-style content using AI.

Today, the list was updated yet again, revealing another deal involving Apple and an AI audio company.

Apple Inc. (“Apple”), through a subsidiary, will acquire certain assets of Samplab GmbH (“Samplab”) and offer employment to and hire certain Samplab employees. Samplab develops audio editing tools. Apple (together with its group companies) designs, manufactures and markets smartphones, personal computers, tablets, wearables and accessories, and sells a variety of related services.

Following the deal, Samplab’s website now redirects to Apple’s, while its social media accounts and YouTube channel appear to have been scrubbed of their previous posts and videos.

Previously, Samplab’s website described its “ultimate audio editor for musicians” as a tool that allowed creators to “edit audio files as if you were working with MIDI.” It also touted its ability to:

Detect and edit chords

They stay in key when you change them.

You can even export them as a midi file.

Make any samples sound good together

Samplab matches their tempo and key.

Easily adapt chords, melodies and drums.

Granular stem separation

Separate stems in any audio and

freely modify individual notes.

While Apple has not commented on the acquisition, it isn’t hard to imagine Samplab’s technology eventually making its way into Logic Pro or GarageBand, or even enhancing the audio editing capabilities of Final Cut Pro.

title: Meta’s Muse hits 10M US downloads in 40 days, a milestone reached by only 11 other apps
snippet: New data also shows Muse is retaining users at higher rates than its AI rivals.
fullText:
Meta’s AI companion, Muse, is now one of only a dozen mobile apps to have reached 10 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. According to new data from market intelligence provider Sensor Tower, Muse has seen 10.9 million downloads since its September debut, 10.2 million of which were in the United States.

Only 11 other apps to date have reached this type of post-launch milestone, said Sensor Tower’s senior insights analyst Kara Lee. The most recent of these was Meta’s Threads, back in July 2023.

Other apps that saw this kind of scale were largely mobile games, Lee noted, like Fortnite, PUBG Mobile, Pokémon GO, and others. Besides Threads, Disney+ was the only other nongame app to make it into the exclusive club.

Meta’s success is tied to the company’s ability to scale its new apps by marketing them across its other services, which it has done with both Threads and Muse. Threads was built on top of Instagram’s social graph, and its content has been integrated into both Facebook and Instagram. However, Muse isn’t only benefiting from Meta’s ability to market the AI agent across its family of apps, which today includes 3.6 billion daily active users; the company is also heavily investing in advertising to drive new users to Muse.

Per Sensor Tower’s data, Meta has allocated 39% of its total advertising spend to market Muse in October, up from 23% last month. In addition, Muse now ranks as the 21st largest brand in the U.S. by advertising impressions this month, up from 73rd in September.

Still, marketing an app and retaining users after the initial shine wears off are two different things. In this case, Muse is seeing better retention rates than its AI competitors like ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok.

In the U.S., the app had a 30% retention rate after 7 days and a 23% retention rate after 14 days. By comparison, its rivals saw an average of a 19% 7-day retention rate and a 16% 14-day retention rate, according to the firm’s data.

Muse also hit another milestone that demonstrates active engagement with the AI app. Its daily active users reached 2.5 million for the first time on October 16, a 15% week-over-week increase.

Meta’s latest AI app, which can handle various tasks on users’ behalf, has seen breakout success since its debut. It shot up to No. 1 on the App Store and at one point even outpaced some of the metrics ChatGPT saw following its launch. Its latest milestone sees it topping its rivals again, as ChatGPT saw 3.7 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. Grok and Claude saw only 500,000 and 200,000 U.S. downloads, respectively, in their first 40 days.

Globally, ChatGPT beat out Muse, having scaled to around 15 million global downloads in its first 40 days. But this isn’t a fair comparison, as ChatGPT benefited from a wider reach. Muse is only available in the U.S. and Canada for now, while ChatGPT’s app attracted attention from markets like Japan, Brazil, and Germany, too. (Japan, for instance, accounted for 25% of its global installs during its first 40 days.)  

Since launching, Muse has retained its No. 1 rank on the U.S. App Store for all days except October 19, when streaming app Kick briefly beat it out. It has since reclaimed the top spot as of Tuesday. Muse has also been No. 1 on Google Play over the past 30 days.

title: YouTube Music rolling out AI labels in the Now Playing screen
snippet: In response to more AI-generated content appearing on streaming services, YouTube Music is adding a new AI label directly to the player. more…
fullText:
In response to more AI-generated content appearing on streaming services, YouTube Music is adding a new AI label directly to the player.

When a song is “created primarily using generative AI,” you’ll soon see a label on the Now Playing screen. This includes “using a generative model to create the composition and vocals.” The goal is to “make it as easy as possible for viewers and listeners to have the right information and clarity when it comes to the music they listen to.”

It appears just below the song name next to the artist/channel. This “AI” badge with an info icon opens a “How this was made” bottom sheet. 

YouTube Music explains how this was “Made with AI: This audio was altered or fully generated using AI” with a link to learn more. 

	

YouTube is using its own detection tools and “teaming up with music partners” to identify AI-generated tracks. 

The rollout starts today. In the future, these AI labels for music will come to the main YouTube app.

title: I Tried Amazing Security Tech for Renters From a Company You’ve Never Heard Of
snippet: It’s the year of window cams, and Baseus has my favorite model yet. Here’s why renters and second-story homes should consider it.
fullText:
Tyler Lacoma/CNET		

	

		

									

						Baseus PimeSentinel W1 Window Camera					

					

	8.5

	
					

			

	

		

			

				Pros & Cons			

			

			

							

					
						4K resolution					
				

							

					
						Great magnetic, indoor design					
				

							

					
						Adjustable camera angle (unusual in window cams)					
				

							

					
						MicroSD card slot for free local storage					
				

							

					
						Free motion and AI object detection for people, vehicles and animals					
				

							

					
						Privacy and motion zone options to customize where and how the camera monitors					
				

							

					
						Simple, effective app					
				

					

			

							

					
						Overly sensitive motion and object detection can trigger false alerts from shadows, though privacy and motion zones help					
				

							

					
						Night vision is only passable, and requires a least a little light to work well					
				

					

	

		

It’s tough to find good security devices for renters because of the restrictions on what changes they can make to their homes and all the fine print in their leases. Window cameras are a happy exception — adhesive-mounted cams that stick to windows and allow you to monitor carports, parking spaces, yards, visitors and more. If you don’t have room for a traditional security camera, it’s a versatile — and affordable — alternative.

My new favorite dedicated window cam comes from Baseus, a company that has stood out in this growing category in 2026. If you haven’t heard of it, you’ll want to keep it in mind. Like Anker, with its many tech lines, including Eufy security, Baseus is a Chinese company that makes a bit of everything, including solid-performing security products at reasonable prices.

The Baseus PrimeSentinel W1 Window Camera ($100) offers a particularly clever design and no-subscription management, although you may need to do a little work in settings to customize everything to your liking. If you’ve dealt with other vehicles taking your spot, people vandalizing your car, strangers on your steps, package theft or similar problems, consider using a camera like this on a window near your door. Here’s how it works.

			

More from CNET

Design and a very easy installation

I was originally very skeptical about using a security camera to look through a window, since glare is a constant problem, the right angle is hard to find and the camera can get in the way of shades or curtains. The first cam to change my mind was Wyze’s version, launched earlier this year. Baseus, however, has a model with a design I like much better, albeit at a higher price.

Instead of using Velcro like the Wyze model, the Baseus cam has a magnetic frame. Stick it to a clean window and the small Baseus cam locks on automatically. All you need is an outlet somewhere near the window to plug the camera in.

The Baseus magnetic frame is a step above other versions I’ve tested.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

But that’s not the only thing I like about its design. You can also manually angle the orb-like camera lense, shifting it downward to focus on things below the window. That’s a helpful feature if you live a story or two up in an apartment building and need to angle the camera down to watch your car parked directly below or a similar area.

A side slot makes room for a microSD card, which allows you to store video locally without paying any subscription fees or risking privacy issues with cloud video storage. I suggest grabbing a microSD card along with this cam if you choose to buy.

Video performance and capabilities

The Baseus cam has a 4K resolution, unusual at this price.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Another useful feature of the Baseus window cam is its 4K resolution, which can be tough to find in cameras under $100. It provides extra detail and worked quite well in my testing. The 130-degree field of view captured a good swath of my yard and should be sufficient for most viewing needs.

The magnetic lock design holds the camera directly against the window, minimizing glare, although some slight distortion may occur when the sun shines directly on the lens. A unique feature lets you flip the video 180 degrees, which can be helpful when positioning the camera based on your windows, the location of the nearest outlet and how unobtrusive you want the cam to be.

Baseus’s app and live view offer plenty of detail.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Video recording and histories also worked well, although snapshots were significantly more blurry than the 4K live view. The camera comes with low-light night vision, which is fine. It’s not going to compete with the more advanced night vision you’ll find on modern cameras, but as long as there’s a little nearby light, I was able to pick out the details. If your area goes completely dark at night, it may be hard for the camera to capture much.

The camera also includes a mic and speaker for two-way audio. It’s funny seeing this feature on a window camera, because while I know it’s common, audio is mostly useless here. You won’t be able to hear much of anything outside, and shouting through the speaker won’t reach outdoors either. At most, you may be able to alert someone inside the house if, for example, you’re at work and see someone smashing car windows in the parking lot.

App controls, settings and smart features

Baseus has a simple and intuitive app.Screenshot by Tyler Lacoma/CNET

The Baseus app is relatively simple, with sections for viewing event history, changing settings, watching the live feed and more. There are no surprises, but it’s worth diving into the settings to improve the camera’s accuracy.

Baseus doesn’t do subscriptions, but you do get detection features for free. That includes not only basic motion detection, but also options to enable person, pet and vehicle detection, along with sensitivity controls.

While glare isn’t a problem when viewing videos, there seems to be just enough reflection for the camera to mistake people or shadows moving around the room for a “person spotted” outside when the light is right. The camera occasionally appeared to be triggered by moving trees as well and was too sensitive overall, even when I lowered it to the lowest sensitivity setting.

Privacy zones are important for the neighbors.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

To avoid mistakes and frequent triggers, I turned to another feature in the app: Baseus includes the ability to add both privacy zones and motion zones. Privacy zones place black sections on the camera’s recording so they don’t show up in videos, which is useful for blocking a neighbor’s yard or parking spot and avoiding issues with privacy.

Motion zones and object settings take a little work to get right.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

However, the privacy zone feature didn’t always block object detection in that area, so I also used motion detection zones to control which spots the camera watched. Between the privacy and motion zones, I was able to wrangle the camera into sending reasonable alerts about the activity I cared about.

I also suggest leaving pet detection off, since it offers the least security value. Hopefully, Baseus will release updates to reduce false alerts overall. In the meantime, you can turn off object and motion detection entirely, or enable privacy mode to temporarily disable the camera.

What about Baseus? Is this brand safe to use?

Before recommending a relatively little-known Chinese security brand, I researched its track record, looking for significant data breaches, privacy concerns or other red flags. Baseus, much like Anker, doesn’t have any obvious security issues. You can view the Baseus privacy policy here, which goes over the information it collects and notes that privacy laws in other countries (and certain states, such as California) do apply to the data it handles. It’s a little rough, but does include plenty of useful information.

I found no notable security incidents involving Baseus. However, the company says authorized employees may access encrypted personal information. It also says it doesn’t collect financial information, relying instead on third-party services to secure that data. But as I previously mentioned, you can use a microSD card for local storage, so you won’t be storing video directly on Baseus servers.

Overall, I’d like to know a bit more about the company’s security practices, relationship with the government and data storage, but there’s nothing right now that would make me hesitant to suggest the company to users.

Final thoughts on the Baseus PrimeSentinel W1 Window Camera

This cam is a particularly good option for monitoring through a window if you can’t install an outdoor camera.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

With its 4K resolution, magnetic design, rotatable lens and free local video storage, the Baseus W1 is my favorite window camera so far—a strong showing from a relatively unknown name in home security. At $100, it costs more than some window cameras, but its features make it a good value. I’ll be testing other options this year, including a new window camera from Eufy, but for now, the W1 is my top choice.

I’d like to see some improvements with its object detection and recognition, which triggered too frequently and seemed occasionally affected by reflections, although I managed to improve results by using the welcome privacy and motion zone settings. Otherwise, this is an excellent choice for renters who may want to watch their cars but can’t use an outdoor cam, and anyone else who has a spot on their window to keep an eye on things.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma
						

						

							Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home						
					

											

								

											Tyler has worked on, lived with and tested all types of smart home and security technology for over a dozen years, explaining the latest features, privacy tricks and top recommendations.
With degrees in business management, literature and technical writing, Tyler takes every opportunity to play with the latest AI technology, push smart devices to their limits and occasionally throw cameras off his roof, all to find the best devices to trust in your life. He always checks with the renters (and pets) in his life to see what smart products can work for everyone, in every living situation. 
Living in beautiful Bend, Oregon, gives Tyler plenty of opportunities to test the latest tech in every kind of weather and temperature. But when not at work, he can be found hiking the trails, trying out a new food recipe for his loved ones, keeping up on his favorite reading or gaming with good friends.

title: Xiaomi 18 Pro gears up for global debut with rumored battery cuts and €1,449 starting price
snippet: Ouch. That’s the reaction many will probably have around pricing for the Xiaomi 18 Pro series when it lands globally, with prices starting at €1,449 according to a new leak. more…
fullText:
Ouch. That’s the reaction many will probably have around pricing for the Xiaomi 18 Pro series when it lands globally, with prices starting at €1,449 according to a new leak.

YTechB reports that the Xiaomi 18 Pro series is headed to Europe with major price hikes in tow. Where last year’s Xiaomi 17 had a starting price of €999 with the Ultra at €1,499, the Xiaomi 18 Pro is starting the lineup at €1,449 this year. That’s a huge price jump seeing as it’s just €50 short of last year’s Ultra device.

Pricing is rumored to land as follows:

Xiaomi 18 Pro (256GB): €1,449

Xiaomi 18 Pro Max (512GB): €1,849

The report goes on to cite the EU’s EPREL labels to confirm that global variants of the Xiaomi 18 Pro series will be cut down from the Chinese models. Xiaomi 18 Pro has a 7,000 mAh battery in China, but will only have a 6,000 mAh battery in Europe. Similarly, the Pro Max has an 8,500 mAh battery in China, but will be cut to 7,050 mAh in Europe. The base Pro is limited to 90W charging in the EU for reasons unclear.

	

The Xiaomi 18 Pro series is among the first to adopt Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip and launched in China last month. The timeline for a global release remains unclear at this point, but the MWC tech conference in Barcelona each Spring is often when Xiaomi kicks off availability. For 2026, Xiaomi 17 launched on February 28, with MWC 2027 start to start on March 1.
