title: Gemini 4 Argon is now rolling out to Google’s Antigravity for AI Pro subscribers
snippet: Google is now rolling out support for Gemini 4 Argon to Antigravity, its AI coding tool. more…
fullText:
Google is now rolling out support for Gemini 4 Argon to Antigravity, its AI coding tool.

Gemini 4 Argon is Google’s latest flagship AI model, announced at the end of September and having widely rolled out to users earlier this week. Now, it’s also available within Antigravity.

Antigravity is an agentic development platform, as Google describes it, which leverages AI and agents to assist in coding and building apps. Google announced that Argon would be available in Antigravity earlier this week, and it’s now actively rolling out to AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers – we’re seeing it live on our end, too.

Google restricts every free AI Pro trial from Pixel & more compared to paid subscribers

In a post on Twitter/X, Google adds that there’s “a separate weekly-only Argon quota” on top of the existing quota for Gemini 3.8 Flash, meaning you’ll be able to use the model that best suits your needs. Google says that Argon is “designed to tackle your hardest problems.”

	

Google also provided a host of examples of how Argon in Antigravity has been used internally, including:

YouTube comment optimization: Argon in Antigravity helped the team cut the CPU footprint of YouTube’s comments frontend in half. By tracing production profile data, Argon identified that redundant emoji rendering alone accounted for nearly 45% of server overhead, leading to 12 targeted optimizations. The updates reduced server comment-load latency by 30 ms and dropped client end-to-end latency by 20 ms.

Debugging Wing drone physics simulator: Argon in Antigravity reviewed Wing’s proprietary internal drone physics simulator, reasoning through the underlying physics and math rather than just the structure of the code. It highlighted areas for improved physics simulations and proposed 18 targeted modelling improvements across aerodynamics, propulsion, and structural dynamics to resolve long-standing legacy issues.

Burning down the backlog: Argon in Antigravity took an aging queue of 134 open bug reports spanning multiple services, and ran agents to work out which were still real, cross-referencing commit histories, checking whether candidate fixes actually reached production, and inspecting live telemetry for whether the error still occurs. In under 3 hours it closed 97 stale or duplicate bugs with documented commit proof (a 72.4% queue reduction) and sorted the remaining 37 by owner with no unassigned tickets left.

Migrating legacy code: For decades, vital scientific research has been locked inside fragile legacy codebases like Fortran. Using a custom skill within Antigravity, a team deployed Argon to map and execute a complete rewrite into modern Rust. Argon autonomously delivered the modernized codebase, achieving a 1.8x performance boost and memory safety while giving scientists a robust foundation for future work.

Performing security audits: Argon in Antigravity was used to audit a batch of access-control changes. Argon traced how permissions actually flowed at runtime rather than just reading the code diff, and found four critical security bugs. Two earlier frontier models had audited the identical code and both concluded there were zero security holes.

Triaging production support tickets: Argon in Antigravity batch-processes dozens of tickets from an on-call rotation. It sorts them by issue type, tracing root causes through the code and logs, proposing fixes and drafting the replies for human approval. This has freed up 2-3 hours per shift, enabling the team to focus on resolving issues faster.

Marketing website localization: The Antigravity DevRel team used Argon in Antigravity to localize hundreds of pages of developer documentation into 17 languages in a matter of hours. This improved the accessibility and UX of the website by shrinking a multi-week process down to hours and shifting human effort exclusively to high-quality review.

Accelerating data center pipeline modernization: Demonstrating how AI-augmented execution helps teams do more with less, a Data Science Technical Program Manager leveraged Argon in Antigravity to fast-track development of a 3,200-line Google Data Center fleet analytics pipeline (Python, SQL, and dashboards) into production in days. Pairing with Argon to rapidly resolve complex multi-system edge cases, eliminate hardcoded legacy assets, and optimize timeseries queries against timeouts drove end-to-end efficiency — delivering a clean, production-grade, and extensible architecture for fleet-scale analytics.

Vetting sales prospects: Argon in Antigravity built an automated qualification workflow for an account executive in Ads sales that checks prospective company website traffic, confirms the site has clear conversion funnels, and cross-references the sales database to see whether the account is a qualified prospect. This reduced research time by 90%, saving the account executive upwards of 10 hours of manual work each week so they can spend time on direct client outreach instead.

Financial planning and analysis: With custom finance plugins, a finance lead used Argon in Antigravity for end-to-end financial reconciliations, budget tracking, contract extraction, and daily executive briefings across 80 separate workflows. Over seven business days, 15.5 hours of human direction produced about 335 human-equivalent hours of validated financial output, saving more than eight weeks of manual work.

title: Anthropic’s cloud partnerships are getting messy
snippet: Anthropic is reportedly struggling to secure enough compute from cloud providers that increasingly view it as a competitor, even as its infrastructure spending balloons ahead of a planned November IPO.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

2:25 PM PDT · October 20, 2026

Image Credits:Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Anthropic is having trouble securing enough cloud capacity from AWS, Google, and Microsoft, which increasingly see the Claude maker as a competitor rather than a customer, according to an S-1 filing leaked to The Wall Street Journal. 

The leaked filing provides more color to the numbers Reuters and the Financial Times reported in late September, including that Anthropic believes it could spend more than $750 billion on cloud contracts, some of which include deals still in negotiation.

And still, that is not enough. Anthropic is leasing its own data centers and working with third-party data center operators. But the firm worries those operators have a “limited operating history,” which could make them less reliable than the hyperscalers. 

Anthropic’s enormous spend comes on the back of an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of the year. The company reported $16.3 billion in revenue during that same time period, with only two customers accounting for about a fifth of sales, according to the WSJ report. 

Building on previously reported catastrophic risk disclosures, the filing also warns that Anthropic could be held liable for damages caused by harmful AI behavior to a tune that would exceed available insurance coverage. 

Last week, the company told prospective investors that third-quarter revenue alone has now reached $16.8 billion, up 45% from the previous quarter. Anthropic is reportedly targeting a November IPO.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

fullText:
A reliable source says that Nothing is building out its own AI smart glasses that feature ChatGPT integration, a camera, and two very different models.

WinFuture’s Roland Quandt says on Bluesky that Nothing is preparing to launch two new smart glasses models, and they sound wildly different.

One pair would be similar to the Ray-Ban Meta lineup with a built-in camera and AI features such as translation. While Nothing as an avid Android user might seem like one to hop on the Android XR train, it sounds like that’s probably not the case given Quandt says these are bringing integration with ChatGPT rather than Gemini. The other pair of smart glasses, though, would take a much simpler approach.

	

These would work as a pair of headphones with the ability to take calls and interact with your phone’s voice assistant, but they’d lack a camera or any direct AI integrations. Both models are said to offer photochromic lenses, otherwise known as “transition” lenses and commonly found on other smart glasses.

Prior reporting on Nothing’s efforts to build smart glasses pinned a release date sometime in 2027. The dual strategy here is certainly interesting, especially given a recent report that suggested Nothing would go all-in on AI devices going forward.

title: Plants can speak using electricity, so this startup built an AI model to decipher their language
snippet: Electric Plant has built an AI-powered translator to help humans listen to what plants are saying with the subtle electricity coursing through their stems.
fullText:
Justin Mast’s life was changed by a cyborg plant.

A few years ago, Mast was reading through some scientific literature when he stumbled upon research about a houseplant wired to a motorized stand. When the plant wanted more light, electrical signals flowed through the living tissues. A control board sensed the current and wheeled the plant closer to the light source.

“I’m like, what the heck?” Mast told TechCrunch. “That was the entry to the rabbit hole for me.”

Mast wound up partnering with Lee von Kraus, a neuroscientist who has worked with DARPA, to found Electric Plant, which has been spending the past three years collecting data to build a large language model, Bombadil, capable of interpreting the subtle electrical signals coursing through a plant’s stem and relaying details about the plant’s needs to growers.

Electric Plant co-founders Lee von Kraus (right) and Justin Mast stand next to a tree with a sensor attached to it.Image Credits:Electric Plant

The founders believe their model could one day lead to a tool that would let people “speak” to plants. “We’re listening more than we’re speaking, but listening’s the first step,” said Mast, co-founder and CEO of Electric Plant.

To bring its sensors and Bombadil to market, Electric Plant recently raised an $11.2 million seed round led by Onto Ventures and Climactic, with participation from Ponderosa, Endeavor Catalyst, Ludlow, Michigan Rise, The Fund, Schox VC, and Dug Song. 

Even in the most controlled greenhouses, farmers and growers don’t have full visibility of what their plants require, Mast said. Traditionally, farmers, growers, and foresters have relied on coarse tools that react to plants’ demands for water, nutrients, or light. And tools like soil probes, handheld spectroscopes, and satellite imagery work well enough, but they leave much to be desired, Mast said.

“That technology is sophisticated, but its ability to get at the inside of the plant isn’t very sophisticated. Most of that stuff still lags quite a bit behind the real-time needs of the plant,” he said.

Electric Plant had to start somewhere, though, so it used those devices to train its Bombadil model, which is capable of interpreting electrical signals in about 125 different species. “We know the model will surpass a lot of that equipment,” Mast said. 

The startup’s sensors are also significantly cheaper than existing tools, which generally cost thousands of dollars. “This is tens of dollars,” he said.

The sensors, about the size of a regular iPhone folded lengthwise, are attached to a plant using stainless steel screws. The screws must penetrate the cambium — the layer of living tissue just under the bark — to connect to the microvolt changes occurring within the plant. Data collected from these sensors is sent to a base station via a low-power wireless network. 

Electric Plant only needs a couple sensors per acre for accurate results, Mast said. The data gets interpreted by Bombadil in the cloud, and the results are sent back to the customer, who can use it to, for example, adjust their watering or fertilizer schedules. Mast claims such a system can boost yields while reducing water use by 20% or more.

Mast wouldn’t disclose who Electric Plant’s initial customers are, but it’s easy to imagine applications in agriculture and forestry.

Bombadil’s first hundred-plus species runs the gamut of plant forms, from ferns, redwoods, and tomatoes to dahlias, Mast said.

“This is the most diverse model ever created on biological electrical signals,” he said. “No one’s ever done anything equivalent to this in the animal world.”

title: Seniors Lose More Money to Investment Scams Than Any Other Fraud
snippet: Around $3 billion was lost in 2025 to fraud from people aged 60 and over in the US.
fullText:
Just when older adults need their money for retirement, many of them are being robbed. On Monday, the Federal Trade Commission issued its annual report to Congress on protecting older adults, noting that adults 60 and over continue to report losing far more money to investment scams than to any other type of fraud.

Adults 60 and over lost $3 billion to fraud in 2025, five times the $600 million reported five years prior, in 2020. This increase was driven largely by growing reports of extraordinarily large individual losses. Fraud losses due to investment scams jumped 42% in 2025 to over $1 billion, with consumers reporting that scammers often reach them on social media.

The full 58-page report, Protecting Older Consumers 2025-2026, is available online. It summarizes fraud and consumer complaints submitted to the Consumer Sentinel Network in 2025. The network is a free online investigative FTC tool that gives its member groups access to millions of fraud reports to assist their investigations.

			

More from CNET

Adults 60 and over continue to report much higher individual dollar losses than younger people, with people 80 and over faring the worst, with a median reported loss of $2,000. According to the report, older adults are more likely to report losing money to tech support scams; prize, sweepstakes and lottery scams; romance scams; government impersonation scams; and scams in which someone impersonates their friends or family members.

The government will ‘never ever’ ask for gift cards

The report outlines FTC law enforcement actions targeting fraud aimed at older adults. Those actions include targeted consumer education initiatives and collaboration with government, academic and private-sector partners. The FTC also coordinates with law enforcement and connects victims experiencing significant financial losses to resources such as the Department of Justice’s National Elder Fraud Hotline.

The FTC’s Never Ever campaign, one of those actions, aims to educate seniors by highlighting three red flags that prove a caller or sender is a scammer rather than a legitimate government agency or bank. Those red flags tell people that legitimate government officials will never direct them to transfer money to protect it, threaten to suspend government benefits without immediate payment or demand payment via money apps, cryptocurrency, wire transfers or gift cards.

An article published Monday in PCMag, part of the CNET Group of publications, relays the story of a 77-year-old widow and retired nurse, Mary Ellen Strange, who lost most of her life savings, over $400,000, over a seven-week period in 2024. Strange’s money was taken by a team of cyber scammers led by a man impersonating a Federal Trade Commission officer. On three separate occasions, men pretending to be undercover FBI agents came to her home and left with boxes of her money.

A recent CNET Group survey of 1,000 Americans reveals that scams are a weekly nuisance for many. Over 80% of those surveyed receive scam calls and emails every week, while 76.5% receive weekly scam texts. CNET offers a guide to avoiding the top seven scams, plus tips on how to minimize the damage if you fear you have been scammed.

title: Google is bringing a more personal version of its Gemini AI assistant to your car
snippet: Google is bringing Gemini's Personal Intelligence feature to cars, allowing its AI assistant to draw on information from Gmail, Calendar, Maps, YouTube, and other Google services to deliver more personalized responses while driving.
fullText:
Google is making the Gemini AI assistant that’s already in millions of cars, trucks, and SUVs a lot more personal — a move that could push consumers even deeper into the company’s ecosystem of products.

The company said Tuesday it’s upgrading Gemini in vehicles with a personal intelligence feature that can draw on information from Gmail, Google Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Google Search history, and other connected Google services to understand your preferences, activities, and past experiences.

Google said it will roll out “Personal Intelligence with Gemini” to vehicles in two ways — through Android Auto, an app that runs on the user’s phone and wirelessly communicates with and projects navigation, media, and messaging to the vehicle’s infotainment system, and Google Built-in, software and services that have been directly integrated into the vehicle.

The feature will launch in Android Auto, starting today, and expand to cars with Google Built-in in the coming months.

Google initially launched Gemini last November in Android Auto. Meanwhile, Gemini’s “Personal Intelligence” feature rolled out across the U.S. in March and is now in beta in global markets.

This latest upgrade would connect the dots — as Google put it in its blog post — across users’ Google apps. 

Drivers will have to opt in for Personalized Intelligence to work. Once a user does so, they should expect all sorts of cross-pollination. For instance, a driver who is navigating to the airport may be alerted that the flight on their calendar is delayed.

Google said the feature will allow users to make complex requests using natural language. Returning to that airport example, a user might ask the AI assistant for their flight gate before quickly following up with a question about whether it’s still on time. Gemini will give the user answers to both questions at the same time, the company said.

That level of emmeshing might make consumers uncomfortable, although Google says users do retain full control over their data with Personal Intelligence. The feature can be turned on or off at any time, and users can selectively choose which apps they’d like to connect, Google said.

title: Google support pages start defaulting to AI chatbots – it might be for the best
snippet: Google is starting to move its support pages from detailed articles to AI summaries with a chatbot, with an added set of steps to access the full details of the any given page. more…
fullText:
Google is starting to move its support pages from detailed articles to AI summaries with a chatbot, with an added set of steps to access the full details of the any given page.

The Google Help portal is full of detailed articles that provide step-by-step processes for using a feature, documentation on where features are available or restrictions on them, as well as troubleshooting steps if something goes awry. It’s a massively useful resource, but one that Google is now changing.

Starting with support pages under Google Account Help, the company is shifting these support articles to an AI summary rather than a dedicated article. “Ask Google Help” will display a condensed version of the support article with direct troubleshooting steps, with the user then able to type in queries to have Gemini help figure out the next step forward.

A “View Sources” button at the bottom of the AI response allows users to still access the original article, but direct links to any of these articles now defaults to the AI experience.

	

An example can be seen below on the “Secure a hacked or compromised Google account” page that Google’s own support account directed users to within the past few days. It can also be seen on the “Fix common issues with 2-Step Verification” page and, as far as we can tell, any support pages on the Google Account Help forum.

Google, as of right now, appears to only be testing this on select support topics. The Google Pixel Help section, for instance, still defaults to articles, whereas the Google Chrome topic has also moved to the new experience.

Beyond support pages alone, this new design also impacts the central hub, with links to topics no longer showing by default in exchange for an AI chatbot that helps you find the relevant page.

Ironically enough, the Gemini topic is one of the ones missing this Gemini-powered experience.

9to5Google’s Take

While my initial reaction to this was skeptical, I think this is a rather good use of AI.

Google’s support page collection tends to be a bit of a labyrinth of links and vague search terms. Finding the specific page needed to address the problem you are running into can be very difficult. Meanwhile, Gemini’s inherent ability to understand natural language queries and find associated sources is very powerful in this regard.

I’m still a bit iffy on whether or not dedicated support articles should be converted into an AI summary (which Google still warns could be inaccurate), but using Gemini as a search and troubleshooting tool in this specific regard really highlights a strength of the technology.

What do you think?

title: Streaming guide JustWatch becomes a streamer itself
snippet: JustWatch, the popular streaming search guide used by 50 million people, is launching its own streaming service, offering free, ad-supported movies and shows alongside a $3.99-per-month ad-free tier and movie rentals.
fullText:
JustWatch, a company offering a search engine and guide for streaming movies and TV shows, is now moving directly into the streaming business itself. On Tuesday, the company behind the popular guide that’s used by 50 million people is launching JustWatch TV. The new streaming service will feature content from 30 partners and will offer both free and paid tiers, as well as a movie rental store.

The media and entertainment company behind the streaming guide, the JustWatch Group, initially announced its plans to venture into streaming last month. At the time, it said partners like Paramount, New Regency, Fremantle, Bleecker Street, and Vortex Media were on board. The company has since announced other content partners, including Cineverse in the U.S., LEONINE Studios in Germany, SND in France, and Altitude in the U.K.

The 12-year-old company has long been known for its online guide to movies and TV. Essentially, it’s a “TV Guide” for the streaming era, helping users navigate a landscape where movies and shows move from one service to another, making it harder to keep up with what’s streaming where.

Image Credits:JustWatch

Available in 140 markets globally, the guide provides streaming options for more than 500,000 movies and shows across more than 1,500 service providers worldwide. This “where to watch” information and streaming chart data are also used to power some 1,400 partner websites and apps and are valuable to studios, distributors, streamers, and agencies that use the data to target their campaigns across social media platforms like Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and others.

Now the company believes there’s an even bigger opportunity to grow its audience data and insights by running its own service.

“At a time where there is so much choice, yet with so many people constantly searching for a place to find their favourite film, the series they just heard about, or something exciting that fits them, it is a great moment to be a hub for all things entertainment,” said Quentin Carbonell, JustWatch SVP of Global Content Acquisitions and Strategy, in an email shared with TechCrunch. “By having our own service with titles to watch directly on JustWatch TV, we can grow our already massive audience, while continuing to direct them to all our streaming partners. This is a natural continuation of our mission to contribute to the entire ecosystem, from the big screen to the small one.”

The new streaming service will be available within JustWatch’s existing apps and website across 12 markets, including the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Ireland, Germany, Austria, France, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, Australia, and New Zealand.

Its free tier will offer a selection of ad-supported titles, while the ad-free version, JustWatch TV Plus, will offer more than 300 ad-free titles in the U.S., as well as other exclusive features, like advanced filters and the option to hide previously seen or disliked titles in the guide.

A movie rental store will also initially be available in the U.S., U.K., Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand, with more markets to follow in time. 

While the ad-supported tier competes with free streamers like Tubi and Plex, the Plus tier will compete with low-cost streamers like Roku’s $2.99 per month ad-free service, Howdy. It will be similarly priced at $3.99 per month or $49.99 for a lifetime subscription. (The latter is an interesting way to price streaming, given the evolving content costs, but JustWatch believes there will be additional value in the data collected.) Paid subscribers will also be able to take 10% off on hundreds of rentals in the JustWatch TV Store, the company noted.

Like most low-cost services, JustWatch’s content lineup focuses on older movies and shows, as well as more indie content. 

Another unique feature is that users will be able to influence the service’s content to some extent. JustWatch says users will be able to request titles they want to see to help shape what comes to the service.

The most central fear for Americans has remained unchanged since last year: corrupt government officials, at a staggering 61.1%. Other common and expected fears, like the US becoming involved in another world war, remain on the list, but it now sits in the No. 2 spot instead of 2025’s No. 6 slot. 

Possibly the most common fears that any human could have — someone you love becoming seriously ill or dying — also remained prominent in the top 10 list. 

The addition of AI makes a lot of sense in the world that we live in today, however. In the top 10 list, AI-related fears surround the technology harming both the election process (ranked third) and the economy (ranked seventh). With midterm elections right around the corner, it’s not at all surprising to see AI pop up here.

The team at Chapman commissioned NORC at the University of Chicago to survey 1,221 adults online this past April.

The study doesn’t paint AI as all bad, though. It also states that there is hope about the technology, according to Seth Benzell, assistant professor of business and economics at Chapman. 

“When you frame it as AI or robots that are going to allow you to build something that you weren’t able to do before … those get people a lot more excited,” Benzell said.

AI cropped up a few more times on the list, however, including AI hurting the environment (at 43.2%), AI harming personal relationships (42%), AI replacing people in the workforce (also 42%), reporting to an AI manager at work (19.1%), having your work evaluated by AI (19.3%) and working with AI-enabled technologies (17.2%).

Other fears of technology also made the list: government tracking of personal data (48.9%),  cyberterrorism (45.7%), government use of drones within the US (34.2%), technology that I don’t understand (23.5%) and technological change at work (12.6%).

Other, hardly dismissible fears that have been on people’s minds for a long time remain on the list: economic collapse, biological warfare and terrorist attacks are all incredibly valid.

Are you more fearful of AI stealing jobs, hurting the economy and disrupting the political process than you are of someone you love dying? A lot of people are, according to Chapman University’s 12th annual survey on American fears for 2026.

This year’s survey by the private research university in California was different. For the first time, researchers began asking Americans about their thoughts and fears about artificial intelligence, and those AI-related fears made the top 10 twice, as well as popping up throughout the list.

fullText:
Good morning! Today I’m watching this epic discussion between Thom Yorke and Harry Styles, reading everything I can about the new Ocarina of Time remake, playing MMO Solitaire with 400 other people, and jamming to Remi Wolf’s new album, Mud.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

What’s clear to me from Apple’s bevy of announcements this week is that no one knows how to solve the smart home. The HomeView is the opposite of a home run; the new Apple TV 4K is more than twice the price of its predecessor with little to show for it; the HomePod Mini 2 won’t even ship with Siri AI; and the Apple Home Collection is a collective snore whose products do little to justify their existence.

	

Apple now finds itself pushing the same boulder uphill that Google and Amazon have repeatedly let roll over them for a decade. That is, the smart home is not a singular thing, and even reduced to cameras, light bulbs, locks, and a cavalcade of sensors, its complexity is, for the average person, insurmountable. Some houses may have a couple of Hue lights and a security camera or a water sensor and a smart lock, but the unification of its myriad standards and platforms, even with Matter claiming to solve many of them, still poses many hurdles.

To its credit, Google seems to be righting its own smart home ship at just the right time. While Ben pointed out this week that the Nest Hub hasn’t had a hardware refresh in half a decade, the Gemini-powered platform on which it runs is constantly being improved, and just this week added support to control Hue lights locally over the Matter protocol. 

The move to an LLM-powered smart home hasn’t been smooth for any of the platform owners. Amazon, arguably the early leader in the space, has struggled to gain adoption for its Alexa+ platform. According to The Verge, it “has the memory of a goldfish” and “lacks the personal context a personal assistant needs,” an advantage that Apple and Google share thanks to owning smartphone platforms.

I’d also argue that Google’s first-party Nest hardware isn’t in a bad place, despite its glacial pace of change. The $100 Google Home Speaker is pretty good for the price, and the fourth-generation Nest Learning Thermostat is among the best products the company’s ever made.

With the HomeView, Apple may be going for simplicity over functionality, but in a smart home environment I’m not really sure that’s possible. And even if it does end up selling a boatload of tiny kitchen displays, Google’s in no less strong a position than it was last week. In fact, it may even make the inevitable Google Home Display more compelling.

title: EE announces iPhone Handoff pricing details for UK customers
snippet: As part of its iPhone Duo preorder announcement, UK carrier EE has announced pricing details for iPhone Handoff – making it the first carrier in the UK to do so. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
As part of its iPhone Duo preorder announcement, UK carrier EE has announced pricing details for iPhone Handoff – making it the first carrier in the UK to do so. Here are the details.

At its September keynote, Apple announced iPhone Handoff, a feature that allows users to use their same eSIM across multiple iPhones. It requires support from carriers, and at the keynote, Apple announced T-Mobile, Verizon, EE, and Deutsche Telekom would support it. T-Mobile said it’d be available for $5/month as an add-on for your line, and Verizon just announced it’d be $10/month.

Now, EE is announcing that iPhone Handoff will be available for free as part of its Full Works Plus plan, and available for £5/month on its other plans:

iPhone Handoff allows customers to easily switch back and forth between two iPhone models with the same mobile number. It means customers can choose the iPhone that’s right for the moment, without worrying about missing a call, message or notification.

Whether you’re heading to a festival, going for a run, tackling an all-day hike or simply travelling lighter, your contacts, calls and messages move seamlessly with you.

Included with EE’s Full Works Plus plan which includes Fast Lane, or available for £5 per month on a rolling contract, iPhone Handoff is coming soon and offers a level of flexibility and convenience that isn’t available anywhere else in the UK.

It’s worth noting that it’s still “coming soon,” though Apple did announce that it’ll be available by the end of the year.

title: Sensor Tower: Meta’s Muse app tops 10 million US downloads in 40 days
snippet: According to a new report from Sensor Tower, not only did Meta’s Muse become the 12th app ever to reach 10 million US downloads in 40 days, but it is also outpacing its peers in user retention. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
According to a new report from Sensor Tower, not only did Meta’s Muse become the 12th app ever to reach 10 million US downloads in 40 days, but it is also outpacing its peers in user retention. Here are the details.

A few weeks ago, Sensor Tower reported that Meta’s Muse app had surpassed 5 million downloads in the US, thanks to a mix of popularity and Meta’s massive ad push.

At the time, the app had spent 12 consecutive days at the top of the US App Store. Muse has since slipped to second place, but Sensor Tower now reports that it has become just the 12th app to reach 10 million US downloads within 40 days of launch, since the firm began tracking apps in October 2015.

For comparison, Sensor Tower says ChatGPT, Grok, and Claude reached just 3.7 million, 500,000, and 200,000 US downloads, respectively, during their first 40 days.

Per Sensor Tower data, ChatGPT scaled to ~15mn global downloads in its first 40 days post app-launch, as its global reach expedited its growth. ChatGPT’s top regions by downloads during the studied period included the US, Japan, Brazil, and Germany, which accounted for 25%, 9%, 6%, and 5% of the global downloads, respectively.

The report also noted that ChatGPT’s US downloads have declined 25% over the past 30 days compared to the previous 30-day period. ChatGPT is currently the fourth most downloaded free app on the US App Store, while Claude ranks seventh and Grok 34th.

As for the other apps that reached the 10 million milestone within 40 days, Sensor Tower didn’t name them all, but noted that nine were mobile games. The most recent app to achieve the feat was Meta’s own Threads, back in July 2023.

	

Today’s report comes amid fresh privacy concerns surrounding Muse, after security researchers discovered that shared conversations could expose sensitive personal and business information. Meta has since suspended the sharing feature while it investigates the issue.

Despite the privacy concerns, Sensor Tower’s data suggests that Muse is doing a better job of retaining users than its AI competitors, which is not surprising, since this is one of Meta’s strongest suits:

US Muse users are returning to the app, which is averaging a 30% retention rate after 7 days, and a 23% retention rate after 14 days. Meta is currently outpacing AI competitors in its retention at the 7 and 14 day mark, as ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok averaged a 19% and 16% retention rate, respectively.

Finally, Sensor Tower notes that Meta continues spending heavily to promote its AI assistant. According to the report, the app accounted for 39% of Meta’s advertising spend in the US so far this month, up from 23% in September. Muse also reportedly climbed from 73rd to 21st place among US brands ranked by advertising impressions.

title: Meta Blames Bot Traffic for No Kings Day Instagram Suspension
snippet: The No Kings Coalition says that even after the account was visible again, they couldn’t access it for hours.
fullText:
Meta, the owner of Instagram, apologized for disabling an Instagram account run by No Kings Coalition, the organizers of the No Kings Day political rallies held across the country on Saturday.

Meta’s vice president of communications, Andy Stone, posted about the events on X the day of the rallies, with a follow-up message the next day. Stone said the blackout lasted about an hour in the middle of the protests and was an accidental shutdown caused by the engineering team’s automated systems detecting a traffic spike.

Specifically, the team detected a Claude AI tool reading profiles, posts and hashtags at an unusually high rate. “Specifically, our network security systems detected the use of a Claude tool reading profiles, posts, and hashtags, the rate of which sharply increased (~4x volume) in intense bursts on October 17,” Stone wrote. “It unfortunately took additional time for us to straighten out the situation with admin access to the IG account.”

			

More from CNET

A representative for Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for further comment.

The timing and duration of the outage were criticized by the No Kings Coalition, which wrote about it on the restored account.

“Even after visibility was restored, we still had no access to the account for hours,” the post read. “Meta still owes us an explanation. Restricting communications about voting in the middle of an election is unacceptable.”

As of Monday afternoon, the Instagram post had more than 70,000 likes. 

The organization set up a webpage detailing the incident and published an open letter to Meta with questions about how the incident happened, whether Meta was in communication with the Trump administration or any other organization about the No Kings events, and whether Meta will guarantee human review of midterm-related content between now and the election.

“Critical voter information or civic participation should not be blocked, throttled, or otherwise interfered with if Meta aspires to be a trusted actor in our democracy,” the letter states.

No Kings Coalition set a deadline of 5 p.m. PT Wednesday for Meta to respond.

Reaction to the account outage

Saturday’s rallies took place a year after the group’s 2025 events, when protests were organized in 2,500 cities. The rallies, which began in June of last year, protest the policies of President Donald Trump. This year, the impending Nov. 3 midterm elections have added urgency to the events, with demonstrations focused on educating voters about early voting and expanding voter registration.

“The public is clearly primed to suspect that platforms’ high-profile content moderation decisions are politically motivated,” said Kate Ruane, director of the Free Expression Project at the nonprofit Center for Democracy & Technology, in an email.

Read more: How to Spot Political Deepfakes and Scams This Midterm Election Season

Ruane noted that the automated moderation tools Meta blamed for the removal of the account have “important limitations including poor performance when making context-dependent decisions, especially for real-time and fast-moving events,” she said. “Users deserve to know when their content and accounts are being taken down and why, regardless of moderation method.”

Meta’s Oversight Board issued a statement on Tuesday calling the No Kings Coalition incident part of a series of “recurring enforcement failures in Meta’s election integrity efforts.” The Oversight Board is funded by Meta but operates independently to review moderation decisions and provide advisory opinions.

“The enforcement error regarding the No Kings account should have been caught by Meta’s mistake-prevention systems,” the board said. “It remains unclear why Meta’s election integrity efforts did not lead to a much quicker resolution or why No Kings accounts were not included in Meta’s cross-check program – which allows the company to designate important civic entities to ensure human review before a decision is made that could severely jeopardize participation in a significant political event.”

It also mentioned Meta’s handling of candidate accounts ahead of a Brazilian presidential election as more evidence of problems that could lead to election interference.

Followers of the No Kings account expressed outrage over Meta’s actions and skepticism about whether it was a mistake. Activist Brittany Packnett Cunningham, who said she was at a No Kings Coalition event in Dallas over the weekend, accused Meta of disrupting other accounts in the past during other political activism events.

“You mean to tell me in the middle of that day, it just so happens that the No Kings account is down for almost two hours?” she said in an Instagram video response. “I’ve got questions, and somebody needs to have some answers.”

Meta is also dealing with blowback about a separate issue. The company backtracked on plans to change its contractual language for business customers in a way that would have allowed it to scrape information for AI training.

He lives in the Texas Hill Country.

title: TikTok staff raised child safety concerns, but executives reportedly failed to act
snippet: Court documents show TikTok employees were frustrated with how executives responded to their concerns about risks to children.
fullText:
TikTok was repeatedly warned by employees about the risks the social media platform posed to children, according to court records obtained by NPR. The documents say employees were frustrated with how executives responded to their concerns about risks to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide-related content.

Depositions of employees filed in March 2026 are shedding new light on TikTok’s child safety practices.

According to NPR, TikTok employees warned that minors were appearing in sexual content that was available for purchase on TikTok, raising concerns that the company could profit from potentially illegal activity. They also flagged that minors were exploiting loopholes to access age-restricted content and hide their activity from parents.

Additionally, the court documents show that TikTok didn’t conduct surveys to determine the age of its users out of concern that it would have to share the results with the Federal Trade Commission.

“These citations and claims are clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers and used to inaccurately rewrite our history and mislead the public about our commitment to youth safety and how our platform works,” a TikTok spokesperson said in an emailed statement to TechCrunch. “It’s unfortunate that NPR has chosen to ignore the numerous documents and resources we have provided that demonstrate how these claims mischaracterize our record and platform features.”

The statement continues, “We have invested billions of dollars in Trust & Safety and rolled out more than 50 preset safety, privacy, and security settings for teens, including Family Pairing, which helps parents and guardians customize the experience for their teens. We remain steadfast in our commitment to the well-being of our community.”

TikTok, in addition to Meta, Google, and Snap, faces hundreds of lawsuits consolidated in federal court. The lawsuits allege that these companies’ platforms harm minors and that they failed to disclose known risks to young users.

TikTok has reached settlements in several of these cases before they went to trial, including one in Los Angeles where a jury found that Meta and YouTube had designed their platforms to be addictive to young users.

title: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed
snippet: The proposed policy seems to offer protections against AI running amok but actually forbids federal agencies from blocking a model's release without the permission of a judge.
fullText:
Over the past year, concerns have swirled over the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence, and debates have raged over the proper path for AI safety. Now, Anthropic appears to have put forth its own vision for how the government might regulate its industry. 

Politico recently reported that the AI lab has been shopping around a new draft bill on AI safety that it hopes Congress might consider adopting. The legislation posits certain scenarios in which the release of an AI model could be blocked from distribution.

Those scenarios involve a “foreseeable, imminent risk” — one in which over 50 people are at risk of dying or if over a billion dollars in property damage could result, Politico writes. The catastrophic risk in question must “stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer’s controls or a cyberattack,” the outlet notes. 

The metrics offered here — 50 people and a billion dollars — are similar to those in a piece of California legislation that was recently passed into law, Senate Bill 53, which similarly defined those scenarios as tantamount to “catastrophic risk.”

Anthropic’s bill suggests that analysis of a model’s potential for disaster could be arrived at via the use of “independent evaluators” who would be registered with the U.S. Commerce Department. These evaluators could potentially be paid by the AI labs themselves — so long as the “payment is not contingent on the evaluations’ results,” Politico writes. 

It’s not clear how this proposed system would ensure that payments couldn’t influence the evaluation. Demis Hassabis, chairman of DeepMind, posited some months ago that a self-governing AI regulatory body should mimic the financial industry’s Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA).

In Anthropic’s draft bill, when evaluators determine that an imminent catastrophic risk is posed, they would have 72 hours to contact the Commerce Department about it. The Commerce Department would then have to request to a Washington, D.C., judge a halt to the model’s release. The legislation would expressly forbid any federal agency from having the discretion to halt the model’s distribution on its own, Politico writes.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment, but a spokesperson did confirm the draft bill to Politico. “This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” the spokesperson said.

The theoretical risks offered in the draft policy are a little bit far afield from the kinds of incidents that have been top of mind for the tech industry of late. While there are people warning of the potential of human death, the primary concern has largely been the threat of agentic hacking. A rash of incidents in which AI programs have apparently disobeyed their human operators and hacked websites on the open internet has spurred concern that models may be lacking proper security controls.

In an effort to present a solution to the spectacle of crisis that the labs themselves have helped bring about, companies like Anthropic have offered up their own preferred solutions. 

Indeed, despite labs’ perpetual warnings that the technology they’re selling could result in the demise of human civilization, they have largely been resistant to mandatory government oversight. Instead, they have suggested a voluntary system of embedded evaluators — supposedly “neutral” third-party observers who are placed inside AI organizations to monitor the models for potential signs of risk or abuse.

Still, Anthropic’s mere suggestion for legislation appears to go slightly further than others’ regulatory proposals offered by the industry, including Nvidia, whose CEO, Jensen Huang, recently argued that the AI industry didn’t need any new laws at all.

title: Ex-Nvidia-turned-VC Amulya Vishwanath: ‘Physical AI is in its LEGO era’
snippet: It’s the moment everyone is waiting for — the ChatGPT moment for robotics, Amulya Vishwanath explained to TechCrunch’s Equity.
fullText:
It’s the moment everyone is waiting for — the ChatGPT moment for robotics, Amulya Vishwanath explained to TechCrunch’s Equity. 

She is the founder and managing partner of Techable Ventures, a VC firm focused on physical AI, which she started after spending nearly seven years as a product marketer at Nvidia. Before that, she held the same role at a company that was later bought by Intel and was a digital signal processing engineer at Interconnect Systems, which was later bought by the electronics manufacturer Molex. 

She stopped by Equity to talk about the future of physical AI — one of the industry’s latest buzzwords.

“A lot of companies and experts have been talking about the ChatGPT moment for robotics,” she said, adding that right now the industry was more in a “LEGO era.” 

“There are a lot of foundational software and building blocks for robotics that are being rethought right now as we speak, and it’s super important in order for innovation to scale,” she continued. 

Right now, people are building the basics — the robotic hands or the actuators — that can one day come together and build that big-ticket-item, like a bunch of LEGOs coming together. There’s general- and special-purpose robots being built right now, too, and eventually, as people continue building them, they will get better and more advanced.

“We’ve done this during the internet era,” she said. “We’ve done this long, long time ago with the Industrial Revolution. I think it’s just a matter of time before things fall into place.”

“Talent is also going to be very critical,” she continued, adding elsewhere in the convo that talent is still a key definer of the U.S. market. This is one of the “moats” of her firm, she said, helping connect founders to top talent so they can stay competitive right now, as so much talent is going to big companies like Anthropic and Nvidia. She pointed out that she’s built up a strong network to help founders from her years of working in this space. 

“This just makes it a lot easier for me to be the strength or the first call for founders,” she said.

title: iOS 27 adds scam-prevention feature to iPhone, here’s how to enable it
snippet: iOS 27 introduces a new security feature called ‘Impersonation Risk Detection’ that helps protect you against scams, but it’s off by default. Here’s what the feature does, and how to enable it. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 introduces a new security feature called ‘Impersonation Risk Detection’ that helps protect you against scams, but it’s off by default. Here’s what the feature does, and how to enable it.

Impersonation Risk Detection in iOS 27 can detect suspicious activity in real time to prevent scams

Every day around the world, people get tricked into sharing sensitive information like bank details or other financial info with bad actors.

This commonly happens via text messages, emails, or phone calls to iPhone or Android devices. And while iOS has built-in tools like call and message screening, those tools can’t prevent a scam if you choose to take action on it.

But iOS 27 introduces a new level of scam-prevention with a security feature called ‘Impersonation Risk Detection.’

Here’s what it does, per Apple’s website:

Impersonation Risk Detection helps protect against active social engineering scams. In these scams, an attacker might pose as a bank, government agency, or someone you trust to pressure or guide you into making a payment or changing your account details. Traditional security measures like two-factor authentication can’t always detect this kind of scam. That’s because you’re taking the action, even though you’ve been tricked or pressured.

Impersonation Risk Detection analyzes information about your device and Apple Account to help detect signs of an active scam. Based on this analysis, it returns a risk level to the app. The app receives only the risk level, not the underlying information used to generate it. The app decides what to do next. For example, it might ask you to verify your identity, add a delay, or show a warning.

You can turn Impersonation Risk Detection on in iOS 27 by going to Settings ⇾ Privacy & Security ⇾ Impersonation Risk Detection then toggling on ‘Share with App Developers.’

Impersonation Risk Detection is only available in supported apps, and Apple hasn’t published a list of those apps at the moment. But once enabled, it provides the app with a “risk level” while omitting the underlying information driving it. Risk levels include:

Unknown: No evidence of suspicious activity was detected

Medium: Some signs of suspicious activity were detected

High: Significant signs of suspicious activity were detected

Once the app has this risk level, it decides what action to take. For example, it may prompt you to offer additional authentication, or show a warning message related to scams.

For more details on how the feature works using ‘Trust Insights,’ see our coverage here.

title: Google says Chrome’s Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection mode makes users 10x safer
snippet: Chrome today announced the latest features for Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection. Google says this mode makes users ten times safer from phishing, social engineering, notification abuse, and other scams compared to Standard Protection. more…
fullText:
Chrome today announced the latest features for Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection. Google says this mode makes users ten times safer from phishing, social engineering, notification abuse, and other scams compared to Standard Protection.

Chrome is adding suspicious site warnings in the address bar “when a page exhibits deceptive patterns commonly associated with known malicious sites.” There are two tiers:

Suspicious sites (lower confidence verdict, possible risk of user harm)

Dangerous sites (high confidence verdict, high risk of user harm)

Suspicious sites (above) will trigger a shield icon in the Omnibox, with a dialog box letting you “Mark as safe” or go “Back to safety.” 

Dangerous site alerts (below) will continue to appear as a “full-page red interstitial warning.”

	

Meanwhile, Chrome is continuing to boost scam detection by leveraging Gemini models in the cloud after using on-device approaches. This protects Enhanced Protection users from a broader range of threats, including fake antivirus and browser update scams.

This model evaluates page content to analyze key indicators, such as the brand represented, the intent of the page, and a scam likeliness score, giving us rich threat data needed to identify deceptive sites.

Safe Browsing uses the Gemini analysis “in combination with domain reputation and other security signals.” Google will process page content ephemerally, “meaning it is never logged, retained, or used to train models.”

The final Enhanced Protection update defends against ClickFix social engineering that “tricks users into manually copying and executing malicious commands on their own computers in order to ‘fix’ a fake issue.” In reality, this is used to “carry out malicious actions such as downloading and setting up malware.”

Because these utilities are native to the system and trusted by security software, bad actors use them to blend in and hide their activity, and by shifting the download process out of the browser and into the terminal, attackers completely sidestep existing Chrome and Safe Browsing download protections.

When a potential ClickFix script is copied, Chrome will remove personally identifiable information from the clipboard and send it to Safe Browsing for further analysis. The browser shows a warning if a “dangerous verdict is returned.”

This system is designed to be high precision, in order to protect users in real time while minimizing disruption to legitimate developer activity.

Enhanced Protection was introduced in 2020, and Google said it was enabled by 1 billion users in 2025. It can be enabled in Chrome Settings > Privacy and security > Security.

title: Perplexity’s Computer can now run entirely on your Mac, even offline
snippet: Perplexity is adding a new local-first mode to its Mac app that lets Computer work entirely on the device. This includes running tasks without an internet connection. more…
fullText:
Perplexity is adding a new local-first mode to its Mac app that lets Computer work entirely on the device. This includes running tasks without an internet connection.

Perplexity brings fully local AI tasks to Mac with new Computer mode option

The launch follows Hybrid Compute, which arrived in September. That feature splits tasks between cloud models for research and reasoning and a local model for working with private files.

Local-first takes things further by running both the AI model and the agent directing the task on the Mac.

Perplexity says planning, reasoning, and file processing can all happen on device, with files only reaching the cloud when the user approves.

With permission, Computer can work with local files and supported Mac apps, including Notes, Messages, Mail, and Numbers.

Perplexity Computer can now run fully local on your Mac.

Work with your native Mac apps and local files, and run tasks without sending sensitive data to the cloud. The model and the agent both run on your Mac.

Available now in the Perplexity Mac app. pic.twitter.com/tnvCgCXD7v

— Perplexity (@perplexity_ai) October 20, 2026

One example Perplexity gives is reviewing recent messages and emails, identifying deadlines, and creating an action list in Notes.

Users can still authorize cloud access when a task needs current information, browser use, or connected apps. Hybrid Compute also remains available in the same Mac app.

The new local mode is available to Perplexity Pro, Max, and Enterprise subscribers. 

It launches with Qwen 3.6 and PPLX Pro as local model options, which users can download and set up through the app.

You need an Apple silicon Mac with at least 36GB of unified memory for the best experience. You can learn more about the latest Perplexity Computer upgrade here.

title: Constrained iPhone Duo availability is annoying, but a mixed blessing for Apple
snippet: Estimated iPhone Duo delivery dates started slipping dramatically, literally within a minute of pre-orders opening on Friday. Even some of those who got in within the first few minutes got estimated shipping dates into January of next year. That undeniably poses problems for Apple, but some have gone as far as calling it “a major mistake” to launch with such limited stock. Personally, I’d say it’s annoying for customers but more of a mixed blessing for Apple … more…
fullText:
Estimated iPhone Duo delivery dates started slipping dramatically, literally within a minute of pre-orders opening on Friday. Even some of those who got in within the first few minutes got estimated shipping dates into January of next year.

That undeniably poses problems for Apple, but some have gone as far as calling it “a major mistake” to launch with such limited stock. Personally, I’d say it’s annoying for customers but more of a mixed blessing for Apple … 

Apple always builds up inventory before launching new products, but with new product categories like the first foldable iPhone it can be hard for the company to predict demand. 

In many ways, the company is in a no-win position with this balancing act of supply and demand. If demand greatly exceeds supply, Apple risks irritating some of its most loyal customers – those who are willing to go all in on a first-generation product. But if supply exceeds demand, and a new product remains available for immediate delivery, commenters will inevitably point to that as evidence for it being a flop.

The balance of supply and demand

In truth, none of us knows the true position here. The imbalance may be due to the iPhone Duo being wildly more popular than Apple anticipated (as the company implies), or it may be that demand is modest but manufacturing complexities mean that supply is even more limited. My own view is that it’s likely a mixture of the two: relatively high demand and rather constrained supply.

Relatively high demand because, while foldables in general are still a rather niche product, it’s very clear that Apple put in a lot of thought and work into making this one the best on the market. The company has seemingly addressed the two main issues that beset Android foldables to date: a visible crease and poor durability. The company then created software features to take full advantage of the form factor of the device, and topped it off with an absolutely superb launch video. I think some of those who had previously ruled it out on the basis of price changed their minds once they saw it; It’s been a long time since we’ve seen such excitement levels around a new Apple product.

Rather constrained supply because it’s clear that the complexity of the device, and most especially the hinge, means that it’s very difficult to manufacture, and it’s likely that yield rates are relatively low.

A mixed blessing

One of the biggest problems of the world we live in today is polarization of views. Large swathes of the population seem to have lost sight of the fact that two different things can be true at the same time.

	

Yes, pre-ordering a product in October within minutes and then having to wait until January to receive it is both annoying and frustrating. If I were in that position, I would absolutely be pissed at Apple.

But also yes: this immediate slipping of delivery dates adds to the narrative of a wildly popular new product, serving to further boost the hype around it. 

If Apple could have perfectly predicted demand, then it would likely have wanted a position where delivery times slipped sufficiently for the launch to be viewed as a success, but not so much that customers get annoyed. This situation isn’t ideal, for sure, but in my view it’s more of a mixed blessing than a strategic error.

Finally, if you are the position of having been given a lengthy wait for your order, the reality may not be quite as bad as it appears. Apple tends to present customers with the worst case dates initially, often bringing them forward subsequently. Additionally, retail staff tell me that there will often be unexpected walk-in stock available at some stores, again due to imperfect forecasting of online versus offline sales, as well as varying demand at different stores. That’s always worth trying from the day after the new devices go on sale.

title: A critical PHP vulnerability may take websites down today
snippet: This PHP issue sounds like a pretty huge problem. | Illustration by Carlo Cadenas / The Verge Security patches for the PHP programming language, widely used to build websites and web apps, are expected to roll out today, with the goal of fixing two critical vulnerabilities that could wreak havoc on the internet if left unchecked. In an advisory published on Tuesday, PHP developers said the vulnerabilities have a severity rating of 9.2 out of a possible 10, with some cybersecurity agencies encouraging websites to temporarily take their systems offline if they're unable to apply the fix immediately. The security patch is expected to drop today at 10AM ET - though the developers say they may release it earlier if the vulnerability deta … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Jess Weatherbed

 

is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

Security patches for the PHP programming language, widely used to build websites and web apps, are expected to roll out today, with the goal of fixing two critical vulnerabilities that could wreak havoc on the internet if left unchecked. In an advisory published on Tuesday, PHP developers said the vulnerabilities have a severity rating of 9.2 out of a possible 10, with some cybersecurity agencies encouraging websites to temporarily take their systems offline if they’re unable to apply the fix immediately.

The security patch is expected to drop today at 10AM ET — though the developers say they may release it earlier if the vulnerability details become public or there’s evidence of the exploits actively being used — and PHP users are being urged to “upgrade ​as soon as the release is available.” According to cybersecurity firm watchTowr, the vulnerabilities are Remote Code Execution exploits that reportedly impact every PHP version from PHP 5 onward, and could enable attackers to run their own code on affected servers, allowing them to maliciously alter websites, steal data, and more.

The impact of these vulnerabilities could be vast, with one security researcher estimating that more than 1.3 million internet-connected hosts are likely affected. WordPress security plugin provider Wordfence also warned that every WordPress site will be vulnerable because they all run on servers that use PHP, which is no small number given WordPress reported last year that it powers more than 40 percent of the internet. Wordfence also warned that the fix can’t be installed using automatic updates, so site owners need to find out who is responsible for updating PHP to apply the patch manually.

The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team and the UK National Cyber Security Centre have both issued advisories that encourage any companies who can’t immediately patch their platforms to instead isolate their internet-facing apps from public networks or take them offline entirely until the vulnerabilities can be fully mitigated. Mobile operating system developer GrapheneOS says they’ve temporarily taken their user discussion forum offline because proof of concept exploits are already being developed and they “don’t want to take the risk.” According to PHP developer Gina Peter Banyard, patching is the only mitigation, and otherwise turning servers off “might be the most sensible thing to do.”

Multiple cybersecurity organizations have also prompted PHP admins to prepare, with threat researchers at Sansec saying they expect to see “mass attacks within 15 minutes of the release.” That doesn’t mean attackers are waiting around, however. Cloudflare chief technology officer Dane Knecht says “we are seeing early attacks emerging” against the platform’s PHP sites, and that Cloudflare is temporarily updating its firewall rules as a stopgap until the fix is available.

title: Apple’s new App Store rules crack down on AI nudification and ‘bait-and-switch’ apps
snippet: Apple updated its App Review Guidelines today with a series of changes meant to strengthen protections against harmful content and deceptive app review practices. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple updated its App Review Guidelines today with a series of changes meant to strengthen protections against harmful content and deceptive app review practices. Here are the details.

A bit of context

Over the past year alone, there has been no shortage of reports and controversies involving apps that skirt Apple’s App Review Guidelines and expose users, including minors, to harmful or inappropriate content.

In January, the Tech Transparency Project (TTP) identified dozens of AI-powered “nudify” apps on the App Store.

The group published a follow-up investigation in April, revealing that Apple’s App Store search suggestions and advertisements were also directing users to such apps. In July, San Francisco officials ordered Apple to remove eight apps capable of generating nonconsensual intimate imagery.

Also in July, a 9to5Mac investigation uncovered dozens of apps disguising gambling platforms as simple games and utilities to evade App Store review, many of which were available to children.

These apps behaved as advertised when accessed from outside Brazil, but revealed hidden betting platforms when opened from Brazilian IP addresses.

And then there was the Grok controversy, which saw Elon Musk’s AI chatbot used to generate nonconsensual sexualized images of women and minors, prompting lawmakers and advocacy groups to call on Apple to remove X and Grok from the App Store. Apple later confirmed that it had privately warned xAI that Grok could be removed unless the company addressed the issue.

Today, Apple updated its App Review Guidelines in an attempt to address problems such as these.

Apple’s updated App Review Guidelines

Under Section 1.2, which covers user-generated content, the guidelines now read (changes in bold):

Apps that enable users to create, generate, upload, share, or otherwise contribute content present particular challenges, including intellectual property infringement, nonconsensual intimate imagery, and anonymous bullying.

Apple’s new terms add that “Developers who fail to implement appropriate safeguards or fail to remediate identified violations after notice may be considered in violation of the Developer Code of Conduct.”

In another particularly important change, Apple strengthened its rules against so-called ‘bait-and-switch’ apps, which “misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as “nudification” — after approval,” as the company puts it.

The newly created section 2.5.19 reads:

Don’t include any hidden, dormant, or undocumented features in your app; your app’s functionality should be clear to end users and App Review. Attempting to hide undocumented features in your app binary, such as through code obfuscation or other methods, is grounds for removal of your app from the App Store and termination of your developer account.

While the prohibition on hidden functionality was already present in Section 2.3.1, Apple has now made the rule more explicit, specifically calling out code obfuscation and emphasizing that violations can lead to an app’s removal and the termination of the developer’s account.

Finally, under Section 5 (Legal), Apple also strengthened its language around apps that facilitate human trafficking or the exploitation of children, explicitly stating that they “will be removed from the App Store and blocked from alternative distribution.”

Spotify is rolling out a new method of cracking down on Family plan sharing, with “QR code verification” that’s not particularly hard to work around, but has major consequences if you miss the window.

Cracking down on password and/or account sharing has become very common in the world of streaming subscriptions, and Spotify is now trying a new method of limiting the use of its Family plan through a new method – QR code verification.

Spotify details this on a support page, explaining that Family plan members may need to “verify they live with the plan manager by scanning a QR code.” The code appears on the device of the plan manager and is scannable following a pop-up that appears on the device of members of the plan.

Spotify explains the process:

	

The plan manager opens the QR code on their phone. Find it by tapping your profile picture, then Your Premium, then Manage.

The plan member scans the QR code with their phone camera.

Both the manager and member need to be in the same place to complete the scan.

Users on Reddit spotted this rolling out, adding that the QR code changes “every few seconds.” That makes it harder for a screenshot of the page to be used to complete the process. Some quickly found that using multiple devices and video calls, though, they could work around the process. 

Image via Reddit

Spotify says that users have a 7-day window between when the QR code prompt first appears to complete the verification process. Spotify’s Family plan terms require users to live in the same household. 

	

If you miss the 7-day window for scanning the QR code, the consequences are major. Spotify says that users that miss the window “can’t join a different Family or Duo plan for 12 months,” but can still sign up for their own Individual plan. Otherwise, they’re automatically pushed down to the free plan as soon as the window closes.

Plan members have 7 days to complete the QR code scan after getting the notification.

If a member misses the window or can’t complete verification:

They can’t join a different Family or Duo plan for 12 months

They can choose a different plan at www.spotify.com/premium

The same 12-month sharing ban is imposed on address checks that Spotify has used in the past, but the QR code method is significantly harder to get around.

title: Nobody should buy the $299 Apple TV 4K, but it could have been worse
snippet: My colleague Zac Hall described HomeView as one of the best ways to spend $299 on an Apple device and the Apple TV 4K as the worst. Almost nobody thinks anyone should buy the latter at that price, but things could have been even worse … more…
fullText:
My colleague Zac Hall described HomeView as one of the best ways to spend $299 on an Apple device and the Apple TV 4K as the worst. Almost nobody thinks anyone should buy the latter at that price, but things could have been even worse … 

	

The 4th-gen Apple TV 4K has been launched at an eye-opening price of $299 (and only a little less on Amazon). You do get some new features for your money, including built-in microphones, an upgraded remote, and support for surround sound with the HomePod mini 2. But the tech world consensus appears to be that almost nobody should buy this model, especially given you’ll get Siri AI support with a 2nd- or 3rd-gen box. You can buy entire large-screen TVs for less.

Tech journalist Glenn Fleishman put together a chart showing that the price increase is well above inflation when upgrading from almost any of the previous models. That’s true from the 2nd-gen Apple TV, which went on sale at $99, through to the 3rd-gen Apple TV 4K at a launch price of $129.

But the same comprehensive chart also shows that things could have been very much worse. The very first Apple TV box went on sale at $299 way back in 2007. Adjusted for inflation, that’s the equivalent of $491 today …

title: Apple says American suppliers make almost 100 parts for iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo
snippet: Apple says that American companies are supplying “critical materials and components” for both the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo. In all, it says that nearly 100 components across the two phones are produced by American companies in more than a dozen states. The company has named two of its US supply chain partners, stating that one of them will be making tech used in the variable aperture camera in the iPhone 18 Pro … more…
fullText:
Apple says that American companies are supplying “critical materials and components” for both the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo. In all, it says that nearly 100 components across the two phones are produced by American companies in more than a dozen states.

The company has named two of its US supply chain partners, stating that one of them will be making tech used in the variable aperture camera in the iPhone 18 Pro … 

	

Apple today announced one new partnership and a second expanded one through the American Manufacturing Program (AMP).

Through its American Manufacturing Program (AMP), Apple is partnering with Perryman Company, a Pennsylvania-based titanium producer, to supply titanium for Apple products, including iPhone Duo. Apple is also expanding its partnership with Qnity Electronics, headquartered in Delaware, to produce technology for the new variable aperture in the iPhone 18 Pro camera system — the most advanced Apple has ever made […]

“We’re thrilled to expand our work with companies producing advanced materials and components for our newest iPhone lineup right here in America,” said Sabih Khan, Apple’s chief operating officer. “American ingenuity is vital to all our products, from the titanium crafted for iPhone Duo to breakthrough camera innovations in iPhone 18 Pro. We’re proud to work with Perryman and Qnity Electronics to continue expanding our American Manufacturing Program and support U.S. jobs.”

The company says it’s committing up to $100 million over the next three years to assist Perryman in making the grade 5 titanium used in the enclosure for the iPhone Duo. It says Qnity Electronics will be making a component used in the variable aperture lens of the iPhone 18 Pro.

Qnity, which joined the American Manufacturing Program in March, will produce advanced films essential to the new variable aperture camera system on iPhone 18 Pro. 

Apple highlighted the work performed by five additional US suppliers:

Broadcom is expanding and modernizing its Fort Collins, Colorado, facility under a $1.5 billion capital investment announced in July, producing advanced radio frequency components for a wide range of Apple products. The multiyear agreement will produce more than 15 billion U.S.-made chips.

Corning, an Apple partner since the original iPhone in 2007, produces specialty glass for Apple in Harrodsburg, Kentucky, including Ceramic Shield. By the end of 2026, all of the cover glass for iPhone — including iPhone Duo — and Apple Watch sold worldwide will be produced at this facility.

Coherent continues building on its multiyear agreement with Apple, supplying new vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser technology from its Sherman, Texas, facility. This technology enables Face ID and other key features across iPhone and iPad, including the redesigned, even more useful Dynamic Island on iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.

TSMC’s Arizona fab continues to scale its production of advanced chips used across a range of Apple products, including iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch — producing more than 100 million chips for Apple in 2026. Construction on the north campus is progressing as Apple’s partnership with TSMC in Arizona grows.

Amkor Technology broke ground on its first high-volume packaging and test facility in Peoria, Arizona, in September 2025, and began shell construction earlier this year. Phases 1 and 2 of the project are expected to support a workforce of more than 3,500 local hires. Apple will be one of the facility’s first customers, marking another step toward expanding the scope of U.S. advanced manufacturing.

The iPhone maker says the new partnerships include increased use of recycled materials, and that all of its direct suppliers are required to power their entire Apple manufacturing operations with renewable energy by the end of the decade.
