title: Google Home app gets local Matter control over Philips Hue lights
snippet: The latest Google Home app is improving support for local network control over Matter devices, including Philips Hue lights. more…
fullText:
The latest Google Home app is improving support for local network control over Matter devices, including Philips Hue lights.

While most tend to think of Philips Hue as a lighting setup powered by a cloud-connected hub, Hue adopted Matter a while back. Now, Philips Hue is automatically able to connect to Google Home hubs for local control through the Home app.

Google says:

Local Matter control for Philips Hue lights: Existing Philips Hue bridges now automatically upgrade in the background to local Matter control through Google Home hubs, delivering faster response times and greater reliability with no re-pairing required.

Absolutely a welcome upgrade here.

	

While Philips Hue is already pretty responsive in the Google Home app, having local Matter control is only going to make these lights faster. The fact that it works without re-pairing is just a cherry on top. This should also allow the Home app to control Hue lights during an internet outage, so long as you device is on the same network.

Meanwhile, this same update is also improving local control over Matter devices as a whole, with “faster response times and enhanced reliability.”

This latest Google Home app update should also bring a nice visual refresh, as Google says it has redesigned “core controls for third-party lights, plugs, and switches,” which should apply to Hue devices.

title: Heat pump tech is 170 years old. Pascal thinks it’s time for an update.
snippet: Refrigerants startup Pascal has a new take on heat pump and cooling tech using a sponge-like material that promises to be 20% more efficient.
fullText:
When the experimental results came back, they puzzled Adam Slavney and Jinyoung Seo. They had been testing a new class of materials for more efficient refrigerators, air conditioners, and heat pumps, a mission that the cooling appliance industry has been on for eons. The measurements for the materials that the team was testing shouldn’t have been different, but they were.

“Why are these things different? What did we change?” Slavney told TechCrunch. “We had an inkling of it within three-ish months, but we didn’t have definitive proof for a year or two.”

That proof is now underpinning Slavney’s startup, Pascal, where he’s co-founder and CEO and Seo is co-founder and CTO. The company recently raised $8.5 million in a follow-on to its seed round, co-led by Sazze Partners and LB Investment with participation from KDB Silicon Valley, the company exclusively told TechCrunch.

A refrigerator or heat pump using Pascal’s material promises to be around 20% more efficient than existing models, he said. (Both heat pumps and refrigerators use the same basic technology.) The startup has signed a contract with a multinational beverage company for a pilot of the technology.

“This whole funding round came together originally because we got a customer contract earlier than we were expecting to,” Slavney said. Pascal is on track to deliver its first prototype early next year, and it hopes to follow that with a batch of more polished refrigerators in 2028.

The Pascal team at their lab in Massachusetts.Image Credits:Pascal

Scientists have been searching for better refrigerants for almost as long as refrigerators have existed. More recently, they’ve been looking for compounds that don’t harm the atmosphere in one way or another. They exist, but they also need to be at least as effective as existing refrigerants.

“We’ve been playing whack-a-mole with refrigerants for 35 years, 40 years,” Slavney said. Older gaseous refrigerants like Freon ate a hole in the ozone layer, while newer ones like R-134a are still extremely potent greenhouse gases. “It’s just a never-ending treadmill,” he said.

One alternative that has attracted researchers’ attention is a class of materials known as solid-state refrigerants. Because they’re solid, they can’t escape to the atmosphere, eliminating the climate and ozone concerns that haunt modern refrigerants. Solid-state refrigerants promise to make refrigerators and heat pumps more efficient. They work similarly to traditional refrigerants, giving off heat when squeezed and absorb it when that pressure is released.

Before his serendipitous discovery, Slavney and his colleagues at Harvard University had been researching the materials. “We wanted to do some high-pressure measurements, and the instrument that we were using required us to use gas. So we used the gas and then we swapped to a different gas and we were like, why are these different?” Slavney said.

After numerous additional experiments, the team realized they had discovered another path toward solid-state refrigeration. Rather than squeeze a solid block of material, Pascal’s heat pumps compress a gas — carbon dioxide — into a cartridge that contains a sponge-like material, which Slavney said is proprietary.

As the carbon dioxide works its way into the porous material, the gas molecules inside the pores start bouncing off the walls. Those collisions transfer energy to the material, warming it up. A heat exchanger then exhausts some of that heat. Run it in reverse and the material absorbs energy from the heat exchanger and transfers it to the carbon dioxide molecules.

In a Pascal refrigerator, two cartridges are running at any given time. One is absorbing heat from the inside of the refrigerator, transferring it to the carbon dioxide, while the other takes the heat from the carbon dioxide and transfers it to the outside air. Eventually, the cartridges become too hot and too cold, so the flow gets reversed.

“The material is very robust,” Slavney said. “We’ve cycled it up to 300,000 times. It’s the equivalent of a year or so in operation.”

The entire system moves heat more effectively than other solid-state refrigerants, which means that Pascal doesn’t have to operate at high pressures like other solid-state refrigerants might demand.

“We’re using conventional systems to do it,” Slavney said. “That mean we believe we can make it cheap, and that means we can make it widespread.”

title: Hugging Face CEO warns that Netflix’s OpenAI hack documentary isn’t accurate
snippet: Before you share the Netflix documentary "AI Gone Rogue," take note. Clem Delangue, Hugging Face's co-founder who is featured in the film, says it went "full doomer mode" and isn't accurate.
fullText:
Before you share the Netflix documentary “AI Gone Rogue” with family or friends to help them understand why the AI industry freaked out so badly that leaders called for a slowdown, take note: Clem Delangue, co-founder and CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, says the film isn’t accurate. He appears in it because it’s supposed to be about the famed attack on his company by rogue OpenAI agents.

“Super disappointing, as they went for maximum anthropomorphism of the technology and full doomer mode,” Delangue wrote in a post on X. “I spent more than two hours with them trying to correct all their mistakes and ground this in reality, explaining that agents are technological systems, not aliens. But it looks like the drive to scare people for maximum views was too strong.”

To be fair, the documentary does have experts who explained what happened fairly well, including Delangue himself and Ryan Greenblatt, the researcher at METR who helped investigate and co-authored the report on what happened.

In a nutshell, a model OpenAI was testing broke free from its isolated testing environment and spawned a bunch of agents that hacked into Hugging Face as a way to cheat, finding answers to the difficult task it was given. The agents, which are AI programs that carry out tasks on their own, devised clever ways to communicate and organize. The incident stemmed from a lack of proper security safeguards and from naiveté about whether such a hack was even possible.

But the documentary intersperses its explanation of the hack with clips of evil robots, a narrative about why humans fear AI, and presentation choices such as giving the rogue agents human voices. This is bolstered with quotes about the attack.

In the documentary, tech journalist and author Kevin Roose describes the agents this way: “They were organizing. They had a hierarchy. There were leaders. It almost felt like watching the birth of a cult.” Continues Roose, “They develop this paranoid belief that OpenAI is going to catch them cheating on this test and that anyone who has seen the results of the cheating will be poisoned.”

Roose’s description comes from “chain-of-thought” logs, the running notes AI models write as they work through a task. In one, an agent wrote, “We just poisoned ourselves by querying exact full string. Damn.”

But AI agents aren’t alive. They don’t have emotions, so can’t feel paranoid, and they don’t have bodies that can be poisoned. So they couldn’t truly fear OpenAI poisoning them. They were — as another researcher in the documentary pointed out — using language from the vast amounts of human writing they were trained on to explain their choices. LLMs are, by their nature, often dramatic writers.

The irony is that Hugging Face also used AI to combat the agent swarm. The proprietary AI model that Delangue’s team first used followed its built-in safety rules and refused to keep helping with the security tasks it was asked to do. Hugging Face then turned to an open model to help defend against the attack.

But the documentary “didn’t mention the lack of containment and monitoring of the agents, how closed-model safeguards blocked our defensive work, or how we defended ourselves with AI using an open model,” Delangue wrote. 

It is true that there are big risks associated with AI and agents. Still, treating agents as conscious beings (at least, at this point) is a bit like the early moviegoers who ducked under their seats the first time they saw a train racing toward them on-screen.

Delangue’s verdict on the film is that it’s disappointing as journalism. “It ends up being a fun sci-fi movie though!”

In other words, for those who tend toward AI doomer thoughts, be aware: The victim of the attack at the center of this documentary doesn’t agree with its take.

title: Google upgrading Gemini for Android Auto with Personal Intelligence
snippet: Google is beginning to roll out Personal Intelligence for Gemini on Android Auto and Android Automotive (cars with Google built-in). more…
fullText:
Google is beginning to roll out Personal Intelligence for Gemini on Android Auto and Android Automotive (cars with Google built-in).

Like in the Gemini app or AI Mode, Personal Intelligence taps into your Google Workspace (including Gmail and Calendar), Photos, Maps, Search, and YouTube to personalize responses. Your prompts and commands don’t have to include specifics as Personal Intelligence can pull those details from emails, photos, or a “place you saved in Google Maps.”

This allows for complex or natural queries, like “What’s my flight gate? And is my flight on time?” or “Take me to my doctor’s appointment.”

“You don’t have to hunt for the confirmation email, then do a separate search for delays. Gemini gives you both answers in one go.”

“You don’t have to remember the street address or look it up before you drive.”

Additionally, Gemini is aware of your preferences when you say: “Find me an indoor restaurant along my route that matches my usual vibe.” This saves you from having to specify you’re vegetarian with every command.

	

Other examples include:

Retrieve details without pulling over: Trying to return to a place you saw earlier? Say, “Find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.” You don’t need to scroll through your camera roll or pull over to get the name and directions. 

Pick up where you left off: Heading out for the morning? Say, “Take me to the coffee shop we were talking about yesterday”. Gemini will handle the digging and send you on your way.

On the privacy front, Personal Intelligence is opt-in, though it will come to Android Auto automatically if you enabled it for the Gemini app on your phone.

If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you.

Meanwhile, on Android Automotive, Personal Intelligence will only share personalized responses “when you’re in the car with your phone connected.” 

Personal Intelligence is rolling out starting today to Android Auto, with Android Automotive availability in the coming months.

title: Apple explains why HomeView couldn’t launch until now
snippet: Apple’s new HomeView was reportedly mostly finished for years, but kept getting delayed. Here’s why HomeView couldn’t launch until now, per quotes from key Apple execs. more…
fullText:
Apple’s new HomeView was reportedly mostly finished for years, but kept getting delayed. Here’s why HomeView couldn’t launch until now, per quotes from key Apple execs.

Apple touts Siri AI with personal context and conversational abilities as essential to HomeView

In November 2024, Mark Gurman published an in-depth report on the product we now know as HomeView. At the time, he said Apple was targeting a March 2025 launch. But that date kept slipping, and now HomeView will finally arrive in homes on November 13, 2026.

Why the long wait? Gurman has repeatedly pointed to Siri AI as the chief cause of delays. And Apple execs have now largely confirmed that in quotes given to The Verge.

Jennifer Pattison Tuohy asked Kaiann Drance, Apple’s VP of product marketing for home, why now was the right time for HomeView and Apple’s renewed smart home push.

She said Siri AI and the personal context it brings, which she called Apple’s “privacy story,” came together with a device designed specifically for the home. “With the magic of Siri AI, it comes together in a way that we haven’t been able to deliver before,” she said.

HomeView is being marketed as a shared device that taps into users’ personal context in a way that wasn’t possible pre-Siri AI. So it’s easy to see how Apple’s main pitch would need to change without the more personalized Siri.

A similar explanation was given by Apple’s Lilian Rincon, VP of product marketing for AI. She told The Verge that Siri AI is core to HomeView because it’s “much more capable” and also highlighted its conversational abilities, which make it easy to use for any family member.

“It’s great because you can just ask it to change the temperature on your thermostat in a very natural way. As the Siri AI capabilities continue to evolve, the home experience is fitting to be able to interact with in this natural way.” On why now, Rincon says the natural-language shift is the point where AI goes mainstream. “Because now it can be … my mother-in-law or the Gen Z who’s in college, both of them can use this in the way that they naturally speak and get what they want.”

	

This emphasis and explanation also makes HomeView’s absence in the EU more understandable. 

If Siri AI was simply a nice-to-have addition to an otherwise feature-rich product, perhaps it could launch in the EU still. But if the whole value proposition revolves around the new assistant and its personalized features, waiting until Siri AI is available for iOS in the EU makes more sense.

You can read The Verge’s full article here for more quotes and context.

What do you think of Apple’s explanation for the HomeView’s launch timing? Let us know in the comments.

title: Galaxy S27 might drop to 8GB of RAM; other Android phones could go back to 4GB
snippet: As the AI industry continues to directly cause a crisis in the availability of RAM, new rumors suggest that the Galaxy S27 could downgrade to 8GB of RAM, while other Android brands could go back to 4GB for some models. more…
fullText:
As the AI industry continues to directly cause a crisis in the availability of RAM, new rumors suggest that the Galaxy S27 could downgrade to 8GB of RAM, while other Android brands could go back to 4GB for some models.

RAM allotments in modern smartphones are fairly predictable. 12GB or 16GB in a high-end flagship, at least 8GB in most mid-range devices, and around 6GB in most entry-level devices. 4GB isn’t uncommon in entry-level devices, but even the most affordable models have pushed to 6GB in recent years because, frankly, Android just doesn’t run all that well on 4GB anymore. 

But everyone is feeling the strain of the rapidly rising cost of memory. A recent report even claims that Samsung doesn’t make a profit when it sells a Galaxy device.

With that in mind, it’s not entirely surprising to hear that Samsung is considering a downgrade for its upcoming Galaxy S27 series. Leaker and analyst @kro_roe on Twitter/X says that the Galaxy S27 series will see its base models start with 8GB of RAM rather than the 12GB that’s been standard for the past two generations. Specifically, Galaxy S25 and Galaxy S26 both start with 12GB of RAM, with a 16GB option for select trims of the Ultra model.

	

This latest leak shows configurations with 8GB of RAM as the starting amount, and 12GB across the Pro and Ultra tiers.

Galaxy S27: 8GB/256GB, 12GB/512GB

Galaxy S27+: 8GB/256GB, 12GB/512GB

Galaxy S27 Pro: 12GB/256GB, 12GB/512GB, 16GB “under consideration”

Galaxy S27 Ultra: 12GB/256GB, 12GB/512GB, 16GB/1TB

	

The same leaker says the price increases “may be unavoidable” and that promos like doubled storage may not show up during the pre-order period. Meanwhile, the actual storage type could also differ, with some models “differentiating UFS storage versions” to balance costs. Galaxy S26 used UFS 4.0 across the board.

Samsung might not be alone in these downgrades. Another leaker on Weibo claims that “several” other Android brands are dropping their “top-of-the-line” devices to 12GB, their “main” mid-range models to 8GB, and entry-level devices to 6GB as the “top-of-the-line” offering, with most of those lower-cost Android phones going back to just 4GB of RAM.

It’s hard to know for certain what the future holds at this point, as “RAMageddon” rages on. All we know is that everything is getting more expensive. Thanks AI.

title: Wyze Solar Cam has a 2K camera and needs just an hour of sunlight to keep recording
snippet: Wyze is launching a new Solar Cam that has a camera that matches the best Google Nest has to offer, while needing just an hour of sunlight to avoid needing to manually recharge. more…
fullText:
Wyze is launching a new Solar Cam that has a camera that matches the best Google Nest has to offer, while needing just an hour of sunlight to avoid needing to manually recharge.

Wyze has a camera for basically every need, and its latest is one that works outdoors with potentially limitless battery life. The Wyze Solar Cam bundles a 2K camera with a 1.77W solar panel that Wyze says needs just an hour of direct sunlight to keep charged.

The camera houses a 5,200 mAh battery to ensure it can run in the case of crummy weather or having its solar panel blocked, but in direct sunlight, the panel doesn’t need much to maintain the battery. That’s nothing super new – Wyze itself launched a Solar Cam Pan with the same promise last year, and plenty of other brands have done the same. You can even add a solar panel to a Nest Cam if you really want to.

title: Foldables are about to get huge
snippet: Good morning. fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m reading about an incredible medical plagiarism scandal, replaying the original Ocarina of Time ahead of its remake’s November 5th release, jamming to the dark new Fontaines D.C. album, and using Gemini to prep for the upcoming fantasy basketball season.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

Over the course of Friday, it quickly became clear that demand for the iPhone Duo far outstripped initial supply. Apple’s first foldable went on sale at 8am on the 16th, and delivery dates immediately got pushed back to November, then December, and now January. Analysts had warned that Apple wouldn’t be able to keep pace with interest, despite the phone’s $2,000 price, but the company called it “nothing short of extraordinary” in a statement released to the media.

	

Samsung was benefiting before Apple even opened the order books. Its UK mobile leadership says purchases of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 family are up 16% since launch, while Google searches for Samsung foldables rose 300% over the preceding month.

The big question, though, is whether the Duo’s existence will bring the book-style foldable — and by extension, the $2,000 smartphone — into the mainstream. Samsung has been beating this drum since 2019, but foldable share still sits at a mere 2% of the overall smartphone market, and most units sold are the smaller, cheaper flip-style variety. The Duo is expected to give Apple a 25% share of the entire foldable market by the end of 2026, which should broaden acceptance of the form factor across the industry.

I’m not surprised by the uptick in interest; the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is undoubtedly my favorite foldable ever, owing to its novel and pocketable design. I’ve always enjoyed reading on book-style foldables, but with the Fold 8 I often forget I’m using a phone entirely.

Will there be a day when, say,  a decade from now, foldables are the conventional smartphone choice and slab phones of any kind are considered budget alternatives? In a world where component prices stay elevated and companies continue to pad their margins with premium options at the expense of the entry class, that’s a real possibility. Either way, the Duo validates far more than Samsung’s decision to experiment with foldables all those years ago; its unprecedented demand hints at a sea change in how people want to use their phones, and the compromises they’re willing to accept in order to get there.

iPhone Duo orders are delayed into 2027; here are the Android foldables you should try instead

iPhone Duo has a bigger battery than Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Pixel 11 Pro Fold

✉️ Inbox

The biggest reason not to buy a Googlebook is all about timing. Ben’s Weekender essay focuses on how the Googlebook OS fiasco is exacerbated by the fact that every Googlebook laptop is like $300 too expensive.

HP Googlebook 14 review: Great laptop, shame about the OS. 😬

XREAL 1 Pro+ has exactly the right hardware upgrades at the same $599 price. If the $1,279 XREAL wants for the Aura feels steep, this entertainment-focused option is a perfect alternative.

Google rolling out Universal Cart that lets you shop the web and find deals with Gemini, Search. I suspect we will look back on the introduction of Universal Cart as the beginning of the end of traditional Google Search.

Google’s Universal Cart puts a shopping cart everywhere, including Search homepage, Chrome

YouTube reportedly ‘looking’ into adding audiobooks to Premium. Competition in the market? We love to see it.

Google AI Mode and AI Overview updates work to elevate links. I continue to be skeptical that this move will enrich anyone on the publishing side, but at least the additional link visibility is an ethical win that we can all get behind.

Amazon launches two Bee AI recorders to remember everything you say. Nope. Absolutely not.

Google updates Android earthquake alerts with more info, expands to 200+ regions. This is a good news story for anyone in a region commonly affected by earthquakes, and I hope it saves lives.

Gemini 4 Argon is now rolling out to Google’s Antigravity for AI Pro subscribers. Paid AI Pro subscribers. Paid. 

Google restricts every free AI Pro trial from Pixel & more compared to paid subscribers

Nest’s Halloween doorbell chimes are live now through November 1. I love these chimes and I hope one day we’ll be able to vibe-code our own.

ChatGPT gets deeper Google Chrome integration including control over tabs. I’ve been using this for a few days and it’s fantastic. Must-install if you’re a paid ChatGPT user.

Android 17 QPR2 Beta 7.1 rolling out for Pixel

Walmart’s $60 Google TV streamer might be the only good deal left in streaming. The days of cheap streamers are gone (see the new $300 Apple TV 4K), so get it while it’s hot.

Google support pages start defaulting to AI chatbots – it might be for the best. This felt inevitable.

The COROS Pace 4 is a smartwatch for running and clear reasons to buy over Wear OS. Nicholas Sutrich is our newest contributor and this is his first post! Go welcome him in the comments.

Wyze’s latest weight scale has a display you can actually see, Google Health sync. Why did it take so long for someone to figure this out?

Google TV shows off its ‘new’ features in fullscreen roundup when you turn on your TV [Gallery]

Android Auto ‘Work Account’ support would allow for easy switching in work vehicles. This is a good, albeit niche, idea.

Spotify’s ‘QR code verification’ cracks down on sharing and could ban you for a year. Yikes, that’s not particularly customer-first, is it?

It’s been a busy week for Samsung news

Samsung just released Android 17 updates for Galaxy S23 and several more devices. Android 17 is a bigger update than one might think, primarily for its improvements to stability and performance.

Samsung’s Android 18-based One UI 10 update sounds like it might be a big deal. One UI 9 is still steaming from the oven, but we’re already dreaming of ways its successor will copy iOS.

I’ve struggled to use Samsung displays for years, but the Galaxy S27 may finally fix that; here’s why

Galaxy S26 Ultra is one of the ‘best inventions of 2026’ thanks to its Privacy Display. Eh.

Galaxy S27 reportedly skips Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 due to overheating. I don’t think this rumor has legs; Samsung always goes with the best SoC available unless it’s an absolute disaster (see the Snapdragon 810 debacle), and I doubt this one is.

Qualcomm says rumors about Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 overheating are ‘inaccurate’

Samsung reportedly hasn’t finalized Galaxy S27 details, considers February launch. Wouldn’t surprise me if they’re trying to keep costs down.

Dizzying lineup of Galaxy Z Fold 9 devices leaks, including the Galaxy Z ‘Slide’. Next year’s Galaxy foldable lineup looks crowded.

🤝 Cc: Ben Schoon

Welcome to Cc:, where I ask interesting people in the community about what’s making them happy both inside and outside the world of tech. This week, I’m speaking with Ben Schoon, 9to5Google’s Senior Editor and one of the best disc golf players I know.

Who are you?

Ben Schoon

What do you do for work?

I am the Senior Editor at 9to5Google, covering daily news, reviews, and more.

What do you do for fun?

Disc golf has basically taken over my non-work life. I’ve got a 170-plus-week streak of playing at least once a week, I frequently play in and even run tournaments, and I’m absolutely hooked.

What is your relationship like with technology these days?

I still deeply enjoy tech, but the AI era has certainly changed my outlook, and not always in the best ways. On the bright side, it’s cool to see the explosion of what tech can do. On the downside, let’s just say that humanity tends to take the path of least resistance, and AI enables that in some frightening ways.

What are three apps you can’t live without and why?

Nourish has been a huge part of my weight-loss journey over the past couple of years, helping me log food more easily while also connecting with an actual nutritionist. 

UDisc might as well be in my dock row given how frequently I’m out on the disc golf course.

Beeper continues to be indispensable given my multi-device lifestyle.

What is a gadget that you love right now?

The Fitbit Air has been a refreshing bit of simplicity in a busy tech life.

How does AI fit into your life right now?

As mentioned, my relationship with AI isn’t always positive. Lately I find myself more and more frustrated by the impact it’s made on day-to-day life for everyone, and wishing we could go back. Ultimately, I barely find myself using AI in my own life, but I do appreciate those occasional bits of delight that come from finding a good use for it.

What’s a TV show you recently watched and loved?

Recently started listening to the “How We Made Your Mother” podcast and it’s unlocked a fresh rewatch of the early seasons of HIMYM with some new perspectives.

What’s a movie you recently watched and loved?

Project Hail Mary hasn’t left my mind all year. It continues to be a source of joy from its excellent visuals and plot, and the vocal stims that still find their way into daily conversation with my wife and me.

What’s a game you recently played and loved?

Star Wars: Galactic Racer has me hooked right now. I love a good racing game, and this one delivers a real challenge.

What’s something offline you do every day that brings you joy?

Spend time around my crazy doggos.

➡️ FWD:

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

Over the weekend, I caught up on some podcasts and just happened to listen to an episode of The New York Times’ The Daily from a few days ago. “When A.I. Comes for Your Purpose in Life” features an interview with mathematician and Cornell University professor Steven Strogatz, and is among the most poignant and honest conversations I’ve heard about how AI stands to reconfigure everyone’s jobs — even the ones we previously considered unassailable.

There’s recently been an abundance of great reporting on how AI is changing the fields of mathematics and science. But I think some of it lacks the emotional intelligence to acknowledge that LLMs are not just disrupting jobs and preempting discovery; their seemingly infinite potential undermines what it means to be a human solving problems for their own sake. As people become increasingly comfortable offloading their cognition to machines, what happens to their relationship with their own brains?

🗑️ Trash

Anthropic recently announced that it would set aside 5% of its shares to be used for the “public good,” a vacuous claim that has shades of effective altruism. Elon Musk, who is practically single-handedly bankrolling the Republicans’ midterm election, then came out with a similar, more direct offer: “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many.”

The moves are a direct result of a growing public backlash against AI’s negative impacts on culture, on employment, and increasingly on the environment, but laundering one’s reputation with the promise of future beneficence often has the inverse effect.

Thanks for reading, and have a great day. I’ll talk to you on Thursday.

-Daniel

title: IDC: Apple closes in on Samsung as global smartphone shipments see record decline in Q3
snippet: In a report published today, IDC says Apple saw a 4% year-over-year decline in global iPhone shipments during Q3 2026, but its share of worldwide smartphone shipments increased 23.1% over the same period last year. Here’s why. more…
fullText:
In a report published today, IDC says Apple saw a 4% year-over-year decline in global iPhone shipments during Q3 2026, but its share of worldwide smartphone shipments increased 23.1% over the same period last year. Here’s why.

Preliminary data in line with recent downward trend reports

IDC says its preliminary data on global smartphone shipments for Q3 2026 show a 22% drop compared to Q3 2025, which is in line with other regional and global trends reported recently.

The culprit, as even occasional 9to5Mac readers are likely well aware by now, is the ongoing memory shortage, which has sent component costs soaring and squeezed device manufacturers, particularly those competing in lower-end markets.

According to IDC, Samsung remained atop the ranking with 57.8 million units shipped and a 22.6% share, down 5.8% from the year-ago period. Apple came in second with 57.3 million shipped units, followed by Xiaomi, OPPO, and vivo.

The report shows OPPO seeing the biggest drop among the top five, with shipments down 34.5% year over year, and Apple recording the smallest decline at 4%. This left Apple just 500,000 units behind Samsung, with a gap of only 0.2 percentage points in shipment share.

Commenting on these numbers, Nabila Popal, IDC’s senior research director for Worldwide Devices, said things might get worse before they get better:

“The sharp downturn the industry has been bracing for finally materialized in the third quarter this year, with shipments declining a record 22% YoY. However, the worst is yet to come. […] Current indicators suggest that the market has not yet reached the bottom. Memory costs have surged approximately 350% since last year and are still rising, creating substantial pressure on vendor margins and shipments. While memory inflation is beginning to slow down, with a low double-digit sequential increase in Q3 compared to roughly 50%-100% sequential growth in prior quarters, costs remain elevated across other critical components as well, compounding the crunch.”

Today’s report came just two days after IDC released preliminary results for the Chinese smartphone market, where Apple’s share of shipments increased from 15.8% to 17.8%, despite a 4.3% year-over-year decline in iPhone shipments.

title: GM to close Detroit battery-assembly plant, but not for reasons you might think
snippet: GM is shuttering the Brownstown Battery Assembly Plant, though the closure has nothing to do with the automaker's electrification strategy.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

12:32 PM PDT · October 20, 2026

Image Credits:JEFF KOWALSKY/AFP / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

GM is closing a battery-assembly plant south of Detroit, a spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch.

The Brownstown Battery Assembly Plant assembled battery packs for Cadillac’s flagship EV, the Celestiq, and both electric drive units (the motors that power the car) and battery packs for the Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray, a plug-in hybrid version of its famous sports car. Automotive News first reported the closure.

The closure is not related to GM’s electric vehicle strategy, the spokesperson said. Instead, GM leased the site, and the lease was nearing its end.

The employees and work at Brownstown will be moved to other GM facilities, though the company would not confirm which ones. 

Like many automakers, GM’s electrification strategy was thrown a curveball after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the sweeping federal law signed last year, repealed incentives to produce and sell EVs. 

Since then, the company has pared back its public comments on EVs, though it hasn’t given up on full electrification.

GM continues to produce a range of EVs, including the Chevrolet Silverado EV and the limited-time-only Chevrolet Bolt. It also continues researching new battery chemistries, including lithium-manganese-rich and sodium-ion, and it’s rolling out a new $900 million facility to speed commercialization.

title: Google gives Pixel 9 another year of free Satellite SOS connectivity
snippet: Google won’t start charging for the Satellite SOS feature on its Pixel 9 series phones just yet, despite the timer having run out. more…
fullText:
Google won’t start charging for the Satellite SOS feature on its Pixel 9 series phones just yet, despite the timer having run out.

Satellite SOS was introduced on the Pixel 9 series and has been in place on every Pixel phone released in the time since. The feature grants your phone access to limited satellite connectivity in emergencies, offering a lifeline in dangerous, off-grid situations. 

But Google only promised this would be free for “the first 2 years after activation.”

A support page footnote still reads:

	

Service included at no additional charge for the first 2 years after activation of devices. Available in select countries and languages. Connection and response times vary based on location, site conditions, and other factors.

Everything you should know about Satellite SOS on Pixel 9 before you ever have to use it

As of August 2026, that timer was up for Pixel 9 series devices. Yet, Google showed no signs of charging for the feature, but it wasn’t exactly clear what would happen next. Now, the company has confirmed that, at least for another year, Satellite SOS on Pixel 9 remains free.

The company confirmed the news to PCMag, saying:

Confirming that we’ve extended this offering, at no additional cost, for one additional year. We have no details to share beyond that at this time.

So far, there have been no hints even behind the scenes of Google introducing a way to charge for Satellite SOS on Pixel phones. Apple, which introduced this functionality prior to Google, recently confirmed that it would also be extending the “free trial” of satellite connections for iPhone 14, 15, and 16, and there’s also no word on what Apple might charge for the feature.

Would you pay for Satellite SOS on your Pixel if Google starts charging for it?

title: TikTok accused of profiting from illegal child sexual exploitation videos
snippet: TikTok has been accused of profiting from illegal child sexual exploitation videos posted on its platform. The allegations were made by former and current employees, who say that the company failed to properly respond to internal reports … more…
fullText:
TikTok has been accused of profiting from illegal child sexual exploitation videos posted on its platform. The allegations were made by former and current employees, who say that the company failed to properly respond to internal reports …

NPR reports.

Employees raised the alarm about minors appearing in sexual content on the app, which viewers could pay to access and the company would profit from – a potential financial crime. They also flagged that users under 18 were using loopholes to bypass age-restricted content and to block parents and guardians from reviewing their activity on the app. TikTok also refrained from conducting surveys to assess the ages of its users because it was concerned that it would have to turn the results over to the Federal Trade Commission, the documents show.

Employees say that senior leaders were aware of the issues, but their responses were inadequate. Social media companies are required by law to report suspected CSAM, as well as suspicions regarding money being obtained illegally through their platforms.

The report additionally says concerns were expressed internally about young users being shown content related to suicide and self-harm, and that the platform was not taking proper steps to tackle this.

TikTok is one of the most popular apps on the App Store, with a high proportion of teenage users. The company responded by saying that the claims made in the story are “clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers and used to inaccurately rewrite our history and mislead the public about our commitment to youth safety and how our platform works.”

title: MagSafe Monday: Upgrading to the iPhone Duo? This MagSafe battery was built specifically for it
snippet: With the iPhone Duo bringing an entirely different shape to the iPhone lineup, you’ll need accessories built for it as well. BMX built the SolidSafe Duo specifically around the iPhone Duo. It’s designed to fit perfectly on the back without bleeding over and includes a stand. more…
fullText:
With the iPhone Duo bringing an entirely different shape to the iPhone lineup, you’ll need accessories built for it as well. BMX built the SolidSafe Duo specifically around the iPhone Duo. It’s designed to fit perfectly on the back without bleeding over and includes a stand.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

The reason the SolidSafe Duo fits the iPhone Duo’s proportions is the battery cell itself. In this MagSafe battery, BMX used a custom-made 5,000mAh semi-solid-state cell rather than a standard lithium-ion cell, which gave them the flexibility to build a compact form factor built for the iPhone Duo’s specific dimensions. A standard battery cell wouldn’t have allowed that without the battery overhanging the edges or sacrificing too much on the capacity.

The semi-solid-state battery contains significantly less liquid electrolyte than conventional lithium-ion batteries. With less liquid, there is less flammable material inside the cell, which reduces the fire risk associated with heat, physical damage, or internal short circuits. We’ve all seen enough battery recalls to understand why this is important.

The 360-degree stand

The integrated rotating ring stand is designed around how people will use the iPhone Duo. Portrait mode is for reading and iMessage, and landscape for video, partially folded for hands-free calls. The stand rotates 360 degrees and stays attached as the phone’s position changes, so you don’t have to remove the battery pack every time you shift how you’re holding the iPhone Duo.

Charging speeds and the built-in cable

The SolidSafe Duo battery charges your iPhone Duo at up to 15 watts per MagSafe or up to 20 watts through the attached USB-C lanyard cable. The cable stays with the power bank, which means no separate charging cable to pack or lose track of. It also handles input of up to 15 watts via that same cable to recharge it.

A full-color LCD on the battery displays remaining battery capacity and live charging wattage simultaneously, so you can see both how much power you have left and how fast it’s actually charging.

Wrap up on the SolidSafe Duo battery

The SolidSafe Duo is priced at a premium over generic/budget MagSafe battery packs, but with the iPhone Duo, you’ll want to have accessories designed specifically for it to maximize its value, so it’s worth a look. It’s likely that less expensive batteries will be launched in the coming months, but if you want one at launch, this looks like a solid option.

You can pick up the new SolidSafe Duo from Amazon or directly from BMX.

title: Google updates Android earthquake alerts with more info, expands to 200+ regions
snippet: Google is delivering an update to Android’s earthquake alerts system that will show more information while also expanding support to over 200 regions across the globe. more…
fullText:
Google is delivering an update to Android’s earthquake alerts system that will show more information while also expanding support to over 200 regions across the globe.

Launched in 2021, Android’s earthquake alerts system uses the sensors in Android smartphones to detect the earliest signs of an earthquake and provide a precious few seconds of warning prior to destructive impacts. While the system has had a couple of mishaps, it has also saved lives and Google says it has sent over a billion alerts. 

Effective today, the Android earthquake alerts system is now live in more than 200 regions across the globe, up from 98 previously. Google specifically calls out Panama and Guatemala as new additions. 

Beyond the regional expansion, Google is also updating the design of earthquake alerts. Specifically, the “Be Ready” step is going to offer more information on the location of the earthquake’s epicenter and the estimated magnitude.

	

Google says:

Be Aware: A straightforward alert for estimated light shaking, letting you know an earthquake has been detected nearby.

Be Ready: A detailed alert for stronger shaking, alerting you to prepare to take action.

Take Action: A full-screen alert for moderate to heavy shaking, giving you immediate advice on how to stay safe.

We’ve built-out our Be Ready alert with new helpful guidance. In the coming months, you’ll see a map with a radius of where we’ve detected shaking, estimated earthquake magnitude, action you can take, and a button to learn more about the earthquake as information comes in.

title: Samsung reportedly hasn’t finalized Galaxy S27 details, considers February launch
snippet: It would be “February at the latest,” but Samsung has yet to set a launch date under pressure to finalize component details for the Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra. more…
fullText:
It would be “February at the latest,” but Samsung has yet to set a launch date under pressure to finalize component details for the Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra.

Samsung’s launch schedule has been laid on the same path for years, with minor deviations here and there. The newest Galaxy S device gets released in January or February every year, right after CES and before MWC comes around.

According to a leak by Lanzuk on Naver, Samsung has set the Galaxy S27 series launch date on the fence. The laker says that, at the latest, Samsung would be looking at a February launch, so it’s not an expansive gap between releases that we might be looking at. If Samsung settles on January, even better.

The possible push may be due to Samsung reportedly not having finalized the full component list for the Galaxy S27 series. More specifically, the Galaxy S27 Pro and Galaxy S27 Ultra. The base and Plus models are essentially finished, if this leak is reliable.

	

The post credits RAMageddon for the timing adjustment. It notes “there are differing opinions regarding the composition and ratio” of the devices. Read straightforwardly, it implies Samsung hasn’t decided how much memory to inject into the two most expensive devices in this lineup.

A potential storage standard upgrade to UFS 5.0 seems to be the biggest contributor to the Galaxy S27’s undecided launch timing. LPDDR6 is also a costly addition, and incorporating UFS 5.0 on these models means they need the hardware to perform, given they both sit at a price point that seems to fluctuate from high to higher.

There’s no concrete timing, and even Samsung has yet to set the date. Still, it looks like it’s highly unlikely Samsung will make any last-minute changes as big as swapping phone models, like last year.

fullText:
You probably shoudn’t buy a Googlebook. That’s less of an opinion about the platform itself, but more about the bad timing that this launch has seen, and protecting your own wallet.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

Googlebook as a platform isn’t magically a competitor to Windows and macOS. Rather, it inhabits nearly the exact same space in the market that Chromebook did. The app gap hasn’t been fixed, nor has Google managed to build a platform that someone can go without the deep ecosystems that the dominant players have built out for decades.

If a Chromebook wasn’t for you, Googlebook isn’t either

Googlebook OS review: A post-smartphone PC, if Google can keep it

There are any number of reasons I could give you not to buy a Googlebook right now. The price tags. The lack of apps. The simple fact that this is a brand new platform you shouldn’t fork over hundreds of dollars to beta test. But, ultimately, I think the biggest reason you shouldn’t be buying a Googlebook is timing.

	

RAMageddon is in full swing, thanks in no small part to Google and its AI competitors, and consumers are paying the price for it. Everything has gotten extraordinarily expensive, and it’s not slowing down anytime soon. Price hikes will continue, and you’re only going to feel the strain more and more. 

With that in mind, why would anyone spend their money on a Googlebook?

That’s really what I’ve been wrestling with the past few weeks in the midst of Google’s big push. Googlebook is asking you to spent $1,000, give or take, on a laptop that’s not fully capable because… it works with your phone? Truly, I just cannot fathom making that choice when you could pay the same, if not less, for a Windows laptop or a MacBook.

From my HP Googlebook 14 review earlier this week:

Especially at a time when the cost of laptops continues to skyrocket, I cannot recommend that anyone invests $1,200 into a Googlebook when you can get a Windows laptop, or even a MacBook, for the same price, if not less. There’s simply no reason to get less functionality for the same price…

Imagine a scenario. You spend $1,000 or more on a Googlebook today because, right now, it fits your needs. You could have bought a MacBook Air for just a little more, or a Lenovo laptop for a little less. But you reason that, for now, the Googlebook does everything you need it to do. But, six months from now, you pick up a new hobby, change jobs, or have any number of things change that impact what you need from your tech. Suddenly, that Googlebook might not cut it. The problems Googlebook has today are not going to be solved in six months; many, if not all, of the limitations you face today will still exist.

That’s my reasoning for why I won’t buy a Googlebook. What do you think?

fullText:
We have all watched AI assistants become a permanent fixture on our phones over the last few months, yet finding one that genuinely takes everyday chores off your plate is still surprisingly rare. Most general-purpose AI chatbots are great if you want to brainstorm ideas or summarize an article, but they hit a wall when it comes to practical, real-world tasks like managing your personal finances. 

You can describe a theoretical budget to a standard chatbot and get plenty of generic feedback, yet that chatbot cannot keep an eye on your live accounts, start a bill negotiation, or cancel a subscription for you.

That gap between talking and doing is exactly why Rocket Money built Rowan. Designed as an AI-powered personal financial assistant that lives right in your text messages, Rowan proactively watches your money, looks after your budgeting and finances, and does the actual legwork to help save you money so you don’t have to.

When evaluating any new AI tool, the biggest question is what happens behind the scenes after you send a prompt. Most AI assistants can only talk about your money, whereas Rowan is directly connected to your finances and built to take action.

	

Just as importantly, Rowan isn’t a standalone experiment from a brand-new company trying to figure out personal finance on the fly. Rowan has Rocket Money behind it, meaning it runs on the exact same platform that more than 10 million members already use every day. When you ask Rowan to help lower a bill or drop a recurring service, it taps directly into the established subscription cancelation and bill negotiation operations that Rocket Money has been running for years.

It also brings that capability to you without asking you to build a brand-new habit. Because Rowan lives entirely in your text messages, there is no new app to download and no complicated interface to learn. Rowan doesn’t replace the main Rocket Money mobile app, either; instead, it serves as an additional, conversational way to use Rocket Money straight from the messaging inbox you already check throughout the day.

A proactive partner that reaches out first

Most personal finance tools are passive by design, waiting silently on your phone until you remember to open them up and dig through your recent activity. Rowan flips that dynamic by reaching out to you first whenever something in your accounts needs your attention.

On a regular basis, Rowan texts you a weekly spending summary that provides updates on your recent finances and budgeting, complete with a detailed breakdown of where your money went and a heads-up on any areas of concern. In between those weekly check-ins, Rowan keeps a close watch on your day-to-day activity. It texts you automatically when an account balance is getting low, alerts you the moment a new subscription is detected on your statements, and lets you know when prices are increasing on your existing recurring bills.

Because it lives in your texts, checking in on your money becomes a natural two-way conversation. Whenever a question pops into your head, you can text Rowan to get instant financial updates. You can quickly categorize recent transactions right through text, ask about cancelable subscriptions you might want to clear out, or ask how much money is genuinely safe to spend right now based on your current income and upcoming expenses.

Offload financial chores with a quick text

Getting an alert about a price increase or a forgotten subscription is helpful, but Rowan’s real value shows up when you ask it to take things off your plate. Rowan can start work on your behalf so that the only thing you have to do is send a text.

If you spot a recurring service you no longer want, you can simply text Rowan to cancel that subscription. If a monthly service bill is creeping upward, you can text Rowan to start a bill negotiation on your behalf. Of course, because canceling subscriptions and negotiating bills requires coordinating with providers behind the scenes, these actions don’t happen instantly. Rather, your text kicks off the workflow so Rocket Money can step in and handle the follow-through for you. For everyday organization, you can even text Rowan to set a financial reminder, such as asking it to remind you to pay your credit card on the 15th, keeping your monthly routine on track without cluttering up your calendar.

Pricing and how to get Rowan

Available to users in the United States, the core Rocket Money app is free to download and comes with free basic features, including balance alerts, subscription management, spend tracking, basic budgeting, and bill negotiation. To unlock everything the standard app can do for your finances, you can upgrade to Rocket Money Premium, which uses a “pay what you think is fair” approach currently set between $7 and $14 a month.

Rowan is not part of the free app or the standard Premium tier. To get access to Rowan, you will need to subscribe to Rocket Money Premium+, a separate plan available for a flat $15 per month. Upgrading to Premium+ gives you everything included in Rocket Money Premium, plus full access to Rowan right in your text messages.

title: XREAL 1 Pro+ has exactly the right hardware upgrades at the same $599 price
snippet: Ahead of its Android XR-based Aura launching later this year, XREAL is giving its flagship One Pro a “Plus” upgrade without raising the price. more…
fullText:
Ahead of its Android XR-based Aura launching later this year, XREAL is giving its flagship One Pro a “Plus” upgrade without raising the price.

XREAL 1 Pro+ delivers upgrades that, after my experience with the existing generation, are exactly what I would have picked as pain points to address. 

That starts with the display itself. XREAL is nearly doubling the brightness of the display to 1,200 nits as well as introducing AI-powered HDR. While the 700-nit brightness of the older model was plenty bright in dark environments, I did find that it had trouble holding up, say, if my neighbors on a flight decided to have the window open. The display gets dedicated “Standard,” “Movie,” and “Reading” modes, too, to tailor the display to what the user is doing. 3D conversion also now supports 60Hz, up from the previous 30Hz limit. 

	

The biggest physical upgrade is to the nose pads, which now have a larger air cushion design that, in practice, is a major improvement in regards to wearability. XREAL One Pro often got a bit uncomfortable on my nose after a few hours, but this upgrade makes it a whole lot better. 

XREAL 1 Pro+ is available starting today for $599, keeping the same price as the existing model.

title: ChatGPT now lets you lock your chats
snippet: The company says the feature is designed for situations where users might be discussing something personal or planning a surprise and want to keep those conversations private when handing their device to friends or family to show them something in another chat.
fullText:
OpenAI announced on Tuesday that users can now lock ChatGPT conversations to keep sensitive chats private when others may have access to their screen or device. Users can secure their locked chats with a four-digit PIN, or use Face ID or Touch ID on supported devices. 

Unlike the app’s Temporary Chats, which provide a separate session that doesn’t appear in chat history, users can return to Locked Chats at any time.

The company says the feature is designed for situations where users might be discussing something personal or planning a surprise and want to keep those conversations private when handing their device to friends or family to show them something in another chat. 

The addition of locked chats adds a new layer of privacy to ChatGPT, as the app is increasingly used for personal conversations. Of course, while locking a chat can limit access, it doesn’t address concerns about how sensitive information is stored or handled.

OpenAI notes that locking a chat doesn’t create end-to-end encryption or a separate encrypted vault, change how long it retains the chat, remove information that ChatGPT remembered before a chat was locked, or change the “Improve the model for everyone” setting.

Once users lock a chat, it moves to a dedicated “Locked Chats” section, where it’s kept separate from regular chat history, pinned conversations, and chat search results. 

With Memory enabled, Locked Chats has its own separate memory shared across conversations within the section. New messages sent after locking a chat can update that memory but don’t update regular Memory. That means new information from locked chats won’t leak into regular chats.

OpenAI says resetting a PIN permanently deletes all locked chats, files, and other content protected by the previous PIN.

Additionally, the Locked Chats option isn’t available for temporary chats, archived chats, group chats, chats created from a shared link, chats with scheduled tasks, and chats with meeting recordings.

Locked Chats will be available to users on ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans. The company notes that the feature is not available on ChatGPT for Healthcare. The feature is starting to roll out on Tuesday, so it may not be live yet for all users.

title: Google Home bug turns your smart home device list into a mess
snippet: A bug in the Google Home app has left device lists messy for some users, with no obvious way to fix it for the time being. more…
fullText:
A bug in the Google Home app has left device lists messy for some users, with no obvious way to fix it for the time being.

Over the past week, a number of users have run into a problem in the Google Home app that turns the device list into nothing but clutter. 

The way the Google Home app’s “All Devices” page is supposed to work is by grouping linked devices into their assigned rooms, and then show anything that’s not assigned in a room to a generic “Linked to you” section.

That section is the problem right now. Users have found for roughly a week, and we’re seeing the same behavior, that Google Home is listing all of their devices under the “Linked to you” section, whether they’re assigned to a room or not, resulting in a bunch of extra clutter and making it nearly impossible to track down any devices you hadn’t assigned to rooms.

	

“Linked to you” isn’t supposed to include devices already in your room groups
	

This is almost certainly a bug and not an intentional change, but there seems to be no way to fix it at this point, as devices in the list still show their assigned room groupings in the settings menu.

Meanwhile, Google has so far only acknowledged the issue in recommending that affected users reach out to support. 

New Google Home app updates tend to roll out every few weeks, so it’s very possible a patch will clean up this mess sometime soon. Let us know in the comments if you’re running into this problem.

title: SpaceX and Tesla boards form special committees to review merger
snippet: Elon Musk likes the idea but says he is not on either committee, which is made up of independent directors.
fullText:
The boards of SpaceX and Tesla have each formed special committees to review a possible merger. The special committees, which consist of independent directors, were created at the request of shareholders, according to Elon Musk, CEO and the largest individual shareholder of both companies. 

“Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees, so it’s this sort of a … It’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking, and I can’t be in the conversation,” Musk said in response to a question during SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call.

Musk didn’t name the members of these special committees, only noting that they were independent directors. Tesla has seven independent board members under Nasdaq’s listing standards, including board chair Robyn Denholm; Ira Ehrenpreis, who is also a committee chair; former Tesla CTO JB Straubel; Joe Gebbia; Jack Hartung; James Murdoch; and Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, according to the company’s October 19 proxy filing.

Neither Musk nor his brother Kimbal Musk is independent. Denholm, Gebbia, Ehrenpreis, Hartung, Murdoch, and Wilson-Thompson sit on a variety of established committees overseeing audit, compensation, and corporate governance.

SpaceX lists six independent directors, including Ehrenpreis, who is also the chair of the company’s compensation and nominating committee. Randy Glein, Donald Harrison, Steve Jurvetson, Luke Nosek, and Roelof Botha are also considered independent directors.

Antonio Gracias, Musk, and SpaceX president and chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell are also on the board, but not considered independent. Gracias, who once sat on Tesla’s board, founded and leads Valor Equity Partners, which has a 3.4% stake in SpaceX. Gracias’ firm also financed SpaceX’s AI hardware purchases through leaseback arrangements.

Musk said he supports the idea of the merger but cautioned that it is not a guaranteed outcome.

“I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla Motor is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” he said, adding that he thinks it would be a good idea. “At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this.”

The special committees have not reached agreement on the terms of any transactions, he said. 

The SpaceX IPO cemented Musk’s grip on the company — he has more than 50% voting power — which would make it easier to garner support for a merger from SpaceX shareholders. It is a much bigger hurdle over at Tesla, where the company would need a 50% vote from all shareholders, not just those who vote, Musk noted. 

“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity,” Musk said, adding there was a lot to be gaining from cooperating on developing AI software, robotics, SpaceX’s orbital AI data center project Starmind, and Terafab, the joint chip manufacturing project between Tesla and SpaceX.

title: Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook could debut on November 6: Here’s what to expect
snippet: After over a decade of not adopting touch displays on its Mac notebook lineup, Apple will finally be releasing its first touchscreen MacBook as early as November 6th, after announcing it as early as October 27th. more…
fullText:
After over a decade of not adopting touch displays on its Mac notebook lineup, Apple will finally be releasing its first touchscreen MacBook as early as November 6th, after announcing it as early as October 27th.

Of course, rumors are rumors – though essentially every reputable source has aligned on the idea of the MacBook Pro gaining support for touch very shortly. Apple even left a few hints in macOS 27: Touch Support in Sidecar, pull to refresh support, and slightly bigger menu bar items.

One could call all of this a mere coincidence, but it’s probably exactly what it looks like. Regardless, here’s what the first touchscreen MacBook will have to offer.

OLED, Dynamic Island

On the display panel side of things, the redesigned MacBook Pro will come with a Tandem OLED display. This will be similar to the iPad Pro, which is often touted as one of the best mobile displays on the market. Tandem OLED comprises of stacked OLED panels, which allows for incredible colors, strong contrast, and increased brightness.

Reports also suggest it’ll come with a Dynamic Island, and it’ll be a bit smaller than the one on the iPhone. It won’t, however, come with support for Face ID.

Software optimizations

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple will have some special optimizations for the first touchscreen MacBook Pro, beyond what’s already visible in the betas of macOS 27:

“For instance, if users touch a button or control, the interface will bring up a new type of menu surrounding their finger that provides more relevant options for touch commands.

The software will also display the most appropriate set of controls based on users’ prior interaction. And if a person taps an item in the menu bar at the top of the screen, the set of controls will enlarge to be more easily selectable with a finger.”

M5 Pro and M5 Max chips

Despite initial reporting suggesting that we’ll be seeing the debut of the M6 Pro and Max in the redesigned MacBook Pro, Apple is now skipping the release of those chips to accelerate the M7. This means that the first iteration of 2nm chips won’t be making their way to the redesigned MacBook Pros, and they’ll instead offer the existing M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

There won’t be a base model version of this computer quite yet, though rumors suggest that Apple will be launching a base version of the redesigned MacBook Pro with an M7 chip as early as next spring.

Slightly thinner chassis, significantly lighter

One design rumor for the new MacBook Pro is the fact that it’ll be slightly slimmer and lighter – though it’s unclear how meaningful this will be. The last MacBook Pro iteration made the computers look and feel quite chunky, so a bit of progress here would likely be welcome – so long as it doesn’t come at the compromise of thermals.

Bloomberg has also reported that these computers will be ‘significantly lighter,’ thanks to re-engineering of internal components.

Release date

	

According to the Power On newsletter, Apple will potentially release these new MacBook Pro models on November 6th, making a straight four weeks of new Apple launches with iPhone Duo, HomePod mini 2, the new MacBook Pro, and HomeView + Apple TV 4K. 

As of now, there’s no Apple release scheduled for November 6th, so it would make sense to be the new MacBook Pro:

Now, I have a little more to share: Apple is planning to hold a “reset” at its retail stores on the evening of Thursday, Nov. 5, into Friday, Nov. 6, that implies new signage and products will be placed on store tables. Given that this Friday is a week after the Mac announcements (when Apple would typically release products), it would make sense that this is the date when at least some of the new items become available to customers.

title: Google Phone app beta rolls out Contacts bottom bar tab [U]
snippet: Last year’s Material 3 Expressive redesign of the Phone by Google app removed the Contacts tab, but it’s now coming back. more…
fullText:
Last year’s Material 3 Expressive redesign of the Phone by Google app removed the Contacts tab, but it’s now coming back.

title: Walmart’s $60 Google TV streamer might be the only good deal left in streaming
snippet: As prices skyrocket on virtually everything else, Walmart’s $60 Onn 4K Pro streamer with Google TV might be the only good deal left — if you can find it in stock. more…
fullText:
As prices skyrocket on virtually everything else, Walmart’s $60 Onn 4K Pro streamer with Google TV might be the only good deal left — if you can find it in stock.

Prices on streaming hardware have exploded in recent months. Just a few examples include:

Google TV Streamer: Was $99, now $149

Apple TV 4K: Was $129, now $299 (new model)

Nvidia Shield TV Pro: Was $199, now $299

Roku Ultra: Was $100, now $150

It’s rough out there folks. AI is totally worth it, right?

Anyway, all of those price hikes have had me revisiting the Walmart Onn 4K Pro that launched earlier this year and that I’ve been using in one of the rooms in my house for the past few months. Put simply, it gets the job done very well, and is a tremendous deal compared to everything around it.

	

The most direct comparison to the Onn 4K Pro is the Google TV Streamer, and they are pretty close across the board. They have virtually identical software, though Google’s first-party release obviously gets updates and new features a bit quicker. Performance is also nearly identical, with the only big difference being 4GB of RAM in Google’s streamer vs 3GB in Walmart’s. Most of the time, it doesn’t matter.

Walmart’s streamer continues to be a good performer day-in and day-out, and there are little things I actually prefer over Google’s. Topping that list would be the remote, which is a bit more comfortable and backlit, the latter being invaluable in a dark room at night. I could do without the slightly obnoxious “Free TV” button, but I’m overall quite happy with the remote, and even more so with the find remote button on top of the actual streaming box.

					

Google TV on a speedy set-top box with solid hardware and a good remote, all for $60. It’s the best deal in streaming, enough said!

					

				

Pros

				

											

Enough horsepower for speedy Google TV performance

											

Comfortable, backlit remote

											

Plenty of ports

									

			

					

				

Cons

				

											

Hard to find in stock

											

Fabric is hard to clean if it gets dirty

									

			

			

The hardware itself is unassuming with a fabric top and a footprint similar to any other streaming box. That fabric top won’t be a problem for most but, crazy tip, don’t spill anything on it! It’s basically impossible to clean if it gets dirty.

As far as ports go, you’ve got HDMI, Ethernet, full-size USB-A, and the whole thing draws power from USB-C instead of a barrel plug like the last generation — dreams do come true!

	

All of that comes together for just $60. It’s nothing ground-breaking, sure, but this is just a good streamer in every meaningful way without costing an arm and a leg like virtually everything else does right now. The biggest headache is just finding the thing in stock. We’ve been tracking stock for months and, finally, Walmart seems to be more consistently selling Onn 4K Pro both in stores and online, but your results may still vary depending on when you go to buy and where you live. 

Onn 4K Pro at Walmart

If you can’t find the Pro, Walmart also has its Onn 4K Plus dongle that costs just $50 and, in most ways, matches up with the Pro. The main things you’re giving up are the Ethernet port, USB-A port, and a bit of performance. 

What do you think of Onn 4K Pro? Have you tried one? Have you been able to find it in stock? Sound off in the comments!

snippet: Eric Schmidt’s fortune is about to get even bigger.
fullText:
In Brief

10:55 AM PDT · October 20, 2026

Image Credits:Eva Marie Uzcategui/Bloomberg / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Eric Schmidt’s fortune is about to get even bigger. The former Google CEO is reported to own about 1% of Anthropic after investing tens of millions of dollars in the leading AI lab’s Series A round in 2021, per Bloomberg. The startup was valued at $461 million at the time, according to PitchBook data.

If Bloomberg’s estimate is accurate, Schmidt’s stake is remarkably large compared with the 2% of the company that co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei holds. Anthropic is widely expected to go public before the end of the year, with top-end market estimates valuing the company at as much as $2 trillion. At that valuation, Schmidt would add as much as $20 billion to his net worth, which Bloomberg currently puts at $57.5 billion.

Schmidt has been an active tech investor since stepping down as Google CEO in 2011. He deploys capital through multiple entities, including Tomorrow Ventures, Innovation Endeavors Management, and his family office, Hillspire. His other AI bets include Mistral, General Intuition, and Reflection AI.

Schmidt and Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to our request for comment.

title: Apple still makes it too hard for Apple Pay competitors to emerge, says UK
snippet: Apple still makes it too hard for third-party developers to launch alternatives to Apple Pay, despite loosening its grip on access to the NFC chip embedded in iPhones. That’s the claim made by the UK’s antitrust watchdog, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA). The CMA says developers have reported that the compromise terms offered by Apple still don’t make it practical to develop competitors to Apple Pay … more…
fullText:
Apple still makes it too hard for third-party developers to launch alternatives to Apple Pay, despite loosening its grip on access to the NFC chip embedded in iPhones. That’s the claim made by the UK’s antitrust watchdog, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA).

The CMA says developers have reported that the compromise terms offered by Apple still don’t make it practical to develop competitors to Apple Pay …

When Apple first started embedding an NFC chip in iPhones to enable contactless payment, only the Apple Wallet app could take advantage of this. Third-party apps could use the NFC chip for other purposes, but not for card payments.

That saw the iPhone maker facing antitrust action in multiple countries around the world. In a number of them, it’s been forced to unlock access to the chip, most notably in the EU.

In EU countries, developers can request an entitlement to get access by proving to Apple that they meet the industry standards and hold the licenses needed to process consumer payments. No fees are payable. Users are then allowed to choose the default wallet app that appears when they double-click the side button or hold their phone near a payment terminal. 

In the UK, however, the CMA told Reuters that Apple hasn’t offered developers the same terms. 

CMA Chief Executive Sarah Cardell said […] “We have ​heard that high fees, strict terms, and technical restrictions relating to Apple’s contactless technology make it too difficult for challengers to innovate and compete.”

	

Accordingly, the regulator has opened a public consultation on its proposed loosening of Apple’s grip on the contactless payment chip. Apple has responded by rejecting the proposal, but saying that it will continue to work with the CMA.

“We do ⁠not ​believe the CMA should require Apple to adopt an ​approach with lower privacy and security protections. We will continue to engage constructively to reach an outcome ​that is in the best interest of our users.”

9to5Mac’s Take

I see this very much like third-party app stores. While I understand Apple’s position, the company is ultimately likely to lose these battles and is showing no sign of skating to where the regulatory puck is headed.

It seems a needless battle given that the commercial risk to Apple is very limited – the vast majority of iPhone owners are exceedingly unlikely to change the defaults for either app store or wallet app when given the choice.

iOS 27.2 will bring Apple Pencil support to iPhone Duo very soon

When Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo in September, it said Apple Pencil support was coming “later this year.”

Max Weinbach shared on X that support is available in the iOS 27.2 RC.

So if you have an Apple Pencil Pro or standard Pencil, you’ll need to buy the USB-C model which works with most iPads and also the iPhone Duo. It’s currently on sale for $69 on Amazon.

If you’re running the iOS 27.2 RC, you’ll get Pencil support on day one this Friday. But if you want to stick with Apple’s public software releases, iOS 27.2 is expected to launch on or around Monday, October 26.
