title: Not upgrading to iPhone 18 Pro or Duo? Here’s what’s coming next year
snippet: iPhone Duo preorders just begun, and iPhone 18 Pro has been on the market for about a month. Of course, iPhone Duo is backordered through January right now, so whether or not you’re considering buying these phones – it makes it really easy to think about what’s coming next. more…
fullText:
iPhone Duo preorders just begun, and iPhone 18 Pro has been on the market for about a month. Of course, iPhone Duo is backordered through January right now, so whether or not you’re considering buying these phones – it makes it really easy to think about what’s coming next.

2027 is going to be a relatively big iPhone release year for Apple. First, the company will be continuing the iPhone 18 lineup after it introduced a split release schedule last month. Then, in the fall, the company will debut a new round of flagships in celebration of the 20th anniversary of the iPhone. Here’s what to expect.

Spring 2027

iPhone 18

For the first time, Apple will be introducing its base iPhone in the spring. Upgrades for the iPhone 18 aren’t quite clear, though more RAM is one of the key rumors. Thermal upgrades will likely happen as well, as well as the new Apple C2 modem.

It’s possible Apple will update the design to fall more in line with the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro, though we don’t yet know.

This phone will of course equip the A20 chip, and it’ll probably start at the same $899 price point that iPhone 17 currently sits at – after it was increased from $799 last month.

iPhone 18e

This phone will most likely just end up being a chip bump from the A19 to A20 chip, and debut in the Spring alongside the iPhone 18. Earlier this year, reports indicated that Apple would share many components between the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e, though it isn’t quite clear what that could mean for the devices.

iPhone Air 2

Out of all of the spring iPhone releases, this one is the one to look forward to. After receiving a lukewarm reception with the initial iPhone Air model, Apple went back to the drawing board and decided to modify the design to fit an ultrawide camera into the device. This meant the phone couldn’t be released last month.

Personally, I don’t think an ultrawide camera is too important – though many people will see one camera on the back of the phone and immediately assume it’s less premium, so it’ll probably end up being an important upgrade for the sake of sales. Plus, ultrawide photos can be fun at times.

While not confirmed, I wouldn’t be surprised if it integrates a smaller Dynamic Island, similar to iPhone 18 Pro. iPhone Air 2 will likely also jump from Apples C1X modem to the C2.

It should also have a larger battery, reportedly as large as 3500mAh. That’s a roughly 10% improvement from the original iPhone Air.

Fall 2027

iPhone 20 Pro

For the 20th anniversary of the iPhone, Apple is expected to debut a fully redesigned iPhone to celebrate. It’ll reportedly be much more glassy, feature significantly slimmer bezels, and ditch the flat edge design of the iPhone 12 and later. It should also offer a much smaller Dynamic Island, likely with a hole punch selfie camera and under-display Face ID.

Personally, I’m slightly skeptical that this’ll truly be a replacement to the “Pro” phone for thermal reasons, but time will tell. iPhone Duo seemingly has strong thermals while not featuring an aluminum unibody, so my concern might not be relevant. It’ll offer two, larger display sizes: 6.4-inch and 7-inch. This largely comes from the bezel reduction.

	

If you’re holding out for iPhone 18 Pro, this “iPhone 20” is definitely the phone to wait out for.

iPhone Duo 2

Lastly, Apple will release a successor to its just-announced iPhone Duo next fall. There aren’t many substantial rumors for this phone, though one could hope Face ID and better cameras are in the pipeline. Of course, you can expect next-generation Apple Silicon with the A21 Pro chip next year.

title: Apple blocks web certificates that could be used by scammers, but Mac vulnerability remains
snippet: Apple has blocked eight web security certificates that could have been used by scammers to impersonate legitimate websites. However, one cryptography engineer has warned that Macs may continue to trust the compromised certificates because macOS does not check for revocation … more…
fullText:
Apple has blocked eight web security certificates that could have been used by scammers to impersonate legitimate websites.

However, one cryptography engineer has warned that Macs may continue to trust the compromised certificates because macOS does not check for revocation … 

The issue concerns what are known as intermediate certificates. These are used to prove ownership of a website, so if you visit apple.com, for example, Safari will check that you are visiting the real site.

However, an error in a script used to generate these certificates led to a number of private keys that could be trivially discovered by testing just 256 possible numbers. The eight compromised certificates have now been revoked, and steps taken to ensure that the vulnerability won’t affect any future certificates issued.

Bleeping Computer reports that Apple, Google and Mozilla have each blocked the compromised certificates in their respective web browsers. However, Mozilla cryptography engineer Dennis Jackson warns that Macs may continue to trust them.

Jackson also warns that macOS’s built-in /usr/bin/curl utility may continue trusting the compromised certificates because its certificate bundle does not check revocation information.

In other words, if your Mac has already accepted one of the certificates, then it will continue to do so. However, there is currently no evidence of them being used in the wild, and it’s something that Apple is likely to be able to fix in an upcoming security update.

title: Sony just canceled a promised Android 17 update for one of its Xperia phones
snippet: Sony isn’t exactly known for speedy Android OS updates, but the company has now completely canceled an Android 17 update for one of its Xperia phones. more…
fullText:
Sony isn’t exactly known for speedy Android OS updates, but the company has now completely canceled an Android 17 update for one of its Xperia phones.

In a notice on its website, Sony says that it will not provide an Android 17 update to the Xperia 10 VI despite initially promising “three Android OS upgrades” for the device. 

Sony announced the Xperia 10 VI in 2024 as an upper-mid-range device. It has a Snapdragon 6 Gen 1 chipset, 8GB of RAM, and 128GB of storage, with Android 14 having been pre-installed at launch. Android 17 was the last promised update even though it wasn’t included in the initial roadmap Sony posted in September. 

The company says that Xperia 10 VI “does not support an Android 17 upgrade experience that we consider adequate” due to a “limitation” related to the phone’s storage. The exact reason isn’t entirely clear, but Sony says security updates will continue on as promised, and that other Xperia devices due to get Android 17 will no be affected.

	

Sony explains:

We announced at launch that the Xperia 10 VI would receive three Android OS upgrades. However, after a detailed technical assessment, we determined that due to limitations related to the device’s storage configuration, the Xperia 10 VI does not support an Android 17 upgrade experience that we consider adequate. Accordingly, we have decided not to make this upgrade available. We recognise that this falls short of our original announcement, and we wish to apologise for this change.

On the other hand, our security update commitment remains unchanged. Sony will continue to provide security updates for four years from the product’s launch date, as previously communicated.

This issue is specific to Xperia 10 VI’s technical specifications and will not impact other Xperia models.

It’s certainly an odd situation, and one that we don’t often see. While it’s not uncommon for Android phones to not be promised as many updates as they should recieve, it’s rare for a promised software update to be canceled outright.

title: Report: Apple gains ground on rivals, but iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo face challenges
snippet: In a new investor note sent out this week, GF Securities’ Jeff Pu and Henry Huang project that Apple will be the only major smartphone manufacturer to grow shipments in 2026, even as the global market is expected to shrink by more than 14%. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a new investor note sent out this week, GF Securities’ Jeff Pu and Henry Huang project that Apple will be the only major smartphone manufacturer to grow shipments in 2026, even as the global market is expected to shrink by more than 14%. Here are the details.

Apple bucks smartphone market downturn

For the past few weeks, several reports from IDC and Counterpoint Research have been mapping out the impact of rising memory costs on smartphone sales.

And while the numbers may vary slightly, it is increasingly clear that Apple has been able to weather the downturn better than its competitors.

This week, Pu and Huang released a new investor note reinforcing that trend, projecting that Apple will gain significant market share in 2026 as most of its major competitors see shipments decline.

According to the report, Apple is on track to close out 2026 as the only major smartphone manufacturer to increase shipments, with a projected 4% year-over-year gain to 257 million units.

That would keep Apple ahead of Samsung, which is expected to ship 241 million smartphones, essentially unchanged from 2025. Apple also topped the rankings in 2024 and 2025.

Apple’s share of global smartphone shipments is also projected to climb to 24% in 2026, compared to 20% in 2025 and 19% in 2024.

Market-wide, the report projects a 14.2% drop in total shipments to 1.08 billion shipped smartphones for 2026, and further pegs 2026-2027 as “one of the most challenging periods for the industry, driven primarily by sharply higher memory prices, which have already pushed OEMs to reduce shipments and raise device prices.”

Back to Apple, the report reiterates that the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max have received a relatively lukewarm reception, which the analysts partly attribute to competition from the iPhone Duo and criticism of their weight. The analysts also cite production constraints affecting both the iPhone Duo and the iPhone 18 Pro lineup:

Due to hinge constraints, we are reducing the iPhone Duo EMS build plan from 7m to 6m units in 2026. We also lower the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max build plan to 72m units given the constraints associated with the adjustable‑aperture camera.

The iPhone Duo went up for pre-order earlier today and is already showing delivery estimates stretching into late January in the US and even further in other countries.

With all of that in mind, the report maintained its “Hold” rating on Apple stock, with a price target of $369. Apple shares closed at $343.46, up 0.43% on the day, making it the only major tech stock to finish in the green amid the ongoing sector-wide sell-off.

With shipping dates slipping well into next year, scalpers on eBay and X are already looking to cash in, with asking prices reaching as high as $10,000.

title: Meet the TechPulse App: News and Video, Created and Curated by Real People
snippet: CNET is partnering with sister sites PCMag, Mashable, ZDNET and others on an all-new app with news, reviews and videos. Our trusted expertise is a free download away.
fullText:
Earlier this year, we relaunched CNET’s tech news team and now we’re releasing an app to make news even bigger and more accessible. I’m excited to announce TechPulse, which replaces the venerable CNET app with an all-new experience. Our goal is to satisfy your thirst for real tech journalism.

We are a primary source for not only breaking tech news, but also videos, reviews, live events, commentaries and more. The new app integrates that content from CNET, as well as from other brands owned by our parent company Ziff Davis, including PCMag, Mashable, ZDNET and Lifehacker. 

Unlike the mindless feeds on other apps driven by a robot algorithm, the main page you’ll see on TechPulse is curated by a human (you!). Its customizable dashboard lets you choose exactly what your TechPulse feed includes. 

Only interested in content from CNET? No problem; our powerful filters let you specify the brands you want to see. You can add or remove PCMag, Mashable and others quickly and easily. 

Only want to see videos? TechPulse lets you filter out the written articles. Only want writing because you don’t care about video? We can do that, too.

The result is less noise, more news.

We developed TechPulse from the ground up based on consumer research. Earlier this year I commissioned a study to find out what CNET readers want from news coverage. We found that folks trust news reports and videos backed by hands-on testing and reviews. Tech fans are fed up with misinformation, complexity and wishy-washy advice. 

If you are too, I encourage you to head to the Apple App Store or Google Play Store to download TechPulse today.

title: iPhone Duo walk-in purchases might be challenging at launch, per report
snippet: According to a new report from MacRumors, Apple employees are being told to warn customers that iPhone Duo likely won’t be available for purchase on launch day if you didn’t already place a pre-order. more…
fullText:
According to a new report from MacRumors, Apple employees are being told to warn customers that iPhone Duo likely won’t be available for purchase on launch day if you didn’t already place a pre-order.

Right now, Apple’s website suggests that you can check back for iPhone Duo availability on October 24th. However, this isn’t a guarantee of any stock actually being available, per MacRumors:

Apple Store employees told MacRumors that they have been advised that there will likely be no ‌iPhone Duo‌ stock available for walk-in purchases on launch day. Staff have been instructed to discourage customers without pre-orders from coming in expecting to buy the device, warning that they will be disappointed.

This isn’t necessarily a surprise, given the fact that Apple stated yesterday that iPhone Duo demand is “extraordinary,” and we’ve long known that there were production constraints that’d lead to limited iPhone Duo supply around launch.

However, this still serves as our first true sign that even if you line up at an Apple Store the night prior to the iPhone Duo launch, you might not actually end up getting a device. Some stores might receive no additional shipments beyond what was already pre-ordered.

	

As of now, iPhone Duo is sold out through January. If these supply constraints remain, it’ll probably be challenging to buy a device for the foreseeable future. Scalpers have also been charging absurd markups on iPhone Duo orders close to launch day.

fullText:

fullText:
Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

If you’re someone who collects tons of varying Apple products, Hoardware is your one-stop shop for keeping track of it all. Hoardware lets you track all of your hardware, as well as the software versions, model numbers, and anything else that might be relevant.

Highlights

Hoardware is mostly useful as a collector’s tool. Say you have a giant vintage iPhone collection. Hoardware will let you track every single iPhone, its iOS version, its serial number, and anything else that you want to note down. There’s also a coverage tab, where you can see how many devices you own on each iOS version.

Of course, it isn’t only useful for collectors. You can add new devices too, and Hoardware has a feature where it can notify you when new software updates are released for your device, so you can see it even quicker than Apple will tell you.

Adding a device to Hoardware is simple. There’s a list you can scroll through, then you select from there – and most of the details are automatically filled in. The app even automatically provides images of devices.

Lastly, you can even set devices as favorites so you can easily find them in a crowded list, if you’re an avid collector. Your library will sync across iCloud, too.

Download the app

Hoardware is available for free on the App Store for devices running iOS 17 and later. There are no ads, in-app purchases, or subscriptions.

title: tvOS 27.2 adds three new features to your Apple TV 4K
snippet: tvOS 27.2 is coming next week, bringing several new features to Apple TV 4K users—including some screen saver upgrades. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
tvOS 27.2 is coming next week, bringing several new features to Apple TV 4K users—including some screen saver upgrades. Here’s what’s new.

#1: Shuffle option for screen savers

tvOS offers a variety of great screen savers across multiple categories, including Aerials, Memories & Slideshows, Portraits, and Snoopy.

But historically, you’ve had to choose just one of these categories for your Apple TV screen savers, thus missing out on all the others.

In tvOS 27.2, Apple has a new ‘Shuffle’ option which will cycle through all available screen savers—regardless of category—throughout the day.

I’ve always favored Apple’s beautiful selection of Aerials. But I love that now I can continue enjoying Aerials while also benefiting from the other screen saver categories too.

#2: Apple TV app supports sign language

For select movies and shows that support it, the Apple TV app now lets viewers toggle sign language options inside the player controls. Per Sigmund Judge:

Update: tvOS 27.2 Beta 3 confirms upcoming Sign Language options for both American (ASL) and British (BSL) – allowing access to sign language options in player controls on selected movies and shows.

— Sigmund Judge (@sigjudge) October 5, 2026

ASL (American Sign Language) and BSL (British Sign Language) are available, expanding accessibility for content in the Apple TV app.

#3: Custom screen savers from Photos library

If you want to curate Photos screen savers, tvOS 27.2 lets you do that in a new and convenient way.

When setting up screen savers in the Memories & Slideshows or Portraits categories, you’re now able to manually select the content that’s included from your iPhone or iPad.

	

Thanks to this addition, you can enjoy Apple TV screen savers from Photos without being forced to let them access your full library.

Coming soon: Siri AI and HomePod surround sound

When the new Apple TV 4K (4th gen) arrives on November 13, it will include support for Siri AI and also a new four-speaker HomePod surround sound setup.

Siri AI is coming to Apple TV 4K 2nd and 3rd generation too, but it’s not yet available in tvOS 27.2.

tvOS 27.2 is now available in RC (release candidate) and is expected to ship next week to all users.

title: Hands-on: UGREEN’s new 25W MagSafe battery for iPhone features liquid cooling
snippet: Last month, UGREEN introduced a new Qi2.2 25W 10000mAh MagSafe battery bank for iPhone. There have been plenty of these, but this one has an interesting new twist: liquid cooling. more…
fullText:
Last month, UGREEN introduced a new Qi2.2 25W 10000mAh MagSafe battery bank for iPhone. There have been plenty of these, but this one has an interesting new twist: liquid cooling.

On the back of the battery, there’s a window that showcases the liquid within the battery bank moving throughout it. This should help keep it a little bit cooler than most MagSafe battery banks.

UGREEN says that it’ll be around 18 degrees cooler than usual, and while that’s probably true – it’s worth nothing that it still isn’t a cold battery bank, it’s just cooler than usual. It’ll still feel warm in your hand.

On the bottom of the battery bank, UGREEN integrates a USB-C cable for charging your phone or any other USB-C device that can’t (or you prefer not to) charge wirelessly. I found it a bit handy at times, since of course wireless charging is never as energy efficient as wired charging.

I will admit, the battery bank is a little bit thick, and the lack of a kickstand is somewhat bothersome at this price point, especially when so many others offer one. That said, if heat is a concern of yours with MagSafe battery banks, this one will definitely solve that for you.

On the side, it offers a small display for showing battery percentage and charging speed.

One last thing of note: if you’re buying an iPhone Duo, this will stick out from the bottom of the phone, based on case dimensions I’ve tested it with. This is true for most MagSafe accessories on iPhone Duo, though.

The UGREEN MagFlow battery bank comes in at $149, which is quite pricey for a MagSafe battery of any kind. That said, UGREEN currently has it on sale for $95 on Amazon, making it much more palatable if you’re looking for a MagSafe battery bank that doesn’t get as hot as the competition.

title: Apple Store is down ahead of iPhone Duo preorder rush
snippet: In keeping with tradition, Apple has taken down the Apple Store this morning ahead of the iPhone Duo going up for preorder. If you are waiting to buy the new Apple foldable, be sure to log on at 5 AM Eastern Time. All reports point to constrained supply and relatively high demand, so everyone is anticipating that Apple will run out of launch day stock very quickly indeed. If you want a Duo for launch day, on October 23, you need to be ready to buy at 5 AM. more…
fullText:
In keeping with tradition, Apple has taken down the Apple Store this morning ahead of the iPhone Duo going up for preorder. If you are waiting to buy the new Apple foldable, be sure to log on at 5 AM Eastern Time.

All reports point to constrained supply and relatively high demand, so everyone is anticipating that Apple will run out of launch day stock very quickly indeed. If you want a Duo for launch day, on October 23, you need to be ready to buy at 5 AM.

The iPhone Duo is Apple’s first foldable, featuring a 7.6-inch inner display and a 5.4-inch outer display when closed. Apple has engineered the product to feature a minimal crease when unfolded, aided by a custom hinge design and a nano-texture matte finish on the inner display. 

It is powered by Apple’s latest A20 Pro chip, and should offer computational performance in the ballpark of the iPhone 18 Pro line. The cameras are a downgrade though, due to the device’s thinner design when unfolded, and the Duo only has Touch ID rather than Face ID biometrics.

The Duo comes in two colors, Night Sky and Star White, and starts at $1999 for the entry-level 256 GB model.

iPhone Duo will launch with iOS 27.1, which will include a bunch of software UI optimisations for the product’s unusual form factor. This includes a new vertical bar where all the controls in updated apps appear along the right-edge of the phone, making them easy to tap with your thumb. 

All of Apple’s apps have also been updated to smoothly expand between the outer display and the larger inner display, and app developers are also submitting compatibility updates as we speak.

While foldables in general make up a small percentage of overall smartphone sales, Apple’s entrance into the category is expected to make a mark. We think the Duo will be a big hit, at least relatively to the competition. 

Whether Apple can manufacture enough of them will be the problem, at least for the first few months. Reports have indicated Apple’s suppliers will ship about 7-10 million Duos for the rest of 2026.

title: How to Spot Political Deepfakes and Scams This Midterm Election Season
snippet: Election Day is just a few weeks away, but AI-edited political ads are already here.
fullText:
Seeing is no longer enough to automatically believe it, thanks to generative AI. Generative AI tools like chatbots, image and video generators make it easy for anyone to create realistic media. The capabilities of AI have improved so much that it’s nearly impossible to distinguish real from AI. That’s never been more frustrating or dangerous than it is now during election season.

The 2026 midterm election is on Tuesday, Nov. 3. All 435 House of Representatives seats are on the ballot, along with 33 Senate seats and many other state and local races across the country. You can check your voter registration and see who’s on your ballot now using Vote.org’s free tool.

This fall, we’ve seen a number of AI-edited political ads, with and without disclosures about their AI use. Unsurprisingly, we’ve seen AI used in some high-profile races, including to give Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff AI cosmetic procedures and to make it seem like Texas Senate candidate James Talarico had defaced a Bible. Political campaigns and groups have spent more than $16 million on these AI ads this year, a CNN analysis found. 

			

More from CNET

We’ve seen how generative AI can wreak havoc during election season. During the 2024 presidential primary, many New Hampshire voters got phone calls from an AI voice replica of Joe Biden urging them not to vote. This wasn’t sanctioned by the Biden campaign, and AI robocalls are illegal, so the Democratic political consultant behind it was charged with voter suppression and fined $6 million. 

Improvements to AI tech since 2024 only make for sharper swords in a bad actor’s arsenal. To protect yourself from being scammed or tricked by AI deepfakes, here are some tips.

Verify if those photos, videos and audio are AI

Obvious errors like seven-fingered hands in AI images are increasingly rare as AI tech improves. That’s bad news for people trying to visually determine whether something is AI or not. 

Instead, it can be more accurate to use online verification websites. These are our top choices:

The Content Authenticity Initiative’s Inspect tool can identify many kinds of AI content.

OpenAI’s Verify tool can identify content made with ChatGPT.

Google’s SynthID Detector can identify Google-made AI content. You can also upload content to Gemini to scan for SynthIDs.

These websites work by scanning an image, video or audio file’s metadata for hidden signatures that indicate it was made with AI. They aren’t foolproof, but they should catch some AI media. 

Other services can also identify some AI content for a price, like Pangram’s $20 per month subscription for individual users. Apple is also adding a verification measure called Reference Images, but it’s limited to its newest iPhone 18 Pro models. 

Be mindful that any AI detection service claiming a 100% success rate is lying. There are too many AI services available and too little standardization across the industry to get it right all the time.

Always double-check with official sources

We know from decades of cybersecurity research that attackers will try to prey on your emotions to get you to fall for a scam. The goal for these bad actors is to cloud your judgment. So one of the best ways to fight back is to arm yourself with knowledge.

For example, if you get a text saying your polling location has been changed with a link to the new one, don’t automatically click it. Go to your state’s board of elections website to verify whether a change has been made – it’s going to have the most official and up-to-date information on polling locations and times. 

Check out this map from the US Election Assistance Commission to see the official election contact information for your state. You can also search for your state’s board of elections or check your governor’s website, which may also have voting info readily available. Nonprofit Vote.org can also help you track down your ballot information, no matter what state you’re voting in.

If you’re looking for official policy stances on a candidate rather than relying on potentially fake images or videos, your best bet is to start with their campaign website and platform. There’s no guarantee that the candidate is going to post entirely truthful information, but it should give you some insight into their beliefs on major issues.

Stay calm, be proactive and make a plan now

It’s cliché but true: Don’t believe everything you see online. Election season is a noisy time, and inevitably, you’re going to run across something that isn’t true. Use your gut and avoid panicking when possible. Fact-checking websites like Snopes.com can be useful resources.

The best way to avoid being scammed or tricked by a deepfake is to plan ahead and stay engaged: Make your voting plan now — many states offer an early voting period beginning in mid-October. Check your state’s voter ID laws. View your ballot in advance and research all the candidates on it, not just the headline races.

If you run into issues at your polling place, you can contact the Election Protection Hotline at 866-687-8683.

For more, check out our guide on what to do when you’ve been deepfaked.

title: HomeKit Weekly: Get your Halloween and Christmas automations set up now
snippet: It’s time to get your Halloween decorations out and automate them because the gear you buy for October is the same gear you’ll use in December. Set it up once now, and all you’ll do in November is swap what’s plugged into your gear. My first real Apple Home project years ago was automating Christmas lights, and it’s still the easiest win in your entire smart home, and it’s really one of the most useful things you can do. more…
fullText:
It’s time to get your Halloween decorations out and automate them because the gear you buy for October is the same gear you’ll use in December. Set it up once now, and all you’ll do in November is swap what’s plugged into your gear. My first real Apple Home project years ago was automating Christmas lights, and it’s still the easiest win in your entire smart home, and it’s really one of the most useful things you can do.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

Start with a home hub

Before buying anything else, make sure you have a device that can serve as a home hub. That means having an Apple TV, a HomePod, or a HomePod mini signed into your iCloud. Without one, you can’t run automations or control anything while you’re away from your local, which defeats most of the purpose here. It isn’t technically required for Apple Home, but for holiday automations, it may as well be.

Outdoor plugs are the real purchase

This is the part that lets you use your system both holidays. In October, Halloween inflatables, projectors, and pathway lights make the perfect Apple Home setup for Christmas lights and yard decorations in December, all running off the same outlet you set up once. Buy outdoor-rated plugs, not indoor ones, and run an extension cord out a window. Indoor plugs aren’t built for cold, moisture, or rain, and you’ll be dealing with both by the time December arrives.

Onvis Outdoor Smart Plug

Meross Outdoor HomeKit Plug

Kasa Apple HomeKit Outdoor Smart Plug

Lutron Caseta Weatherproof+ Outdoor Smart Plug

Minoston Outdoor Smart Plug Outlet

Most of these plugs have two independently controlled outlets, which matters more than you’d think if you don’t set them up. One side runs your inflatable, the other can run a light, and you can put them on different schedules. I have one out year-round on my back porch for lamps

Indoors, a single smart plug turns your Christmas tree into an Apple Home automation, and the same plug handles a Halloween window display or a fog machine in October.

Eve Energy with Thread

TP-Link Tapo

Minoston Matter Smart Plug Outlet

Shelly Smart Plug

Eve Energy costs more than some others, but it supports Thread.

Halloween setup

Halloween is when Apple Home motion sensors are especially useful. If you put a sensor near the walkway, you can trigger a light when someone approaches the door. It’s the one holiday where having a reactive automation beats a scheduled one.

Bulbs that can change color on the porch are the other easy win. If you swap your normal porch bulb for a color-capable one, set it to orange or deep purple for October, then back to warm white in November. The Linkind Smart Light Stick would be an interesting option to have as well.

Christmas setup

Your Christmas tree is the obvious one to automate. Plug it into an Apple Home/Matter smart plug, name it something Siri will easily understand, and you’re set: “Hey Siri, turn on the Christmas tree.” That single automation is the one my family uses most, and it costs about $20 to set up. You can also simply automate using the tips below.

Building the automations

Once your devices are in the Home app, go to the Automations tab, tap the + button, choose Add Automation, and pick A Time of Day Occurs. Sunset is the setting you want for almost everything holiday-related, since it shifts automatically as the days get shorter. The step a lot of people can forget about: create a second automation to turn everything off. Sunrise works, but a fixed time like 11 PM is usually better in my experience.

Here’s a tip that I’ve learned from years of smart home use: name your devices very simple. Call the outdoor plug “Front Yard Lights” instead of “Christmas Lights,” and you won’t have to touch anything or rename devices when the season changes. The automation you built for Halloween keeps working in December. In fact, I’ve gotten to the point where I leave mine plugged in all year just so I don’t have to remove, reset, and re-add.

Wrap up

The best thing about Apple Home is that you can start with a single outdoor plug and an inflatable ghost, or with a Christmas tree, and build it out from there over time. The hardware is really inexpensive, the automations take about five minutes each, and doing it in early October means you’re not standing outside in the cold in December trying to pair a plug to your network. Set it up once in the fall, then run it for both Halloween and Christmas.

title: Galaxy S27 reportedly skips Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 due to overheating
snippet: According to a new report, Samsung’s Galaxy S27 series might not use the latest Snapdragon chipset due to overheating problems. more…
fullText:
According to a new report, Samsung’s Galaxy S27 series might not use the latest Snapdragon chipset due to overheating problems. 

The Snapdragon vs Exynos debate has been around for years, with Samsung often mixing its two flagship chipset choices, but also occasionally going all in on one or the other. Snapdragon is almost exclusively used in the US, with the last time Samsung used Exynos entirely in the States being the Galaxy S6 over a decade ago. That was due to overheating problems with Qualcomm’s flagship chip at the time, and it seems we’re in for a case of deja vu.

Seoul Economic Daily reports that Samsung has “informed Qualcomm of the overheating issue” with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and is looking at Exynos 2700 as an alternative. The report claims:

Samsung is in talks with Qualcomm to resolve the heat issue within this month, according to sources. If Qualcomm meets the required performance, Samsung will adopt Snapdragon as originally planned; if not, it will have little choice but to consider the Exynos 2700 as an alternative, weighing performance stability and mass-production timelines.

Qualcomm announced its latest flagship chips in September and the top-tier Elite Extreme Gen 6 features a 2nm process and two 5GHz cores. Qualcomm claims a 13% boost in CPU performance over the Gen 5 chip, 44% improvement in GPU performance, and boosts to AI processing and power efficiency.

	

There have already been a few phones announced with the chip, including the US-bound Motorola Signature 27, but it’s too early to tell if overheating issues are going to be widespread.

Update: Qualcomm, in a statement sent to 9to5Google, says that the report is “inaccurate.”

Recent reporting about thermal issues related to Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 is inaccurate. We are proud of the innovation and strong momentum behind our next-generation flagship platform and continue to work closely with global OEMs to deliver premium user experiences.

fullText:
HomePod owners, have you ever wished you could disable touch controls on the top of your device? With iOS 27.2, Apple is finally adding that option. Here are the details.

HomePod touch controls can be disabled with ‘Lock Controls’ setting in iOS 27.2

If you have ever had an issue with your HomePod and phantom touches, or perhaps like me you have a young child, you may have wished for a way to disable touch controls.

All HomePod models will support the Lock Controls setting, according to HomePod software 27.2 RC.

You should see the setting in the Home app after updating both HomePod and iPhone. https://t.co/lAPVuRg3av

— pdfu (@itspdfu) October 19, 2026

As seen in the screenshot above, iOS 27.2 adds a new setting for ‘Lock Controls’ inside the Home app’s HomePod accessory settings. When enabled, here’s what it does per Apple:

Prevent HomePod from playing audio or taking action when the top cap is touched. Intercom, timers, alarms, Check In and FaceTime calls will still respond to touch.

If you control your HomePod primarily through your iPhone or another device, Lock Controls is a great option to have. Particularly if you have toddlers or cats at home, or if your HomePod experiences phantom taps, you might want to disable touch interactions.

As pdfu’s post today says, this new setting is coming to all HomePod models, even the first-gen HomePod from 2018.

title: HP Googlebook 14 Review: Great laptop, shame about the OS
snippet: HP’s first crack at a Googlebook laptop is a winner, or at least as much of one as the platform allows. While Googlebook as an operating system leaves a lot to be desired, the HP Googlebook 14 checks every single box for a fantastic laptop. more…
fullText:
HP’s first crack at a Googlebook laptop is a winner, or at least as much of one as the platform allows. While Googlebook as an operating system leaves a lot to be desired, the HP Googlebook 14 checks every single box for a fantastic laptop.

Kicking things off with the hardware, HP really has built a very good laptop here.

The design is subtle at a glance, but I appreciate the sharp corners of the underside where the feet hold the laptop up for air circulation. There’s a decent-sized gap in the back for airflow as well which almost feels like a handle when you’re carrying the closed laptop. It’s a far cry from something as flat and edgeless as a MacBook Air, but I’ve really come to like it while using the HP Googlebook 14. 

The machine is just 10.9mm thick, and weighs in at 2.74lbs (despite an error that doubles the weight on HP’s website). The aluminum build is sturdy with minimal flex in the deck, and it mostly passes the one-handed opening test. 

	

					

The HP Googlebook 14 is a well-built, speedy laptop sold at a good price for its specs, but it’s let down by a young and incapable operating system and launching at a time where your money is best spent elsewhere.

					

				

Pros

				

											

Excellent keyboard + trackpad

											

Vivid display

											

Thin and well-built hardware

									

			

					

				

Cons

				

											

Googlebook OS is not as capable as Windows or macOS

											

The Snapdragon X Elite runs well, but is also over 2 years old

									

			

			

The keyboard has been a tremendous highlight. Despite the thin design, there’s a ton of travel in this keyboard and it’s wildly comfortable to type on. The keys have a satisfying clack without being too loud to be used in public spaces, and the spacing is great, while the backlight is also perfectly pleasant. It took just a few minutes to feel completely at home typing, though Googlebook’s keyboard shortcuts do take a moment to settle into. The top row of function keys are simple and straightforward for the most part, but the window fullscreen toggle (F4) and screenshot tool (F5) both need better iconography — the screenshot key is incredibly vague.  

The trackpad is also quite good. While I still struggle with Google’s premium push on Googlebook’s first wave, I’m glad that haptic trackpads were mandated, though HP’s implementation feels just a tiny bit hollow. The placement of the trackpad going right up to the spacebar might prove troublesome for some users, but I never ran into any issues in my testing period.

As for the display, the 14-inch OLED panel is gorgeous. It’s crisp and colorful, and just bright enough. I’d love if it were a bit brighter for outdoor usage, but it’s perfectly acceptable as long as you’re not in direct sunlight.

Battery life is good enough, though not quite at the level of something like a MacBook Air. That’s a bit of a tough pill to swallow given Googlebook OS’ inherent limitations, but this is a far cry from the dark days of laptop battery life and easily on par with a Snapdragon-powered Windows machine. Standby time is good, and it’s actually quite nice having Android’s typical battery usage stats at the ready. Windows is far behind in this regard. Charging has been very quick and I commend HP for including a charger that feels like it belongs in this decade, though I typically stuck with whatever USB-C chargers I had at the ready both in at-home use and on a recent trip.

Performance on the Snapdragon X Elite with 16GB of RAM is unsurprisingly excellent. Seeing as Googlebook is built on Android, it’s a clear formula for a speedy machine. While I’ve absolutely run into my fair share of hiccups here or there, boot times are near-instant, and the overall performance is impossible to complain about.

HP Googlebook 14 has every piece of a great laptop, but sadly it all comes down to the software, and Googlebook is a drag on this machine.

Our Abner Li has already delivered a pretty in-depth review of Googlebook OS as a whole, so this is basically my own personal addendum on that.

Googlebook OS review: A post-smartphone PC, if Google can keep it

My view of Googlebook is that, frankly, it seems a bit pointless in this day and age. Google has rebuilt ChromeOS on top of a new foundation that, yes, presents more possibility for the future, but also fixes virtually none of the existing problems. Like ChromeOS, Googlebook has an incredibly limited library of desktop-class software, even more so given that Linux support has regressed tremendously. One could point at obvious examples like the Adobe suite here, but it really comes down to the niche apps and tools that have been built out for Windows, macOS, and Linux for decades now. That’s an impossible task for any new platform to deal with, but Googlebook feels as though it is actively ignoring that clear gap in functionality. As mentioned, Linux app support has been largely decimated, which was a major boon to the app situation on ChromeOS. There’s also no way to emulate apps for other platforms here, which would be another good way to meet the needs of users not satisfied by what can be found on the Play Store or the web. Google literally has the tools to do this and, yet, none of them can be found here.

	

In launching this platform, Google’s repeated line about who this is for is “it’s a laptop for Android users.” I’m absolutely sick of hearing that. It’s utterly meaningless.

In a smartphone-dominated society, smartphones are the tentpole. Yes, you want integration between devices, but you’re not buying a laptop for smartphone integration. You buy a laptop to do the things that your phone can’t, and Googlebook can’t really do much more than your phone, at least not yet. 

HP did a great job building out a very good laptop for Googlebook. The hardware is just let down by the software. You’d have a much better time using this laptop with Windows or even Linux compared to Googlebook right now. Especially at a time when the cost of laptops continues to skyrocket, I cannot recommend that anyone invests $1,200 into a Googlebook when you can get a Windows laptop, or even a MacBook, for the same price, if not less. There’s simply no reason to get less functionality for the same price. Fast-forward to when Googlebook is available on less expensive hardware and it might be a different story, but right now, eh.

title: You should pick up this $850 Pixel 10 Pro XL over its $1,300 sequel
snippet: Whether you’re in need of a new phone or you’re trying to get some early Christmas shopping out of the way, Amazon has a killer deal on a Pixel 10 Pro XL that might make you forget all about RAMageddon. more…
fullText:
Whether you’re in need of a new phone or you’re trying to get some early Christmas shopping out of the way, Amazon has a killer deal on a Pixel 10 Pro XL that might make you forget all about RAMageddon.

It’s no secret that consumer tech prices are continuing to balloon in the face of AI-driven RAM shortages, which makes any deal on last-gen tech always worth considering. It says a lot that, even removed from that context, this $850 Pixel 10 Pro XL in Moonstone remains an all-around great deal, saving you a whopping $450 over its successor without much in the way of meaningful sacrifices. In fact, considering the 256GB variant actually has more RAM than this year’s base Pro XL model, you might come out ahead in the long run.

Buy Pixel 10 Pro XL for $850 at Amazon

Still, it’s worth breaking some of those sacrifices down. In addition to the obvious downside of losing a year’s worth of software upgrades — since we’re a full 12 months further along the Pixel 10’s seven-year lifecycle — you’ll have to be willing to lose a handful of changes on both the hardware and software fronts. Other hardware changes include a Tensor G5 over the G6, a slightly dimmer display, a smaller telephoto sensor, and, of course, the lack of everybody’s favorite underbaked Google feature, HiLight.

But hey, at least you get a temperature sensor and a brighter flash.

On the software side, Camera Looks is the big missing tool, with no plans to bring my favorite Pixel camera feature to previous generations on the horizon. However, I wouldn’t say Camera Looks is worth the extra $450, especially when Camera Looks being backported certainly remains a possibility in play. The same goes for Google’s typical slate of AI features; tools like Rambler remain Pixel 11-exclusive for now, but considering third-party developers have already made their own moves in this regard, I would expect to see an improved take on the company’s latest voice-to-text model show up sooner rather than later.

	

Don’t sleep on this deal; we’ve already seen a $700 sale price for the smaller Pixel 10 Pro in 256GB sell out (though the 128GB model is still available for $750). If you’re looking for a new phone to help you weather RAMageddon — and you don’t want to break the bank to buy it — this Pixel 10 Pro XL might be your best hope.

fullText:
Google TV is rolling out its latest feature roundup, showcasing new features and additions that have rolled out in recent months.

title: iPhone Duo has a bigger battery than Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Pixel 11 Pro Fold
snippet: Apple’s iPhone Duo may be thicker and heavier than most Android foldables, but it makes use of that space with a bigger battery compared to its main competitors, with a bigger battery than both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and PIxel 11 Pro Fold. more…
fullText:
Apple’s iPhone Duo may be thicker and heavier than most Android foldables, but it makes use of that space with a bigger battery compared to its main competitors, with a bigger battery than both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and PIxel 11 Pro Fold.

The iPhone Duo measures in at 254g and is 11.3mm thick when closed. That’s considerably heavier and a fair bit thicker than virtually every other Android foldable on the market today, as we previously discussed.

iPhone Duo is thicker and heavier than basically every Android foldable

But Apple isn’t wasting that space.

Despite the short and stout footprint of the iPhone Duo, the device is packing a 4,883 mAh battery. That’s the rated capacity as confirmed on an EU energy label, that is, as Apple almost never publicly confirms the battery capacity of iPhones. MacRumors did find the same info on Apple’s own documentation of the same EU energy label.

	

That’s not exactly a huge number in the foldable space, but it’s bigger than the iPhone Duo’s main competitor offers. Citing the same EU data, here’s how Samsung and Google compared:

iPhone Duo: 4,883 mAh

Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra: 4,854 mAh

Galaxy Z Fold 8: 4,660 mAh

Pixel 11 Pro Fold: 4,658 mAh

Ouch.

Neither the Fold 8 nor the Pixel 11 Pro Fold have particularly bad battery life, but Apple having a bigger battery along with the host of other reasons that iPhone users are in Apple’s ecosystem makes it harder to convince anyone to look at Samsung or Google’s devices – the main competitors in the US – as a complete alternative to the Duo.

What do you think?

iPhone Duo pre-orders are already delayed well into 2027.

title: YouTube reportedly ‘looking’ into adding audiobooks to Premium
snippet: Based on a recent report, YouTube is apparently considering adding audiobooks as a new medium alongside music and video. more…
fullText:
Based on a recent report, YouTube is apparently considering adding audiobooks as a new medium alongside music and video.

According to a report by The Wall Street Journal, YouTube is “looking” into audiobooks for a future addition to the app. There’s little detail as to when it could become a concrete feature, or whether it would be offered as a standalone benefit.

The report does mention that Google is considering offering it with YouTube Premium, which costs $16/month. It would join ad-free music playback with YouTube music, in addition to the main selling point – ad-free videos.

	

YouTube has seemingly not confirmed the possibility. It wouldn’t be unheard of, considering Spotify and other major platforms have partnered with audiobook services to offer users a little more than just music.

	

While it isn’t entirely the same thing, Google Play Books’ YouTube channel has been a dedicated spot for audiobook previews, and this integration would just make it easier to connect the two products.

It also wouldn’t be the first time YouTube has donned another hat. Shorts was seen as a direct way to compete with TikTok, and it’s become a major part of the app for the company. But the YouTube Music app might be a better fit for audiobooks, rather than the main video hub.

title: Here’s the difference the variable aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro makes at night
snippet: I previously tested the difference the wider aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro makes when it comes to depth of field. The executive summary is that the difference is small, but definitely present. I said at the time that I’d intended to test the difference it made to Night mode shots when an unmissable night video opportunity had me write about that instead. So belatedly, let me turn my attention to Night mode photos … more…
fullText:
I previously tested the difference the wider aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro makes when it comes to depth of field. The executive summary is that the difference is small, but definitely present.

I said at the time that I’d intended to test the difference it made to Night mode shots when an unmissable night video opportunity had me write about that instead. So belatedly, let me turn my attention to Night mode photos …

Once the ship had passed through the bridge, I stuck around to return to plan A: testing Night mode still photos. The new variable aperture lens offers two complementary advantages for night photography: allowing us to either increase or reduce the shutter speed depending on the effect we’re looking for.

Faster shutter speed

The widest aperture is boosted from f/1.8 to f/1.48. The wider the aperture, the more light captured for any given period of time. That should mean that Night mode shots have a shorter duration, meaning we don’t have to hold the phone still for quite so long. The shorter the duration, the lower the chances that inadvertent movement will spoil the shot.

I tested this with a number of shots and found that while the difference in duration was indeed rather small, as we’d expect from less than one stop of extra light, it may be enough to help in some circumstances.

For example, for this shot, switching from f/1.8 to f/1.48 reduced the duration from 2.1 seconds to 1.7 seconds.

Other test shots showed similar results. The biggest differences are likely to be in the darkest of environments, like astrophotography. However, living in London, this is about as dark as it ever gets, and we never get to see stars, so that wasn’t something I could test.

Slower shutter speed

Conversely, there may be times when we actually want a slower shutter speed. For example, having the shutter open for a longer period helps to smooth out choppy water, which can give a more pleasing appearance.

By manually reducing the aperture to the maximum of f/4 (a larger number is a smaller aperture), I was able to increase the exposure time to 4 seconds. This did indeed help give the water a smoother appearance.

This helps significantly with reflections on the water. For example, check out the reflections of the four spotlights on the floating pontoon under the Discover London from the Water sign. Drag the slider left and right to compare:

The other benefit of the smaller aperture is the starburst effect you get from lights. Again, compare those pontoon spotlights as well as the street lamp on the left.

However, if you want the ultimate glassy water effect, then you need a significantly longer exposure. On a standalone camera, the usual exposure we choose for this type of shot is 30 seconds, typically at f/16 or f/22, and on an iPhone that requires a third-party app to combine multiple shots into one. The shot below was taken from the same place using the Spectre app I reviewed back in 2024. This was a 30-second exposure taken on my iPhone 16 Pro Max, and you can see that it gives the water an ice-like glassy-smooth appearance:

Conclusions

Is the variable aperture lens enough reason to upgrade from the iPhone 17 Pro to the iPhone 18 Pro? Probably not. But if you’ve been considering an upgrade from an older iPhone, then these benefits might be enough to tip the balance.

A custom-size 5,000mAh cell is shaped to the iPhone Duo’s folded footprint, so it sits flush on the cover panel instead of hanging past the edges. It was built around the Duo, and it snaps onto the iPhone 12 through 18 series just as securely.

The BMX Duo also features a built-in ring that rotates a full 360 degrees. The full-color display on the back shows the exact battery percentage and live charging wattage. title: YouTube starts hiding the dislike button on normal videos
snippet: After removing dislike counts years ago, new UI tests at YouTube are making it harder to even using the dislike button at all. more…
fullText:
After removing dislike counts years ago, new UI tests at YouTube are making it harder to even using the dislike button at all.

In 2021, YouTube removed the dislike count as a way to “de-weaponize” the button – effort that had been ongoing for years – with YouTube even acknowledging that it was a decision that users might disagree with. Now, following similar changes to Shorts, YouTube appears to be testing further hiding the dislike button.

A report on Twitter/X highlighted by Neowin showcases YouTube hiding the dislike button under an overflow menu, hiding it from view despite the like button remaining front and center. This appears to be on the desktop website, though we couldn’t replicate the same behavior on our end.

title: iOS 27.2 adds new features in six iPhone apps, here’s what’s coming
snippet: iOS 27.2 launches next week with new features for iPhone users, including improvements across six Apple apps. Here’s what’s coming. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 launches next week with new features for iPhone users, including improvements across six Apple apps. Here’s what’s coming.

Messages

One of my favorite additions to Messages this year, Suggested Actions, debuts in iOS 27.2.

Suggested Actions appear underneath messages in a conversation when relevant. They can suggest creating a calendar event or reminder, adding to a note, and more based on the context of the message.

The feature was originally part of the iOS 27 beta this summer, but didn’t make the public build. Now it’s back in iOS 27.2, new and improved. There’s also an option to fine-tune which types of suggestions you’ll see.

Read more: iOS 27.2 adds new Messages feature that’s already a favorite

Apple TV

Every major streaming service has its own profiles feature, letting users on the same account keep their viewing history and recommendations separate. Apple TV has long offered such a feature in tvOS, but now with iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 it’s coming to iPhone and iPad too.

When you launch the TV app in iOS 27.2, you’ll be greeted by a new profile selection screen. You can easily disable it if you don’t want to see if again. But if you ever share your iPhone with kids, the new profiles feature should come in handy.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone

FaceTime

Dual Capture is one of FaceTime’s best new features in years. Added in iOS 27, on compatible iPhones it lets you keep your front and rear cameras both active at the same time while on a FaceTime call.

iOS 27.2 brings a key upgrade to Dual Capture: it’s now available for Group FaceTime calls.

To use the feature, just hit the flip camera button like usual, and by default on iPhone 17 and newer you’ll stream both camera feeds simultaneously.

Read more: iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime’s best new feature even better

Home

Timed with its new Home products push, Apple adds a pair of new Home app features in iOS 27.2 for compatible smart locks.

‘Lock After Closing’ is a new automation setting that lets you choose how long after a door is closed that it should lock automatically. Previously you could only set a duration based on the time since a door was unlocked, not closed.

‘Door Left Open’ tackles a related, but distinct problem: a door being left open too long. With compatible locks, you can configure the Home app to automatically notify you if a door has been left open for a certain period of time.

Read more: iOS 27.2 has three new changes just added this week

Apple Podcasts

Apple Podcasts keeps getting better, with AI-powered automatic chapters and transcripts some of my favorite features. And in iOS 27.2, Apple has a welcome change to the Up Next queue on the Home tab.

Up Next is now being split into two separate queues: New Episodes and Continue Playing.

New Episodes contains only the latest episodes from shows you follow, while Continue Playing is a hub for all the episodes you’ve previously started but haven’t yet finished.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple Podcasts the big fix I’ve wanted for years

Games

Apple’s Games app has a couple smaller upgrades for its Home tab in iOS 27.2 as well.

The Home tab now shows you recently downloaded games that you haven’t yet played. Previously, you would only see games with some play activity. And Apple says achievement progress and leaderboard scores have been updated in the Home tab to be easier to track.

snippet: iOS 27.2 is launching soon for all users, but Apple keeps introducing new updates with each beta release. Here are three changes added to iOS 27.2 this week. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 is launching soon for all users, but Apple keeps introducing new updates with each beta release. Here are three changes added to iOS 27.2 this week.

#1: Messages settings for new ‘Suggestions’ feature

The Messages app adds a ‘Suggestions’ feature in iOS 27.2 that was originally meant for iOS 27.0, but was ultimately pulled from the summer beta.

Suggestions let you quickly, conveniently take action on a message you received. For example, by creating a new calendar event or reminder based on the message’s content.

In iOS 27.2 beta 4, Apple added a new option to enable or disable different types of suggestions. Inside Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Messages ⇾ Suggested Actions, you’ll now find toggles for five suggestion types:

Add to Calendar

Add to Reminders

Add to Notes

Show in Maps

Flights and Packages

#2: New Home app features for smart locks

It was a big week for Apple Home announcements. Joining the HomeView, new Apple TV 4K, HomePod mini 2, and Apple Home collection, the iOS 27.2 beta added a pair of Home app features for smart locks.

As discovered by leaker pdfu, ‘Lock After Closing’ is a new setting in the Home app when you have a compatible smart lock. It lets you choose how quickly your door should automatically lock itself after it’s been closed.

Similarly, pdfu found a new ‘Door Left Open’ notification option. It lets you program automatic alerts to notify you if a door was left open. You can choose from ‘Off’ or after 5, 10, 15, or 30 minutes.

#3: Apple Music’s new icon and design updates

Apple Music introduced some unexpected design changes in iOS 27.2 beta 4, including a new app icon, changed accent color, and refreshed widgets.

Essentially, Apple has stripped the iconic red accent color from the Music app’s branding. Now, app icons are a simple black and white, and widgets lose red backgrounds too in favor of black.

Additionally, the Music app’s tab bar now uses a blue accent color for the currently active tab—it was previously red.

So far reception online to these changes seems overwhelmingly negative. It will be interesting to see if Apple reverts any of these design updates moving forward. Though they clearly appear part of a broader rebranding effort for Apple Music.

title: New App Store chief discusses Apple’s gaming strategy, future of Apple Arcade, more
snippet: In an interview with Polygon, Apple’s new head of App Store Worldwide, Carson Oliver, discussed the company’s broader gaming ambitions, the growing number of premium iPhone games, and where Apple Arcade fits into its strategy. Here’s what he said. more…
fullText:
In an interview with Polygon, Apple’s new head of App Store Worldwide, Carson Oliver, discussed the company’s broader gaming ambitions, the growing number of premium iPhone games, and where Apple Arcade fits into its strategy. Here’s what he said.

New App Store chief talks App Store gaming

Apple’s ambitions to be seen as a proper gaming platform owner aren’t exactly new. Over the years, the company has repeatedly attempted to attract major game developers and convince players to take gaming on its devices more seriously, with varying degrees of success.

And those efforts show. As Apple has repeatedly highlighted during WWDC keynotes and product announcements, the company has introduced hardware-accelerated ray tracing, made significant improvements to its Metal graphics framework, and developed tools that make it easier to port PC and console games to its platforms.

Early last week, shortly after Carson Oliver’s promotion to vice president of the App Store was reported, Apple announced Indie Games Week, highlighting seven new and upcoming games for iPhone and iPad, including:

Sifu

Vampire Crawlers

No Man’s Sky

Little Kitty, Big City

9 Kings

Dome Keeper

Yes, Your Grace 2: Snowfall

In light of that, Polygon conducted an email interview with Oliver, who shared some interesting details about the state of gaming on the App Store and Apple’s plans for the future.

Oliver told Polygon:

“We’ve seen incredible growth of games coming to the App Store, in general, with more premium games releasing on the App Store this year than last. […] While many of those are indies, we’re also seeing more console and PC franchises coming to mobile, as it is a burgeoning audience for those games. These seven games featured in Indie Games Week capture where gaming on iPhone and iPad is heading: incredible diversity and creativity with no compromises on quality.”

Oliver also touched on the technical improvements Apple has made over the years, some of which we mentioned above, as well as the role that younger generations of players have had in shaping the mobile gaming market.

According to Oliver, “an entire generation of players” grew up with an iPhone as their first gaming device, rather than a traditional console or PC.

He added:

“These users embrace direct touch as their primary controller, making iPhone and iPad the ultimate canvas for indie innovation.”

As for Apple Arcade, and how it fits into Apple’s broader gaming strategy alongside the growing number of premium games launching directly on the App Store, Oliver told Polygon it comes down to giving game developers more flexibility:

“We want to give developers a trusted place to reach users around the world, support them at each stage, and help them build successful businesses. […] To achieve that goal, we provide developers with flexible business model options. That means a breakthrough phenomenon like Balatro can thrive as a premium download, and it can also find a home as part of the Apple Arcade service. The important thing is that we give developers the flexibility to make the best choice for every game and players the freedom to play how they want.”

snippet: Google Home is getting a fresh update with improvements to reordering your favorite devices, redesigned controls for third-party smart home devices, and some much-needed fixes for Gemini commands. more…
fullText:
Google Home is getting a fresh update with improvements to reordering your favorite devices, redesigned controls for third-party smart home devices, and some much-needed fixes for Gemini commands.

I can’t speak for everyone else, but the Favorites tab in Home probably accounts for nearly all of my interactions with the app, which is why it’s so exciting to see Google making some big changes here. This month’s changelog suggests any “instability” seen while dragging and dropping tiles across your Favorites view has been smoothed out, and as someone who has absolutely given up on trying to manage that page in the past, I couldn’t be more grateful. 

Of course, if you prefer controlling your lights or speakers with voice commands, you’ll know it’s Gemini that really needs some attention within Home. Google says it’s rolling out a bunch of fixes to how Gemini works with its smart home app, including more reliable “stop” commands to prevent misinterpretations and easier-to-read answers on smart displays. For my money, though, it’s the move to implement “more natural ways” to stop your conversation with Gemini that’s the highlight of the bunch, allowing you to quickly end your chat with a simple “thank you” to cease talking and close the mic.

Other Gemini fixes include the ability to better differentiate between relaxing music and ambient sounds — you’d think AI would know the difference between soothing spa music and white noise without a specific update, but alas — and consistent temperature units for weather based on the preference set within your Home settings. Outside of Gemini, you’ll find large smoke alarm banners within the app, complete with event time information, a more responsive progress bar when scrubbing along paused video on Android, and Matter control for Phillips Hue lights with existing bridges.

title: I’ve struggled to use Samsung displays for years, but the Galaxy S27 may finally fix that; here’s why
snippet: The Samsung Galaxy S27 display may be getting a DC-dimming upgrade, and that will be a huge boon for people sensitive to PWM dimming. more…
fullText:
The Samsung Galaxy S27 display may be getting a DC-dimming upgrade, and that will be a huge boon for people sensitive to PWM dimming.

Ever since the Galaxy Z Fold 4, I’ve had difficulty using Samsung phones for long periods of time. The problem, for me, is the company’s use of low-frequency PWM dimming, which causes me horrid headaches, followed by eye pain, and eventually nausea. It’s not fun, and I’ve learned through resources like r/PWM_Sensitive and LEDStrain.org that I’m not alone.

Thankfully, Samsung’s Galaxy S27‘s display may give users the option to use DC dimming, according to one rumor (via GSMArena). Motorola has offered DC dimming as an option on all its OLED-equipped phones for years, and it’ll be great to see Samsung do the same. DC dimming is a more traditional dimming method used by lightbulbs and displays since the dawn of each technology, and is often considered more comfortable than PWM dimming by advocacy groups.

Sure enough, as I learned more about PWM dimming in my personal struggle over the years, phones that use DC dimming are often the most comfortable for me. The only other alternative is to use much higher frequency PWM dimming; 2,000Hz or higher, while the $1,300 Galaxy S26 Ultra only uses 480Hz.

	

Samsung has long prioritized PWM dimming on its displays for several reasons. First, PWM dimming offers better display quality in low-light situations, as DC-dimmed OLEDs can sometimes exhibit “mura” at low brightness levels, which means individual pixels don’t dim at the same rate. This creates what’s referred to as a “noisy” display, and often looks a bit like old film cameras (see the image below for an example).

Second, is efficiency. While it hasn’t been proven to have a drastic effect, PWM dimming can be loosely linked to better battery life. This has become a bigger deal in recent years as Samsung has lagged behind other companies in battery technology, but will be less of a sticking point as the company finally adopts silicon-carbon batteries more widely.

Third, is cost. DC dimming traditionally requires extra hardware to regulate voltage, while PWM dimming is (typically) done entirely via software. Extra hardware means a phone costs more to manufacture, even if it’s just a small amount per unit.

But people who are sensitive to PWM dimming typically cannot use Samsung phones at all, so none of these “positive” points matter to them. Companies like Apple and Google have begun making changes to cater toward PWM-sensitive individuals, but neither have adopted full DC dimming as this Galaxy S27 display rumor suggests Samsung might do.

If the Galaxy S27 display doesn’t adopt DC dimming next year, that will make the Motorola Signature 27 the only flagship in the US to support the technology. OnePlus used to offer DC dimming on its flagship phones in the US, but the company no longer sells its phones outside of China.

title: You Can Play Mafia, Horizon Forbidden West and More Now With PlayStation Plus
snippet: Some scary games, like Poppy Playtime: Chapter 2, are also coming to the service for Halloween as well.
fullText:
PlayStation Plus is dressing up as a gangster for Halloween. It’s not the scariest move the service could make, but I’m with it.

There’s something autumnal to me about mafia films and, therefore, the Mafia game series. Maybe it’s the muted color palette in some films, like the shades of brown throughout the Godfather, or all the suits and coats everyone wears that make me think of cooler weather. Either way, it feels fitting to me that Mafia: The Old Country, with its tale of organized crime in the hills of Sicily, is now on PlayStation Plus.

PlayStation Plus, which is Sony’s version of Xbox Game Pass, offers a large, constantly expanding library of games. Subscribers can choose from the Essential, Extra and Premium tiers, each with unique perks and benefits. Starting at $11 a month, the plans give subscribers access to monthly games and rewards, and each month, all subscribers can access a handful of games at no additional charge.

			

More from CNET

Mafia: The Old Country

The fourth entry in the Mafia series is a prequel, which means it doesn’t require you to have any knowledge of the previous games. You play a man named Enzo as he becomes embroiled in organized crime in Sicily in the early 1900s. You will find shootouts, horse races and more in this sepia-toned crime game.

This sequel to Horizon Zero Dawn sees the main character Aloy, head west to find a cure for a mysterious plague that kills everyone it infects. While she travels this new frontier, you’ll reunite with old friends, encounter a war between rival factions and fight even more giant feral machines. 

Poppy Playtime: Chapter 2

Coming to PlayStation Plus on Oct. 27.

It wouldn’t be October without at least one horror game. After freeing Poppy in the first entry of this series, you’ll have to dive deeper into the Playtime Co. toy factory to find out what happened there. You’ll need to grapple and swing to safety, as well as solve puzzles to move forward. Just don’t let Mommy catch you. 

Other games added to PS Plus

Those are a few of the games PlayStation Plus Premium and Extra subscribers can play in October. Here are the other games those subscribers can play now, unless otherwise noted.

Dino Crisis 2*

The Midnight Walk

Monster Energy Supercross 25: Available on Oct. 27.

Mycopunk

RollerCoaster Tycoon 3 Complete Edition*

Tales of Arise – Beyond the Dawn Edition: Available on Oct. 27.

* PlayStation Plus Premium subscription required.

title: Google Fitbit Edge hands-on: Pixel Watch Lite, take two
snippet: Google’s new Fitbit Edge tracker launches later this month and, as we get our review together, here’s a quick hands-on look at the new middle child of Google’s wearable lineup. more…
fullText:
Google’s new Fitbit Edge tracker launches later this month and, as we get our review together, here’s a quick hands-on look at the new middle child of Google’s wearable lineup.

The Fitbit Edge sits in between the screen-less Fitbit Air and the pricey & premium Pixel Watch 5. It’s the same slot that Google last addressed with the Fitbit Charge 6 back in 2023, but it does bring some changes this time around that make it even more of a “Pixel Watch Lite” than the Charge 6 already was.

As detailed in our launch coverage, the Fitbit Edge’s biggest upgrade over prior Fitbit trackers is the screen.

Google announces $179 Fitbit Edge tracker with display, GPS

It’s a much bigger canvas that fits a lot more on it, including new software tweaks that make it feel a lot more like a Pixel Watch than the Charge did. That includes both the faces and the different panels that Google has already shown. I’m thrilled to see a tactile power button on the side, too, as that was one of my biggest frustrations on the last Charge (even though Abner actually preferred it).

	

The hardware as a whole is simple, and we’ll get to how it feels to wear at a later date – we’re not allowed to share any in-depth insights or impressions from use on the Edge just yet, so this is really just a hands-on look.

Fitbit Edge is a fitness tracker first, supporting the usual heart rate, sleep, and workout tracking, as well as featuring the same live connection to both the Google Health app and third-party equipment for heart rate broadcasting and workout tracking. But it does more than that. With its display, it can also display notifications and calls from your phone, and it also has GPS that works with Google Maps.

I’m a bit disheartened to see that Google Wallet isn’t supported as it was on the Fitbit Charge 6, so that’s certainly a knock for the Fitbit Edge in my book. As for how that affects the overall experience, we’ll have to actually get into use to see more.

	

Continuing the Pixel Watch trend, Fitbit Edge uses the same style of Active Band, though with a connector that’s ripped from the Charge series. I was also pleasantly surprised to see that the Edge uses the exact same charger as the Air – I’m not sure who would use these two side-by-side, but it might be nice if you have a companion using the other tracker.

We’ll be digging into the Fitbit Edge over the coming weeks, so stay tuned!

Fitbit Edge officially launches on October 27, so you can probably take a guess when you’ll see our review. Pre-orders are open now.

title: PSA: Apple’s official silicone iPhone Duo case will require adhesive to stick
snippet: iPhone Duo is just about a week away from launching, and now that preorders have opened, Apple’s official iPhone Duo accessories have started to hit stores for early purchases. After purchasing, some users have noticed that the silicone case has a little bit of a caveat. more…
fullText:
iPhone Duo is just about a week away from launching, and now that preorders have opened, Apple’s official iPhone Duo accessories have started to hit stores for early purchases. After purchasing, some users have noticed that the silicone case has a little bit of a caveat.

Apple designed two cases for iPhone Duo: a $79 silicone case, and a $129 folio case. This concern is about the former.

With the silicone case for iPhone Duo, you’ll actually need to expose adhesive on the case for it to stick to your iPhone. Apple decided to opt for adhesives rather than using magnets. Presumably, the case would fall off if you don’t use the adhesive. This isn’t a new concept for foldable cases.

The unfortunate thing about this is that you likely can’t swap cases or go caseless as easily, and even if you do, the adhesive wouldn’t be as effective after you take it off.

	

This isn’t a super major deal, but something to keep in mind if you’re going to purchase Apple’s official silicone case for iPhone Duo. On the other hand, Apple’s folio with kickstand does seem to be rather nice, though it does carry a premium price tag.

If you aren’t interested in Apple’s official cases, some good options include Spigen’s Ultra Hybrid Pro and ESR’s Classic Hybrid with kickstand.

title: Pocket Casts app now available on Android TV
snippet: After first coming to Apple TV, the official Pocket Casts app is now available to download on Android TV and Google TV devices. more…
fullText:
After first coming to Apple TV, the official Pocket Casts app is now available to download on Android TV and Google TV devices.

Officially teased when launching for Apple TV, it has taken a few months to be converted for Android set-top boxes. Unlike casting from your phone or tablet, this is a native app built from the ground up to work once paired with an existing account.

The dedicated experience is tailored to your TV, with a few refinements, including a dedicated “Made for TV” section for video podcasts with promoted content and highlighted content that you can watch and listen to simultaneously. It looks almost identical to the Apple TV version from what we can glean.

You pair using a QR code, and all of your podcast subscriptions, playlists, and account data will be synced with the application. You’re able to start a podcast playing and then close the application or minimize it, and it will continue playing. Any upcoming podcasts in your queue will appear as quick links, allowing you to switch quickly or pick up where you left off, as playback information across your devices is retained.

	

It’s worth noting that this has taken a couple of weeks to become widely available, as the app was noted in a recent changelog. You may have difficulty when searching directly on a Google TV or Android TV device, but you can “force” Pocket Casts to download from a browser by selecting any of your connected devices on the Play Store.
