Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

When installing macOS 27 (Golden Gate), Rosetta is automatically removed. If you manage a fleet with any legacy Intel-only software still in use, you need a plan in place before your users start experiencing issues. Here is what I’m doing, and I have some thoughts on vendors who are waiting until the last minute to deploy Apple Silicon-native tools.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

The silent failure problem

One thing I need to clarify is that macOS 27 removes it, but macOS 28 will no longer support it. For traditional apps, macOS 27 will prompt the user to reinstall it with an easy-to-follow GUI prompt. That’s actually the workable scenario, because at least the user knows something is wrong, and macOS reinstalls it. The tools I’m worried about are the ones that won’t do that. I have a handful of menu bar utilities from vendors who haven’t shipped a native Apple Silicon build yet, and in my testing this summer, they are just silently failing. There’s no error prompt. It just fails to work. That makes auditing your fleet before macOS 27 rolls out more important than it might seem at first glance.

What I’m doing in my device management system

My short-term fix is to automatically push a Rosetta reinstallation script to every Mac that joins my macOS 27 Dynamic Device Group. In Mosyle, the setup is really straightforward. You create a new script profile, name it something obvious like “Rosetta Install macOS 27,” and enter the following command in the script tab:

softwareupdate --install-rosetta --agree-to-license

Under Execution Settings, pick your preferred trigger, then assign the profile to your macOS 27 Dynamic Device Group and save. When a device appears in that group, Mosyle automatically pushes the script, and Rosetta (hopefully) gets installed before the user ever runs into a problem. It’s not a permanent fix, but it buys time while I work on the real solution: getting vendors to ship native builds.

On the vendors

I want to be direct about this. Apple Silicon shipped in late 2020. We are now in late 2026. Any vendor still telling customers that a native Apple Silicon build is “on the roadmap” before Rosetta stops working in macOS 28 has had five-plus years to solve this problem and has chosen not to. That is not a resource issue or a technical challenge at this point. It is a prioritization choice, and one that falls squarely on the IT teams managing their software. Even if these vendors ship Apple Silicon-native versions before macOS 28, the shipping delay makes me question their commitment to macOS.

Wrap up

If you haven’t audited your fleet for Rosetta-dependent software yet, do it now while there’s still time to either push a script workaround or have the harder vendor conversations before users start running into problems. Most enterprise fleets are likely doing a 90 day block on Golden Gate for final testing/QA, so now is the time to work on your final plan. The script fix in Mosyle takes about five minutes to set up. Vendor conversations will take longer, and migrating to new solutions will take a bit longer.

title: iPhone 18 Pro one month later: These features keep impressing me
snippet: I’ve had the iPhone 18 Pro for about a month now, and during that time three main features have consistently impressed me. more…
fullText:
I’ve had the iPhone 18 Pro for about a month now, and during that time three main features have consistently impressed me.

#1: Battery life

When Apple introduced the iPhone 18 Pro, it compared its battery life to that of the iPhone 17 Pro Max—a model universally praised for its impressive runtime.

After a month of use, iPhone 18 Pro’s battery truly is top-tier. I never even think about charging it during the day, and at the end of almost every day I have about 60% battery left.

I can’t even imagine what I’d end the day with if I had the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max. Suffice to say, Apple’s battery upgrades this year are excellent, and anyone with an older model iPhone should be very happy regardless of which Pro size you choose.

#2: Main camera upgrades

Apple makes the iPhone’s cameras better every year. But it’s actually not too often that the Main camera improves substantially. In the last couple years, for example, Apple has focused more on upgrading the Telephoto, Ultra Wide, and Front cameras.

But iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera with variable aperture is the star this year, and I’ve been loving it.

I don’t have professional photography training, so the addition of pro controls isn’t appealing to me. And I never manually change apertures with the camera. But just using the ‘Auto’ setting, I keep taking photos that look especially great to me. Most of the time they’re  ƒ/1.48, with some ƒ/1.8 thrown in too. And while I don’t have the expertise to describe why they look so good to me, I’ll just say I’ve been very happy with the camera.

#3: Vapor chamber cooling

	

I use my iPhone outdoors a lot, on frequently sunny days, and iPhone 18 Pro’s vapor chamber has been a welcome upgrade in keeping the iPhone usable.

Previous iPhone models would often struggle out in the elements, especially on warm, bright days. This proved especially frustrating when I was trying to capture a special moment with the Camera app and my warm iPhone was too sluggish to snap the photo.

With iPhone 18 Pro, while it still occasionally gets slightly warm, I’ve never noticed a delay in performance as a result. Instead, the vapor chamber keeps everything cool enough to deliver the iPhone experience I expect.

fullText:
Terrence O'Brien

 

is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Serato DJ for iOS brings the company’s pro-level DJ suite to the iPhone and iPad. Before now, the company had only dipped its toes into mobile software, with apps like Pyro that basically just added some autofades between songs in a playlist. This is the first time most of the features of its flagship DJ app have been available on a mobile device. Competitors like Rekordbox and Algoriddim have had proper mobile DJ apps for some time.

If you’re a DJ used to Serato on a laptop, the workflow should feel instantly familiar. You can even transfer your library directly from Serato DJ 5.0 on your laptop to your iOS device either over USB-C or wirelessly. The mobile version supports stem separation and the company’s full suite of effects. It also includes EQ tools, BPM matching, key sync, cue points, recording, and more for live performance and capturing those performances for posterity.

You can DJ directly from your touchscreen in various layouts, but Serato DJ for iOS also supports over 120 hardware controllers. With some older controllers, you might need an adapter, but it seems like compatibility with your DJ hardware shouldn’t be a major issue. It even supports Digital Vinyl Systems (DVS) for scratching and DJs who prefer the feel of real records.

Serato DJ for iOS is available as a feature-limited download from the App Store. You can buy a license for $149 or get it bundled along with Serato DJ Pro, Serato Studio, and all of its expansions for $14.99 a month.

title: I can’t get enough of the iPhone Duo’s matte inner display
snippet: Easy on the eyes. The iPhone Duo has all the messiness of a first-gen product. And while I'm not sure I love all of the decisions Apple made around its design, it got one thing right: the matte finish on the inner screen. I've been using it for the past week to watch movies on a plane, peruse my photo gallery, and catch up on a little reading, and I'm convinced. The matte screen is the best thing about the Duo, and I hope every other foldable maker copies it. When we first got our hands on the Duo, the nano-texture finish on the 7.6-inch inner screen was genuinely a surprise. I've used a dozen or so book-style foldables over the past five years, and every on … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
The iPhone Duo has all the messiness of a first-gen product. And while I’m not sure I love all of the decisions Apple made around its design, it got one thing right: the matte finish on the inner screen. I’ve been using it for the past week to watch movies on a plane, peruse my photo gallery, and catch up on a little reading, and I’m convinced. The matte screen is the best thing about the Duo, and I hope every other foldable maker copies it.

When we first got our hands on the Duo, the nano-texture finish on the 7.6-inch inner screen was genuinely a surprise. I’ve used a dozen or so book-style foldables over the past five years, and every one of them came with a glossy inner display. Aside from occasionally noting that they can be hard to see in direct sun, I never really questioned it. That’s just how screens are, I figured. But opening up the Duo for the first time, it clicked. Matte makes sense.

If you want to watch a podcast video outside, the matte screen has you covered.

The benefits proved out while I used the phone for the past seven days. I propped it up on my tray table to watch an episode of Widow’s Bay. The matte screen effectively fought off the glare from the open window in my row. Reading a longer article felt a little easier on the eyes, and that’s what the inner screen is really there for. And there’s something about that slight matte finish that signals to my brain that it’s time to read. I can sort of fool myself into thinking that I’m holding an e-reader when I open the Kindle app and turn the phone sideways to its portrait orientation. It’s cute to imagine using your reading app in the landscape-oriented, partway-closed posture like a physical book. But I wouldn’t actually read anything like that; portrait all the way.

The thing to know about the Duo’s matte finish is that it’s pretty subtle. You don’t feel it under your finger quite as much as the more paperlike finish on TCL’s Nxtpaper devices. My colleague Dominic Preston wondered if it would be jarring flipping between the glossy cover screen and the matte display, and personally it hasn’t bothered me. The fact that the Duo’s big screen isn’t full-on e-reader matte probably helps ease that transition.

Maybe blacks don’t look as rich as they could on a glossy display, but I’m okay with that.

In fact, changing between the two screens somehow feels nice in both directions. Opening up to the inner screen feels like a welcome break from the reflections on the outer screen. When closing it and going back to the outer screen, the richer blacks and colors feel inviting.

I can concede that if you’re watching something with a lot of dark, shadowy scenes, the matte might feel like it obscures a bit of the detail that would otherwise stand out. It didn’t really bother me. But the bottom line is that this is a device that you will, by its nature, take outside. You’ll use it in ideal lighting conditions and crappy ones. I’ll take a slight hit in richness and detail for a more comfortable overall viewing experience. When my seatmate throws the window shade open, I’ll be ready for it.

title: The iPhone Duo is a messy, expensive, good time
snippet: The iPhone Duo is the riskiest Apple product in years. It's a huge rethink of what an iPhone is and could be, and it contains the seeds of many fascinating ideas that might be great in the future. But that future is yet to come. The iPhone Duo is also one of Apple's messiest first-generation products in a long time, and right now it will delight gadget nerds and early adopters and likely frustrate everyone else. It's been a minute since the iPhone has looked or worked significantly differently. The last major change was the iPhone X, which dropped the home button almost a decade ago, and even that was a fairly subtle improvement. In fact, … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
The iPhone Duo is the riskiest Apple product in years. It’s a huge rethink of what an iPhone is and could be, and it contains the seeds of many fascinating ideas that might be great in the future.

But that future is yet to come. The iPhone Duo is also one of Apple’s messiest first-generation products in a long time, and right now it will delight gadget nerds and early adopters and likely frustrate everyone else.

It’s been a minute since the iPhone has looked or worked significantly differently. The last major change was the iPhone X, which dropped the home button almost a decade ago, and even that was a fairly subtle improvement. In fact, “subtle improvement” is really the entire story of the iPhone — it’s the foundation of Apple’s entire business, after all, and there’s a lot of risk in just up and changing it. You can see it in this year’s iPhone 18 Pro: It’s been refined in many ways, with better thermals and an interesting variable aperture lens, but it’s barely different than the iPhone 17 Pro.

But you can’t play it safe designing a foldable. You have to make some big decisions about screen sizes and what the inner and outer displays are for, and then make an even bigger set of decisions about how that big inner screen should work. All of those decisions are risky, and Apple’s riskiest decision was the Duo’s size and shape.

7

Verge Score

$1999

The Good

Fun to play with

Matte inner display is very cool

You will watch less TikTok on it

The Bad

You will watch less TikTok on it because the cover display is too small

Heavier and bulkier than a standard phone

Gets hot

Cameras are just OK

Hardware and design

Apple’s single most important design decision for the Duo was to make it shaped like a passport.

The wide aspect ratio makes the inner screen friendlier for 16:9 YouTube videos, but it also marks a departure from the taller foldable design phone makers have embraced over the past five years. Prior to 2026, most folding phones opted for a tall-and-narrow shape to optimize for using vertical apps on the cover screen. But rumors started pointing to Apple going with its landscape-first form factor, and other foldable makers shifted gears — seemingly to get ahead of Apple. Now that the iPhone and a handful of competitors have adopted the wide format, they have to solve a new problem: designing a cover screen that will work well enough for vertically oriented apps.

The Duo’s 5.4-inch outer display is glossy, while the 7.6-inch inner display has a striking nano-texture matte coating. Apple’s very proud of this inner matte display, and for good reason — it looks and feels incredibly solid, a big step up from foldables with glossy, seemingly soft screens with glaringly obvious creases, like the Pixel Fold, and even the more subtle but still visible crease of the Galaxy Fold 8.

The matte display is indeed there to help hide the crease, which Apple keeps calling “perceptually flat” because it’s more fun to invent science-y marketing phrases than just saying “you mostly don’t see it.” But it’s true: You mostly can’t see the display crease, although you can definitely feel it. If you’re looking at a white image off-axis, you can see it, and there are moments in some lighting where it’s much more obvious. It definitely shows up more prominently on camera than it does to your eyes.

What you will see is the under-display camera, which reflects light in a more glossy way if you’re outdoors or in a bright area. Overall, though, the camera and display crease stopped being noticeable after a while. The crease also wasn’t any more noticeable after a week of constant flipping and folding, although we’ll see how it holds up over time.

That’ll be a real test, because Duo owners are going to be constantly flipping this thing open. Between Apple’s display aspect ratio and iOS design choices, the outer screen feels like much more of a status display than you’d expect — everything about the Duo gently nudges you to flip it open and use it in tablet mode. And not just tablet mode, but portrait tablet mode. That’s because iPhone apps are largely portrait, and the Duo is still very much an iPhone, even though its shape makes it fight all that history.

iPhones have gotten bigger over the years, but they’ve mostly stuck to the same basic rectangular aspect ratios: 2:3 from the first iPhone through the 4S, 16:9 from the iPhone 5 through the 8, and 19.5:9 from the iPhone X on to today’s iPhone 18 Pro. Basically, the iPhone has mostly gotten taller over time.

It’s wild to have iPhone apps with controls in all kinds of different places

The Duo changes all of that — it’s the first iPhone that’s gotten shorter and wider. Both the inner and outer displays have a 1.4:1 aspect ratio, which was a very deliberate choice on Apple’s part, because they’re the same shape open and closed. This is clever in terms of display math and potentially great for app developers, but in practice it means that the outer display is really quite small, especially compared to modern Max-sized phones. If you’re texting someone in Messages with the keyboard onscreen, you’re lucky to be able to see two or three texts at once.

Apple has tried to reclaim some vertical space by scooting the UI elements of updated apps off to the right, but if you’re left-handed, that means using the phone closed with one hand can be challenging, even for someone with big hands. Having that strip of real estate along the right side occupied by navigation controls also means that using the Duo single-handed in your right forces you to reach farther when there’s something on the left side of the screen you need to tap. This means that you’re sometimes holding a fairly heavy phone, stretching for a small target that’s just out of reach, which isn’t particularly confidence-inspiring.

It’s also wild to have iPhone apps with controls in all kinds of different places; reaching for the back button in Apple’s Mail app and realizing it’s moved from the top left to the right is kind of disorienting. A lot of using the Duo is just figuring out how to use an iPhone again, which hasn’t happened in a long time.

If you’re using an app that isn’t updated for the Duo, you’ll see a black bar along the right side of the cover screen where those navigation controls would otherwise live. But even updated apps don’t feel particularly useful for anything other than a quick check-in on the cover screen. Apple says you’re getting 90 percent of the screen area of an iPhone 18 Pro, but that’s pretty small for today’s apps. It’s like having an iPhone 5 in a world of iPhone Pro Maxes.

This means that when you pull the Duo out of your pocket, you’ll almost always be looking at a tiny amount of information. And the second you want to really do anything, you’ll find yourself unfolding the phone to use the vastly larger and more useful inner display.

But you don’t get any additional height when you open the Duo up. Switching from a tiny portrait display to a bigger landscape view isn’t useful for most phone apps, which are all designed around big portrait displays. Most phone apps look silly this way, especially those still running as standard iPhone apps, which look normal but with lots of black padding on either side. It’s either cramped and tiny on the outer screen or a little silly and awkward when you open the Duo.

This means almost every time you open the phone you instinctively rotate it, and while it will work no matter how it’s rotated, it’s better to rotate it counterclockwise so the cameras are on top and the volume buttons are on the top left. Over our week of testing, this started feeling more natural, but it’s exactly the opposite of what you’d initially expect. It’s especially odd in Apple’s bumper case, which has a large notch to expose the Touch ID sensor and camera control, and it looks for all the world like it belongs at the bottom.

You might think this is a little thing, but it’s strange to find yourself slightly unsure of how to hold a smartphone. A nontrivial part of the Duo experience is just reorienting yourself to where the volume buttons are as you flip the thing around. When closed, they’re on top of the phone, but if you rotate the Duo clockwise, they end up on the bottom right, and it’s the top button that turns the volume down because they don’t change orientation with the display. There’s a buried setting in iOS that makes the volume buttons reorient themselves as you turn the Duo around; Apple needs to set it so it works right by default.

One other thing to get used to is simply unlocking the phone. Touch ID is integrated into the wake button on the side of the phone. There’s no Face ID at all, and it might take a minute to remember that when you stare at your phone for a beat and wonder why your notifications aren’t unfurling. Ask us how we know. But a week is long enough to get used to Touch ID life again, and it’s mostly painless once you remember you’re supposed to be using it.

Now, here’s the thing: This is all pretty fun! The iPhone has been the same for so long that being forced to come up with little moves and tricks and ways to think about holding the Duo is a gadget nerd thrill. Other foldables do this too — Samsung and Google and Huawei have been pushing the envelope of gadget-y smartphones for ages — but Apple’s played it so safe for so long that the Duo is legitimately surprising. But Apple hasn’t found some magical software solution to making a product with this much inherent complexity any less chaotic. It just happens to be the kind of first-generation chaos that will delight early adopters and lead most everyone else back to their regular old iPhones.

Software

That first-generation wonkiness is most obvious in the software, especially in how the Duo supports third-party apps. Almost everyone who sees the Duo assumes that it simply opens up into being an iPad, but that’s not how it works at all. In classic Apple fashion, the company decided to throw everything out and start over.

That means getting rid of a lot of weird iPad baggage, but it also means that solved problems on the iPad are back on the Duo. It’s big stuff and little stuff: For whatever reason, the Duo doesn’t support pinching the keyboard to make it smaller and friendlier to use one-handed — a feature iPads have had for ages. It also means there are new ways to think about multitasking, and sometimes you’ll be unsure what will happen when you swipe around the screen because apps interact with iOS and each other in very different ways.

If you want to run two apps at once on the Duo, you swipe up and over to pin an app to one side, and then pin another app to the other side. If you tap on the little divider, you connect the apps into a set, and you can come right back to it in the app switcher. It’s neat, but it only works in landscape. If you want to have two apps open when you’re holding the Duo in portrait mode, you’re basically out of luck — unless what you want is to watch a video on the top while scrolling an app on the bottom. In that case, you need to make sure you have an app that supports background video, open that app, start the video, close that app to initiate the floating video window, open your other app, and then (and only then!) find a little button in the floating video window and hit that to pop everything into place.

This is legitimately cool once you figure it out. But you will note that this is a totally different approach to multitasking than any previous iPhone or iPad, and nothing about the Duo’s interface makes it obvious that it can work this way. It’s a lot of these little moments of figuring it out for yourself that really solidify the Duo as an early adopter special — especially since some features only work in some apps sometimes. That floating video feature? Yeah, it works with YouTube TV, but it doesn’t seem to work with regular YouTube.

This is initially surprising, because the YouTube app appears to be at least a little updated for the Duo. But it turns out that right now there are basically three ways apps work on the Duo.

iPhone Duo AMA

Got more questions about the Duo? Verge subscribers can post their questions over to our AMA where senior reviewer Allison Johnson will be answering them starting at 11:30AM ET.

First, there are regular iPhone apps that haven’t been updated at all. As with an iPad, you can zoom and rotate these apps to make things a little more useful, but they look pretty silly. This is the vast majority of apps right now, although we saw lots of apps get updated to the second category during the course of our review.

The second category is what you might call the messy middle: apps that have been updated for iOS 27. They get some automatic layout fixes so they’ll automatically expand to fill the inner screen in landscape orientation and don’t look quite as silly as standard iPhone apps. But you can tell they haven’t actually been designed for these displays, and those rough edges are super obvious. The telltale sign of these apps is the black bar on the right when you use them on the cover screen — proper Duo apps add controls to that space, but these in-between apps don’t.

1/5Apps that aren’t updated to iOS 27 will open on the inner screen without resizing.

Then there are fully updated Duo apps built for the Duo-specific iOS 27.1 — we got to test a few of these, and they can be pretty good. Instagram’s Edits app is a perfect example of why a folding phone is useful. It opens into a full video editor with a big timeline and nice preview window, and you can just get things done. And even in the span of the past week that we’ve been using the Duo, we’ve seen some apps, like Slack, go from the messy middle to fully updated. This makes a big difference in how useful they feel on the inner screen, but obviously doesn’t address the reality of the small outer-screen real estate.

Developers will need to have either a lot of energy to create neat stuff that takes advantage of the Duo’s form factor or a lot of encouragement from Apple. Maybe both. Either way, we have to hand it to the Deck-Man app, which reformats Apple Music into a little virtual Walkman. The page-turn animation in Books is terrific. And if you’ve ever dreamed of reading PDFs on a big screen in the back of an Uber, know that they look particularly great on the matte display.

But the reality is you’re going to see a lot of tiny iPhone apps and apps in the weird unoptimized middle zone for a while. It’s all just messy, in a lot of the same ways Android foldables are. That’s particularly surprising because the Android tablet app story has always been messy, but Apple had the whole ecosystem of iPad apps waiting at the ready. For whatever reason, the company just didn’t go that way, and that means it will take a while for the Duo’s app story to settle down.

Versus the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8

The Duo’s most obvious competitor is the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which Samsung managed to sneak out a few months ahead of the Duo. They’re both wide folds, but they’re not exactly the same. The Fold 8’s front screen is slightly taller and narrower, and the Duo is noticeably thicker and heavier. Those details add up to a big difference in how it feels to use the cover screen, especially one-handed. The Duo is pretty hard to use single-handed, but it feels doable with the Fold 8.

Apple also insists on preserving the more narrow vertical aspect ratio when you use an app on the cover screen by reserving that strip on the side for controls, whereas Samsung lets content occupy the entire width of the screen. On the larger inner display, Samsung offers a couple of options to make the keyboard friendlier to use. You can switch to a one-handed option that’s easier to reach or a floating keyboard you can move around and resize. And lots more Android apps readily take advantage of the full inner screen because foldables have been a thing on Android for quite a while now.

Apple is really emphasizing the ability to use the Duo in a variety of postures, including that kind of “I’m reading a book” situation where it’s partially closed. You can prop the phone up in tent mode and use it as a clock or digital photo frame. If you use it as an alarm, you’ll get a nice glow from the inner screen that’s supposed to help gently wake you up. You can watch videos on half of the inner screen in laptop mode, or on the outer screen in tent mode. Weirdly, Apple is actually more liberal in this than Samsung. The half-open position is called Flex mode on other Galaxy foldables, but the Z Fold 8 doesn’t let you use it, probably because the hinge isn’t stiff enough all the way through its range of motion.

Another important difference: The Duo is rated IP68 for full water and dust resistance, while the Z Fold 8 is IP48, so it isn’t fully dust-resistant. Neither phone should be used carelessly at the beach, but that higher dust rating offers a little more peace of mind.

Overall, these feel like pretty familiar moves for both of these companies. Apple wants you to use its phone its way. Samsung is less hung up on details like aspect ratios and where the keyboard can be. As always, Apple’s phone works best the deeper you are in the walled garden. The Duo feels a little more polished, but the Z Fold 8 has the better cover screen experience. Given how much of the experience of a foldable is reliant on the cover screen, that counts for a lot.

Performance and battery life

We each tested our own review units under pretty different circumstances over the past week, so it’s not surprising our battery life experiences differed. Nilay used the Duo just like he would during any other workday, using Slack, Google Docs, and Safari, and watching YouTube TV, Instagram, and TikTok. He needed to charge the Duo at least once to get through the day. This matched his usual experience with regular Pro iPhones, although the MagSafe battery packs he uses to get through the day are made for taller iPhones and don’t fit the Duo very well.

Allison was traveling more with the Duo, and spent more time watching video on Wi-Fi on her flights and scrolling social media. She had about 30 percent left after about 6.5 hours of screen-on time, which is decent. But as ever, iPhone battery life tends to vary dramatically for everyone, and change a lot over time. That’s even more so the case with a foldable — the more you use the inner screen, the worse of a time you’ll have with the battery.

Performance-wise, the Duo has an A20 Pro chip, and Apple says it has the same improved vapor chamber thermal management system as the iPhone 18 Pro. For most things it’s plenty fast, but the reality is that it’s also a thin phone driving two big displays, and it definitely gets warm, and sometimes hot. We saw this happen in two places: third-party apps, particularly video apps and Google’s apps, caused things to get hot. The first-generation nature of the Duo really came through here, and it’s something we would hope would improve as various apps get updated.

The phone also heats up when you use the camera for a long time — especially features that use the camera and both displays at once, like Duo Preview and Kid Cue. You can just feel the phone getting significantly hotter when this happens. Add in processor-intensive camera features like Smart Take, which automatically hits the shutter button, and the phone gets hot enough to start noticeably lagging after a while.

You’d hope Apple can improve battery life and thermal management over time — it has certainly done that with other iPhones in the past. But the Duo today gets hot, and doesn’t seem ready to last a full day of heavy use. Those are real compromises on a phone that starts at $2,000.

Camera

The Duo’s other big compromise is camera quality. It has a smaller main camera sensor than the one you’ll find in the 18 Pro and is instead on par with what you get from the iPhone Air. That’s fine for grabbing everyday shots, but it’s fundamentally a notch below flagship tier. The Duo relies on heavier sharpening to make up for its weaker hardware, so fine details look a little crunchier than they do on the 18 Pro. The Duo retains a bit less color detail in low light too, though Night Mode kind of evens out the playing field between them.

1/2Taken with iPhone Duo, cropped to 100 percent.

Some of the manual controls on the 18 Pro are absent here, too. There’s no shutter speed and no moving aperture, but you do get white balance and manual focus controls. The biggest concession is that there’s no telephoto camera here. You get that 2x crop zoom and up to just 10x digital zoom. There’s a 48-megapixel ultrawide that’s fine, but you just don’t have the flexibility you’ll find on basically every slab phone that costs half as much as the Duo.

The 12-megapixel Center Stage selfie camera on the front screen is a little worse than the 18-megapixel one on the 18 Pro — again, it looks like it’s compensating for its lower resolution by oversharpening details. There’s also an under-display FaceTime camera on the inner screen that’s okay in good light but really quite bad in dim light. (Apple won’t say the FaceTime camera’s resolution, but it’s just 4 megapixels.) Overall, it’s serviceable for a video call, but not much else.

But the good thing about a folding phone is that every camera on this thing is a selfie camera. You can open it up and preview your image on the front display while you use the much better main camera to take a photo of yourself. You’ll actually want to use the camera control button on purpose for a change, because it’s the only sensible way to press the shutter when you have the phone facing you like this — there’s no on-screen shutter and the volume controls are right next to the lens.

Apple’s Kid Cue takes a page out of Google’s book by using the front screen to play animations designed to get your kid looking at the camera. It works, but your subject will be looking off to the side since the Duo (wisely) uses the better main camera lens rather than the selfie camera for this. But if you’ve ever tried to get a young kid to look at a camera and make a normal face, you’ll probably agree that this is close enough.

1/19

Outside of that, the form factor lets you do a couple of fun things with the camera. You can set it up in laptop mode or standing up like a book to shoot a time-lapse. There’s a feature called Smart Take that will automatically snap photos when it senses that subjects in the frame are striking a pose that’s kinda fun. (It would be cool if you could switch the image preview to the other panel to use it halfway open like a waist-level viewfinder, but you can’t.)

The main camera records up to 4K/120 video and it will let you apply Cinematic mode to your clips after capture like the 18 Pro does. You also get the new texture controls in Photographic Styles if you want your foldable phone camera to act more like a film camera. Still, you’re definitely not getting the latest and greatest iPhone camera, which is weird on a $2,000 phone — though that’s certainly not unusual for a foldable.

On the other side of the aisle, Samsung basically split its Fold series into two models: the wide one with less-good cameras and the portrait-oriented one with a better main camera. You can’t have everything — unless you have access to foldables sold in China, in which case, yeah you can. The bottom line is that the Duo offers a totally acceptable camera for a new iPhone, but it’s far from the best iPhone camera you can get.

Bits and bobs

There’s a lot of other little stuff to say about the Duo — it’s full of new ideas and weird little details keep coming up the more you use it. The Duo has MagSafe, unlike the Z Fold 8, which is a big quality-of-life improvement. Allison found that a PopSocket made the Duo way easier to hold, while Nilay had a less-good time trying to use his existing MagSafe battery packs on the phone. He also has MagSafe mounts around his house and stuck the phone up all over the place, with entertaining results. Who hasn’t dreamed of having a tablet in the shower?

You can use the Duo like a tiny little laptop, which is adorable, and it connects to a portable keyboard for some purse computer action. You can also watch movies and TV shows with it slightly bent, so it stays open on a table in tent mode. (It takes a second for the phone to figure out that you want to do this, but it gets there.) If all of this sounds stressful, then the first-gen foldable life might not be for you. But if you’re itching to try some of this out for yourself, then you just might be the kind of early adopter who will have a good time with the Duo.

The wrap-up

The hard rule at The Verge for 15 years now is that you have to review the product that’s in the box — not the idea of the product, or all of our hopes and dreams, or even the promise of software updates to come. (And boy, does the Duo have a lot of software and app updates to come.) There’s a lot of potential in the Duo, but right now it is a first-gen device in every possible way.

It is expensive, it’s full of compromises, and it can be incredibly frustrating to use. Switching from the Duo back to one of our standard slab phones to get something done often felt like a relief. Sometimes you just need your iPhone to do what you need it to do — that’s why Apple has been so risk-averse in changing it.

It is very much an open question whether Apple made the right choices about the Duo’s screen sizes and aspect ratios

But all of the risk and weirdness of the Duo is also fun, in the way the best early adopter devices are fun. It’s incomplete as a product, but complete enough as an idea that you can see where things are going. It’s reminiscent of the very first MacBook Air, which took exactly no one by storm — it took a full redesign for Apple to get it right, and then it took over the entire industry.

We’ll see what happens with the Duo, but as it stands, it is very much an open question whether Apple made the right choices about the Duo’s screen sizes and aspect ratios. Most Duo owners will find that the cover display is simply too small to use all the time. Avoiding the entire iPad app ecosystem is another choice that might not age well; so is asking developers to jump on board with a device that’s clearly destined to eventually run into the iPad. Apple also made some very real compromises around the camera, and we’ll need to do a lot more testing to understand the Duo’s performance and thermal management story.

But the Duo is a more cohesive idea about foldables than most of its Android competition, precisely because Apple has a better app and developer story to lean on. Right now the problem for most Android foldables is that the inner screens aren’t that useful so there’s no super compelling reason to open them. The problem with the Duo is that the outer screen isn’t useful enough, so you want to open it all the time, and Apple’s ecosystem means that eventually the apps will be useful on the inner screen.

But the real answer is somewhere in the middle — for both screens to be interesting and useful. Someone’s going to get there, and we’ll see if Apple can be the first.

excerpt:
The iPhone Duo is the riskiest Apple product in years. It’s a huge rethink of what an iPhone is and could be, and it contains the seeds of many fascinating ideas that might be great in the future.

But that future is yet to come. The iPhone Duo is also one of Apple’s messiest first-generation products in a long time, and right now it will delight gadget nerds and early adopters and likely frustrate everyone else.

title: Samsung says the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is more popular than ever thanks to iPhone Duo
snippet: Apple’s debut in the foldable market was always going to have an impact on Android foldables, with many brands having been optimistic that it would have a positive ripple effect. For Samsung, that appears to be true, as the company says that interest in its Galaxy Z Fold 8 remains significantly higher following the iPhone Duo’s announcement. more…
fullText:
Apple’s debut in the foldable market was always going to have an impact on Android foldables, with many brands having been optimistic that it would have a positive ripple effect. For Samsung, that appears to be true, as the company says that interest in its Galaxy Z Fold 8 remains significantly higher following the iPhone Duo’s announcement.

Speaking to Forbes, Samsung’s UK VP over mobile said that demand for Galaxy Z Fold 8 has risen following the debut of iPhone Duo, with search interest even higher — apparently up by 300%.

Samsung’s foldable momentum is undeniable… Customer demand for the Galaxy Z Fold8 family has increased 16% since launch, and with a 300% increase in active Google searches for Samsung foldables in the last month alone, our market leadership is stronger than ever.

It’s not hard to imagine why this might be the case.

Apple’s massive and loyal fanbase means that the launch of iPhone Duo put foldables under the spotlight for effectively the first time for a lot of potential buyers, so it only makes sense that at least a portion of those users are curious to see what else is out there. Samsung’s lower prices and more refined design might also have a few folks interested enough to give the alternative a shot.

	

Galaxy Z Fold 8 is currently available for $1,699 on Amazon, $300 less than iPhone Duo, while Samsung.com is offering the Fold 8 for even less than that, with a special discount on the 1TB trim that offers the device for just $50 more than Apple’s base 256GB model.

title: Apple’s ‘Designers of Tomorrow’ highlights creative projects from emerging designers
snippet: Apple, in collaboration with Design Miami, is highlighting four creative projects from emerging designers in this year’s ‘Designers of Tomorrow’ exhibition, which opens today at Hôtel de Maisons in Paris. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple, in collaboration with Design Miami, is highlighting four creative projects from emerging designers in this year’s ‘Designers of Tomorrow’ exhibition, which opens today at Hôtel de Maisons in Paris. Here are the details.

Apple showcases 2026 Designers of Tomorrow

Apple today published an interesting press release highlighting the work of five designers, who “integrated Apple products into their creative processes” to develop their projects.

Now in its second year, Apple’s “Designers of Tomorrow” initiative is organized in partnership with Design Miami. As Apple explains, this year’s participants were selected by a jury that included the company’s vice president of industrial design, Molly Anderson.

Here’s Apple on this year’s theme and the designers’ approach to it:

“Apple’s Designers of Tomorrow showcase, in collaboration with Design Miami, returns for a second year to spotlight the best in emerging talent, this time focusing on the theme of presence. Exploring what still holds the public’s attention amid the hurried pace of the modern world, designers Salem S. Charabi, Isabel Rower, Yoonjeong Lee, and Parafernalia (Genki Matsumura and Sebastián Zorrilla) crafted original works that invite reflection and aim to shift perspectives, engage the senses, and kindle curiosity.”

According to Rodman Primack, the program’s curator, the artists’ works “demonstrate the power of objects to shape our physical environments and transform the human experiences that are possible within them.”

Throughout the press release, Apple details how the selected designers used its products to develop their projects. Egyptian-Danish architect Charabi, for instance, relied on a MacBook Pro for sketching and 3D modeling, while Seoul-based designer Lee used an iPad Pro and Apple Pencil to sketch ideas and take notes.

Lee’s New Form sketches (left) and Parafernalia’s MonoAmbiente 1 sketch (right)

Brooklyn-based designer Rower says she used an iPhone to document her creative process and Keynote to experiment with images and text, while the duo behind Mexican design studio Parafernalia said they used the iPhone, iPad Pro, and Procreate to collaborate remotely between Monterrey and Mexico City via FaceTime.

As with Apple’s recent showcase of the “From Earth to Sky” fashion collection, it may be tempting to dismiss the exhibition as a marketing effort. But if you’re into design, it’s always interesting to see how professional designers use the same tools we’re familiar with to come up with such different kinds of creative work.

Update, 4:56 p.m. ET: Apple’s Greg Joswiak shared a post on X featuring a video highlighting the designers’ work:

Different paths. Different crafts. One shared spark.

Check out four emerging designers at Design Miami Paris, each bringing their vision to life with iPhone, iPad Pro, Apple Pencil Pro, and MacBook Pro. pic.twitter.com/pZfMV1Gsf8

title: John Ternus talks his involvement with design teams at Apple
snippet: Last week TIME shared select quotes from a new interview with Apple CEO John Ternus, but today the full video has been published, including a discussion on Ternus’s involvement with Apple’s design teams. more…
fullText:
Last week TIME shared select quotes from a new interview with Apple CEO John Ternus, but today the full video has been published, including a discussion on Ternus’s involvement with Apple’s design teams.

John Ternus says that at Apple ‘design means everything to us’

Ever since John Ternus officially became CEO last month, reporting has indicated that he’s spending lots of his time hands-on with Apple’s design teams.

In a recent interview with TIME, Ternus discusses his new role, the transition, and his current priorities. And design comes up in the conversation.

At one point he’s asked directly: “How involved with design are you still?”

Here’s what Ternus said:

It’s funny because as a product designer—I’m a mechanical engineer by background—the team that the product designers work most closely with are the industrial designers. So, I’ve been working hand in hand with industrial designers at Apple since I started. And it’s an amazing relationship. 

I think what’s so special about this place is design is at the center of it. Design means everything to us. And what’s incredible is our designers, both on the software side and the hardware side, they really understand the engineering. And the engineers have a very deep appreciation for design. And so it’s a really powerful collaboration. It’s not [like] a designer sketches something up and then throws it over the wall and says, “Go make that.” From the very beginning the teams are collaborating, and it’s just a wonderful thing to be a part of.

Without explicitly saying that he’s been especially hands-on with the design teams, Ternus emphasizes that he’s always worked closely with Apple designers, and reiterates how central design is to the company.

title: Older Pixel phones appear to be getting Google’s new 3D emoji
snippet: Google’s redesigned 3D emoji library debuted on the Pixel 11, but might now be slowly appearing on older Pixel devices. more…
fullText:
Google’s redesigned 3D emoji library debuted on the Pixel 11, but might now be slowly appearing on older Pixel devices.

One Pixel 6a user on Reddit shared his new 3D emoji library, noting that his choices switched over from the traditional designs. Given that this is on a Pixel 6a, it signals Google might be slowly switching devices over from 2D to 3D emojis. Only one other commenter shared the same experience, which means the rollout, if it’s actually going live, is very gradual.

Without many other reports, it’s hard to nail down Google’s intended device targets. We know the Pixel 11 is how Google wanted to release the new 3D emoji set, but what comes after has seemed slow. So far, it looks like a majority of devices represented in that thread haven’t received an update. The one user who said they got the new Noto 3D emoji set said they appeared after a Google Play Store update.

Like them or hate them, Google is replacing the standard cartoonish emoji library with 3D designs that closely emulate them on all Pixel devices going forward, starting with Android 17. There are subtle differences across Android’s emoji selection, and they’ll likely take some time getting used to if you’ve been using Android devices for some time.

title: Apple lists unreleased iPad mini accessory ahead of rumored launch
snippet: While Apple is rumored to be gearing up to introduce an OLED iPad mini later this month, an oversight on the company’s French site might have just confirmed the product’s existence. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
While Apple is rumored to be gearing up to introduce an OLED iPad mini later this month, an oversight on the company’s French site might have just confirmed the product’s existence. Here are the details.

Next-gen iPad mini likely to get a new Smart Folio

As spotted by MacRumors, Apple’s French regulatory website currently lists a Smart Folio for iPad mini with the model number A3632, which doesn’t correspond to any existing products.

The regulatory document is dated September 8, 2026, although it’s unclear when Apple actually added the listing to its website.

Compared with the Smart Folio for iPad mini (6th generation), whose regulatory document is dated December 22, 2022, the unreleased accessory has some notable differences.

According to Apple’s documentation, the new Smart Folio contains at least 3% recycled materials, compared with a minimum of 9% in the current model. It also contains at least 6,610 milligrams of rare earth elements, compared with 3,947 milligrams in the previous version, which could indicate changes to the magnets used to attach the cover to the iPad.

While these figures don’t reveal anything specific about the accessory’s design, the fact that Apple has assigned it a new model number suggests that changes may be coming.

For context, the sixth- and seventh-generation iPad mini models are compatible with the same Smart Folio, so a new accessory could indicate that the upcoming model will feature physical changes that affect case compatibility.

The next-gen iPad mini is rumored to feature an OLED display, Apple’s A20 Pro chip, thinner bezels, a relocated front-facing camera, and a redesigned speaker system. Bloomberg has also reported that Apple is working on a more water-resistant design, while recent rumors suggest the device could cost considerably more than its predecessor.

There are currently conflicting reports on whether the new iPad mini will retain a 60Hz refresh rate or gain support for 120Hz ProMotion.

While previous reports had left the possibility of ProMotion open, leaker yeux1122 recently reiterated that the device will be limited to a 60Hz OLED display.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has indeed tested both options, but he hasn’t been able to confirm which one the company ultimately chose.

fullText:
The iPhone Duo is the biggest change to the iPhone’s form factor in its nearly 20-year history. It combines a compact, notebook-style design with an iPad-like inner display. It might look a little awkward, but that’s for good reason. 

I’ve spent the last week using the iPhone Duo. Here’s everything you need to know about Apple’s first foldable iPhone.

Design

In my iPhone 18 Pro review last month, I wrote that the iPhone 18 Pro Max was right at the edge of what I was willing to carry in terms of weight. The iPhone Duo weighs 254 grams, five grams more than the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

But one key difference is weight distribution. Despite being slightly heavier, I find the iPhone Duo significantly more comfortable to hold than the iPhone 18 Pro Max. The iPhone Duo is shorter and squatter, which makes a big difference in how it feels in my hand.

That said, the iPhone Duo is heavy, and I start to feel it in my wrist when using it one-handed for extended periods. Still, I find it more manageable than the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

The other aspect of the iPhone Duo’s size is thickness. When closed, the iPhone Duo measures 11.3mm thick, making it about 29% thicker than the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. Unfold it, however, and it’s just 5.2mm thick. That’s even thinner than the iPhone Air, which measures 5.64mm.

Then, we have the overall footprint — which I think is particularly notable for the pocketability conversation. When folded, the iPhone Duo measures 117.8mm tall and 84.1mm wide. That makes it 45.6mm shorter than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, but just 6.1mm wider.

Despite its added thickness and weight, I’ve found the iPhone Duo surprisingly comfortable to carry in my pockets. Its shorter, wider footprint makes a bigger difference than I expected.

And then, of course, you can take the iPhone Duo out of your pocket and unfold it to reveal that massive 7.6-inch display. That extra weight and thickness is well worth the trade-off.

The iPhone Duo’s hinge is what makes that folding and unfolding possible. Apple says the hinge is made up of more than 100 individual components, with a variable torque system that adjusts resistance as you open and close the device. There’s an integrated magnet system that keeps the two sides securely closed.

Unfolding the iPhone Duo is very much a two-handed operation. The hinge has enough resistance, and the two halves fit together securely enough that you really need both hands to open it comfortably.

When I first unboxed the iPhone Duo, I instinctively wanted to baby it. I was worried about breaking something. It’s a weird sensation to repeatedly fold and unfold an iPhone. That’s not because it didn’t feel durable; it just goes against nearly 20 years of how we’ve used an iPhone.

But after a day or so, I just … stopped thinking about the hinge — and I mean that as a compliment. I’m already treating it like any other iPhone.

The hinge can also hold the iPhone Duo steady at various angles, enabling “seated” and “tent” configurations. This lets you prop up the iPhone Duo on a table to watch videos, take FaceTime calls, or use StandBy, without needing a separate stand or accessory. iPhone Duo features a completely revamped StandBy experience that works without being plugged in. I’ve loved propping it up alongside my MacBook at the coffee shop. 

Apple uses Grade 5 titanium for the iPhone Duo’s frame, with a polished, mirror-like finish. The iPhone Duo is available in Night Sky and Star White. My review unit is Night Sky, a dark blue Apple probably would’ve called midnight a few years ago. It’s nothing particularly exciting, but it shifts between dark blue and black in different lighting.

The iPhone Duo is also IP68-rated for dust and water resistance, like every other iPhone Apple sells today. I didn’t test this, but I’ll take Apple’s word.

All of this comes together to make the iPhone Duo the most versatile iPhone that Apple sells, without compromising durability. On paper, some aspects of the iPhone Duo’s design sound unappealing — it’s thicker and heavier than I’d normally accept from an iPhone.

But it’s hard to overstate just how impressive the whole thing feels in practice. The hinge feels fantastic, the smaller footprint makes it surprisingly easy to carry, and you can unfold it into a 7.6-inch display. It’s an incredible piece of engineering, and even after a week, I’m still impressed by how well the entire package comes together.

Outer display

The iPhone Duo’s outer display measures 5.4 inches diagonally with the same 1.4:1 aspect ratio as the inner display.

On paper, that 5.4-inch outer display sounds small. I’ve seen a lot of people compare it to the iPhone 12/13 mini, which had a 5.4-inch display. It’s a fair comparison on paper, but it doesn’t translate to the real world because of the different aspect ratio.

Thanks to its aspect ratio, Apple says the Duo’s outer display has 90% of the screen area of the iPhone 18 Pro.

The iPhone Duo’s squatter, wider form factor feels very different from any other iPhone. The wider proportions give you more horizontal space to work with, but significantly less vertical space than a traditional iPhone (including the aforementioned iPhone mini). Grab your passport and imagine it runs iOS. That’s the best way to describe the form factor.

For a right-handed person, the iPhone Duo is a delight to use one-handed. I can comfortably reach all corners and edges, unlike my iPhone 18 Pro, where I have to stretch to reach the top-left corner.

Typing on the iPhone Duo’s outer screen is very pleasant. Given its shorter design, the keyboard does take up just a little under half of the total screen area. I’ve found both two-handed and one-handed swipe typing to be comfortable.

But while I’m right-handed, I’ve made a point of using my iPhone Duo in my left hand as much as possible, since I’ve seen a lot of left-handed people worried about the right-aligned software controls on iPhone Duo. It’s definitely not as comfortable as using it with my right hand. You’ll struggle to reach the top-right corner to pull down Control Center, but the controls lower down on the right side are still mostly reachable.

The iPhone Duo’s outer display has been great for quick interactions like responding to texts and emails, checking items off a shopping list, and jotting down thoughts in the Notes app. It literally feels like I’m pulling a small, physical notebook out of my pocket.

The outer display has also been excellent for other things, like extended social media scrolling and reading. Those things are undeniably better on the larger inner display (obviously), but if you can’t or don’t want to unfold the iPhone Duo, I don’t feel constrained by the outer display.

But the awkwardness of the iPhone’s 5.4-inch outer display shows up in Safari. The web simply isn’t optimized for this form factor. I’ll talk more about this later, but the right-aligned controls on iPhone Duo eat into the usable screen real estate in Safari especially.

It’s easy to find yourself on a Safari webpage where you can’t see anything but a cookie popup or newsletter banner. Granted, you can’t really blame Apple for that. It’s clear the modern web isn’t optimized for such a small, squat form factor. Once you get to a long-form article, reading in Safari on the outer display is pleasant. Getting there can be a bit annoying, depending on the website design.

I can see why Apple chose the design it did for Safari on the iPhone Duo. I don’t think overlapping the controls with the website would’ve made sense. Still, scrolling in Safari is one of the best examples of something that’s better on the inner screen. 

Ultimately, one thing I was worried about going into my time with the iPhone Duo was that using the outer display would feel like a “last resort.” I worried I’d only want to use it if I was in a situation where unfolding to the larger inner screen wasn’t an option. This hasn’t been the case.

Inner display

Minimizing the crease

There are two aspects to Apple’s work on the iPhone Duo’s crease. First, there’s minimizing the crease itself.

The iPhone Duo’s 7.6-inch inner display is a classic example of Apple’s engineering work at its best. It’s made of more than 10 ultra-thin layers, each designed to balance durability and flexibility for folding.

At the surface, there’s a scratch-resistant coating and a nano-textured polymer layer that Apple says is up to 40% stiffer than competing materials. Underneath, high-strength glass sits above and below the OLED panel, using special adhesives that let the layers slide against one another as the display folds. Finally, a titanium plate underneath provides additional structural support.

Apple compares the way the layers move to the pages of a book, which helps explain how the display can repeatedly bend without putting excessive stress on any individual layer.

The second aspect is reducing the visibility of the crease that is there. To do that, Apple is returning to a familiar friend: nano-texture.

We’ve seen Apple’s nano-texture on several products in recent years, including the iPad Pro and MacBook Pro. Beyond serving as a matte finish and offering the usual benefits of nano-texture, it plays a central role in reducing crease visibility.

One way it minimizes crease visibility is by diffusing reflected light. In an interview, Tom Marieb, Apple’s VP of hardware, explained that the “specularity” of traditional glossy displays makes it “very easy to pick up topology differences.”

The nano-texture finish counteracts that on iPhone Duo by diffusing light and preventing the mirror-like reflections you get from a glossy display. Over the long term, the nano-texture finish will also be more forgiving of topology changes.

I’ve only used the iPhone Duo for a week, so I can’t speak to that long-term durability. In an interview with @angietutorials on TikTok, Kate Bergeron, Apple VP of Hardware Engineering, explained that the matte display coating is replaceable. 

I don’t think Apple expects iPhone Duo users to replace that cover layer because of crease visibility. Instead, it’s a repairability benefit. If the inner display is damaged, that cover layer can be replaced (for a surprisingly low price), without having to replace the entire display.

So, how does the iPhone Duo’s inner display fare in real-world use?

Using the inner display

Crease visibility

Put plainly, all that work Apple did to minimize crease visibility pays off.

Here’s the best way I can think of explaining it: anyone who says the iPhone Duo’s crease is invisible is misleading you. Even Apple doesn’t say that. It talks about the work it’s done to reduce the crease’s visibility, but nowhere does it claim the crease is invisible. At the same time, anyone who says the iPhone Duo’s crease is visible enough to be a problem is similarly misleading you.

The iPhone Duo’s crease isn’t visible when you use the device head-on in most lighting conditions. Yes, you can photograph the iPhone Duo at unflattering angles and clearly see the crease. People aren’t using the iPhone Duo at those angles, though.

The only time I could really see the crease during normal use was in brighter lighting, like sunlight, while looking at darker user interfaces, like a black loading screen or video frame. The combination of bright lights and darker software seems to be a perfect storm that accentuates the iPhone Duo’s crease.

The difference is between being able to see the crease when you’re looking for it and actually noticing it when you’re using the iPhone Duo. In my experience, the latter almost never happens.

You can feel the crease when using the iPhone Duo’s touchscreen, especially in portrait mode while scrolling webpages or social media. It is more noticeable than seeing the crease, but it’s still not a problem once you get used to it.

Beyond minimizing the crease, iPhone Duo’s nano-texture coating provides all the same benefits as nano-texture on other Apple products. It reduces glare and gives the screen a paper-like feel. It’s very similar to my 11-inch iPad Pro with a nano-texture display. The matte coating feels nice to the touch, though fingerprints are a bit harder to remove than on a normal glossy screen.

Another unique aspect of the iPhone Duo’s inner display is its under-screen FaceTime camera (more on that below). I’ve been impressed by how well the FaceTime camera blends in with the display. You can tell it’s there, but it’s not distracting when you’re looking straight on. There’s also a really nice animation where it shrinks down into itself after you finish using it.

Form factor

When you unfold the iPhone Duo, you’re presented with a 7.6-inch display. By screen area, Apple says the iPhone Duo’s display is 50% larger than the iPhone 18 Pro Max’s, 80% larger than the iPhone 18 Pro’s, and the largest display ever on an iPhone.

Unfolding the iPhone Duo and seeing that inner display is a remarkable experience. You’re taking a passport-sized device and unfolding it into what’s basically an iPad mini. Even after a week of using the iPhone Duo, that “wow factor” hasn’t worn off.

The iPhone Duo’s inner display has a 1.4:1 aspect ratio, giving it a wider, more rectangular shape than other foldables on the market. I’ve never found the taller, squarer shape of foldables like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra appealing. It’s essentially taping two normal-sized smartphones together for what I think is an unwieldy experience. The foldable aspect feels like an afterthought, whereas on the iPhone Duo it’s a key part of the experience.

If you’ve used an iPad, you’ll feel right at home when using the iPhone Duo’s inner display. It makes for a very natural experience when watching video with minimal letterboxing. The book-style design also bodes well for reading, browsing the web, and scrolling social media.

In my week with the iPhone Duo, I’ve found myself using the outer display when out and about, running errands. I’m using it basically like a normal iPhone. When I’m stationary, whether at home or at a coffee shop, I unfold it to use the larger screen.

I think this comes down to ergonomics. The iPhone Duo’s 7.6-inch inner display is simply too large to use comfortably one-handed, and it’s not particularly practical while walking around a grocery store. The outer display is much better suited for those situations.

I’m watching considerably more video on my iPhone Duo than I have on any previous iPhone. Compared to my iPhone 18 Pro, the added screen real estate makes it more enticing.

From a productivity standpoint, I can get more done with the iPhone Duo. Navigating WordPress is much easier than on an iPhone 18 Pro. I can see the full WordPress interface, rather than the awkward, long-and-tall mobile version that requires much more tapping between menus.

In the Mail app, I get a proper two-pane interface, so I can scroll my inbox on the left and read full emails on the right. It makes the triage process much easier. With Split View (more on that below), I can put Notes on one side and Safari on the other to prepare show notes for a podcast on iPhone Duo, rather than grabbing a Mac or an iPad.

The iPhone Duo gives you two very different experiences depending on what you’re doing. That’s what has surprised me most about it. I’m not going out of my way to find reasons to use the larger display. Those reasons have come naturally.

Software

It’s iOS 27

Amid all the rumors about iPhone Duo, there were many questions about its software and apps. Would it run iOS when folded and iPadOS when unfolded? Would it run a hybrid operating system? Would it run iOS but with iPad apps?

Ultimately, all of that was a waste of time. Instead, iPhone Duo runs the same iOS 27 foundation as every other iPhone, but with some key changes to accommodate the different screen sizes and aspect ratio. It’s not just normal iOS stretched (or shrunken) for the iPhone Duo’s screens.

The biggest change is that iOS 27 on the iPhone Duo moves many familiar navigation controls from the bottom to the right side of the interface. Using the Music app as an example, the navigation bar with things like “New” and “Library” now appears in a right-hand sidebar rather than at the bottom. Controls that normally appear at the top, such as the playlist button and three-dot menu in the Music app, have also shifted to the right-hand sidebar.

The changes go beyond just individual apps. On the Home Screen, the dock has been moved to the right-hand side. The status bar icons, like the time, Wi-Fi icon, and cellular bars (now dots), are in the upper-right corner above the dock.

The interface is adaptable, too. If you use the iPhone Duo unfolded and in portrait orientation, the dock and in-app navigation bars shift back to the bottom like “normal” iOS.

After a few days, Apple’s interface changes to accommodate the iPhone Duo’s form factor start to feel natural. They account for the shorter, wider aspect ratio; the smaller outer display; and the larger inner display.

Typing on the inner display while in portrait orientation is very natural. In landscape mode, you have to stretch a little bit, but it’s still doable for me.

The fluidity between all of it is fantastic. No matter how I held the iPhone Duo, UI elements were exactly where I expected them to be. There’s also that gorgeous software transition when you unfold or fold the iPhone Duo.

The iPhone Duo also supports Split View when unfolded—a first for any iPhone. You can place two apps side by side, or two windows from the same app. It’s the most powerful multitasking has ever been on an iPhone. Being able to put Safari on one side and Notes on the other has been a huge productivity boost for me on iPhone.

You can also pin a video to the top part of the screen, and use another app below it. That app will morph to fill the size of the display below it.

Apps

Speaking of apps, we need to talk about the different ways apps behave on the iPhone Duo. First, all of Apple’s pre-installed apps have been updated to take full advantage of the iPhone Duo’s two displays. This includes proper right-aligned controls that float alongside the content as you scroll in apps like News, Maps, Music, and Reminders.

The second part of the app story is third-party apps, which gets a bit more complicated. Every existing iPhone app works on iPhone Duo. This means that any iPhone app you have today will run on iPhone Duo. From here, there are basically three tiers.

First, apps built with the iOS 26 SDK or earlier don’t take full advantage of iPhone Duo. The example above shows the MLB app running on iPhone Duo. In landscape mode, it has large black bars on either side of the app. In portrait orientation, it runs floating in the center, surrounded by letterboxing on all sides.

You can then zoom in like you can when running an iPhone app on iPad. If the app supports landscape mode, you can also manually switch between portrait and landscape interfaces, as shown in the Google Docs screenshots above.

Second, there are apps built with the iOS 27 SDK. These apps resize to fill most of the inner display, but leave space along the right edge for the status bar. The above screenshots show the Reddit app running on the iPhone Duo:

Here’s what YouTube looks like: 

And here is what X looks like: 

Finally, there are apps built with the iOS 27.1 SDK or later. These apps can be fully optimized for iPhone Duo, using the entire inner and outer displays. In just the week I’ve had the iPhone Duo, developers big and small have rolled out a ton of apps fully optimized for iPhone Duo.

There is a huge difference between using an app updated for iPhone Duo and one that isn’t. Going forward, I think proper iPhone Duo support will be a deciding factor when I choose which apps to use. If I’m choosing between two apps that do the same thing and only one is optimized for the iPhone Duo, I’ll choose that one.

I’ve tried a ton of third-party apps with iPhone Duo support over the last week, and below are some of my favorites.

More iPad, please

I wish there were more iPadOS elements sprinkled throughout the iPhone Duo’s software. It’s great having Split View, but I wish there was an iPadOS-like way to drag and drop apps into that Split View interface. Slide Over also seems like a piece of low-hanging fruit.

There are places where iOS isn’t doing enough to take full advantage of that 7.6-inch inner display. For comparison, the iPad mini has an 8.3-inch display, and it runs the full iPadOS interface. Even the previous generation 7.9-inch iPad mini got the full iPadOS experience at the time.

One of my favorite things about using an iPad is that websites (mostly) treat Safari as a desktop-class browser. That’s not the case on iPhone Duo, where you sometimes get the awkward mobile layout even when browsing on the unfolded inner display. This doesn’t always happen (hence my WordPress example earlier), but I wish it were closer to the desktop-class iPad experience.

To be clear, I don’t think the iPhone Duo should run iPadOS. I think going all-in on iOS was the right decision. I just want iOS to do more in certain areas to really show off the benefits of the bigger screen. Right now, I sometimes have to fight to get iOS to recognize I’m using an iPhone with a 7.6-inch display. 

Touch ID vs Face ID

Perhaps the biggest trade-off with the iPhone Duo is that it uses Touch ID instead of Face ID. Flagship iPhones have used Face ID since the iPhone X in 2017, so this is a big change.

iPhone Duo has Touch ID integrated into the side button. I’ve added both my thumbs and index fingers, so it’s easy to unlock the iPhone Duo no matter how I’m holding it. It also supports “Rest to Open,” so you can authenticate with Touch ID and keep your finger on the side button to unlock it automatically.

I think switching from Face ID to Touch ID has been the hardest thing to get used to on iPhone Duo. I’ve become so accustomed to just looking at my iPhone to unlock it. Having to deliberately reach for the side button feels like a step backward, even though Touch ID works quickly and reliably.

One benefit I have enjoyed: Touch ID is a lot easier to use when your iPhone is lying flat on a table. Instead of picking up your iPhone to unlock it with Face ID, you can rest your finger on the Touch ID sensor and to glance at your locked notifications.

iPhone Duo also supports Apple Watch unlock. If you enable this feature, you can swipe up on your iPhone Duo’s lock screen, and it will automatically unlock if you’re wearing your Apple Watch (so long as your Apple Watch has a passcode on it and is unlocked).

I used my iPhone Duo without Apple Watch unlock enabled for the first few days to get a feel for what it’s like to use an iPhone with Touch ID for the first time in nearly a decade. Ultimately, I turned on Apple Watch unlock, and it does make the experience significantly better.

Finally, because iPhone Duo doesn’t have Face ID, it also doesn’t have any Attention Aware features. On Face ID-enabled iPhones, your iPhone will check for attention before dimming the display, expanding a notification when locked, or lowering the volume of some alerts. Of all those features, I really miss being able to glance at my iPhone and have my notifications automatically expand.

Ultimately, Touch ID works just fine on the iPhone Duo. It takes a while to get used to, but Apple Watch unlock helps quite a bit. I assume Face ID is on the shortlist of features for future iPhone Duo generations.

Cameras

Despite being Apple’s most expensive iPhone, the iPhone Duo does not have its most powerful camera system. On paper, many of the Main camera specs are similar to the iPhone Air and iPhone 17, but Apple emphasizes that it designed the camera specifically for the iPhone Duo’s ultra-thin form factor.

Here’s how the iPhone Duo’s camera hardware compares to some of Apple’s other recent iPhones:
