title: Here’s Apple’s official response to OpenAI’s trade secret theft allegations
snippet: Apple has responded to OpenAI’s allegations that one of its former employees who departed for Apple took confidential files along with him. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple has responded to OpenAI’s allegations that one of its former employees who departed for Apple took confidential files along with him. Here are the details.

A bit of context

Earlier this year, Apple filed a trade secret misappropriation lawsuit against two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products.

And while this case has had its twists and turns, things took an even more unexpected turn yesterday when a new OpenAI filing alleged essentially the same thing, but in reverse.

As we covered in more detail here, OpenAI claims that a former employee who departed for Apple sent “over a hundred highly confidential files about at least one unreleased OpenAI device under development to his personal accounts.”

Soon after OpenAI made its filing, Reuters reported that “Apple said it has policies and procedures ​in place to ensure new employees do not use confidential information from previous employers and it has found no evidence to support OpenAI’s ​allegations.”

Now, Apple’s response, along with two supplementary exhibits, has been made public in a new court filing, providing more details about its investigation and challenging OpenAI’s decision to bring the allegations before the judge.

Apple shoots back

In its response, the company notes that OpenAI made the filing “without any notice to Apple,” and adds that OpenAI’s allegations are “unrelated to the claims” in its main trade secret misappropriation case.

Interestingly, Apple shares more information regarding the employee at the center of these new allegations, who “had left Apple for OpenAI and subsequently decided to return to Apple.”

[REDACTED] is an engineer on Apple’s Manufacturing Design team, which is the same role he held at Apple before departing for OpenAI. He focuses on iPhone.

Apple said that it investigated the issue as soon as OpenAI brought it to the company on October 9, and that on October 12 “Apple wrote OpenAI to inform it that it had been unable to locate any OpenAI confidential information.”

Apple said it requested additional information from OpenAI to continue its investigation, but received no response before OpenAI brought the allegations to court:

Apple requested more specific information so that it could perform alternative searches. OpenAI did not respond, and instead filed Docket No. 176 with the Court. Apple will continue to work with OpenAI to investigate its allegations.

In one of the supplementary exhibits, Apple also challenges the specificity of OpenAI’s claims about a potentially confidential file, noting that its description appears to refer to two quality control methodologies that have been widely used since at least the 1990s.

Based on your description of the [REDACTED], it appears [REDACTED] and [REDACTED] may refer to two quality control methodologies widely implemented at least by the 1990s. Other than searching for the specific file name, which Apple is doing, it will be difficult to locate potentially relevant files, if they exist, based only on the terms “[REDACTED] and “[REDACTED]  […]

The company also reiterated its willingness to conduct additional searches if OpenAI provides more specific file names or search terms.

Finally, Apple says that even though “[n]one of this relates to the present lawsuit, […] which concerns OpenAI’s misuse of Apple’s confidential information,” and adds in a supplementary exhibit that it is “taking appropriate steps, including preservation of evidence, to comply with its legal obligations in connection with [OpenAI’s] Letter.”

title: Apple execs talk Samsung’s role in creating iPhone Duo display
snippet: Apple is widely reported to have Samsung as its key supplier in building the iPhone Duo’s folding display. As a result, some have claimed that Apple is just “using a Samsung display.” Here’s how Apple addressed that question in a new interview. more…
fullText:
Apple is widely reported to have Samsung as its key supplier in building the iPhone Duo’s folding display. As a result, some have claimed that Apple is just “using a Samsung display.” Here’s how Apple addressed that question in a new interview.

Here’s what Apple said about Samsung’s contribution to iPhone Duo

Last month, YouTuber MrMobile (Michael Fisher) had the chance to interview a trio of key Apple staff who were involved in iPhone Duo’s development.

The sit-down took place following the iPhone Duo introduction, but the interview just went live on YouTube yesterday.

It’s a great video that’s well worth watching if you’re interested in the iPhone Duo. But one noteworthy portion involves the question of Samsung’s involvement in building the Duo’s display.

Here’s what Rich Dinh (VP of Hardware Engineering) and JP Guillou (Senior Director of Display Technology for iPhone) had to say:

Michael Fisher: What on the iPhone do is like straight out of the Samsung factory and what is Apple designed? 

Rich Dinh: Everything that we design internally comes from the place of servicing the experience at the end of the day. And so whether it’s the display, whether it’s the hinge, whether it’s the enclosure, the chip, there are manufacturers that we work with, a number of them, incredible manufacturers that we work with. But at the end of the day, we start with, “What are we trying to accomplish?” And we start internally with, “What are we trying to accomplish in the design? What are some of the challenges we’re trying to solve for?” And then we work with our manufacturers to help us develop those parts.

Fisher then presents a contrast between the display and hinge, He suggests that Apple gets shipped a pallet of “display things” from Samsung to make the iPhone Duo, then says, “That doesn’t include the hinge, right? The hinge is not in that thing. You guys whip that up yourselves.” Here’s how Apple responds:

JP Guillou: Maybe I can say: the display doesn’t exist at the vendor until we start working on it.

Fisher: They don’t start working on it until you make an order with your specifications.

Dinh: Yeah, there’s not a, unfortunately [laughter] there’s not a pre-cooked shelf of components that we can go to.

Guillou: And certainly not ones that would meet our demands, expectations, requirements, specifications.

Fisher: Everything is a custom order for you guys.

Guillou: Everything is, everything is.

Dinh: We really did start from the ground up. Now, there’s partners that we work with out there that are incredible partners in helping us to manufacture these designs, but it always starts with, like, we customize down to the nanometer.

Other key topics addressed in the video include iPhone Duo’s durability, the choice to use an under-display camera on the folding screen, how Apple approaches product design, and more.

What are your takeaways from MrMobile’s interview? Let us know in the comments.

title: Spotify podcast memberships let you support your favorite shows and get added perks
snippet: Spotify may not be a dedicated podcast platform, but it is launching a big new feature in podcast memberships that let you support your favorite shows in exchange for added perks. more…
fullText:
Spotify may not be a dedicated podcast platform, but it is launching a big new feature in podcast memberships that let you support your favorite shows in exchange for added perks.

Available starting today, Spotify podcast memberships work similarly to Patreon and other membership programs. Hosts can create support tiers with a monthly fee that deliver perks to their audience and, in turn, support the show. 

Spotify says examples of what creators can provide in these memberships include “exclusive audio or video, bonus episodes, fewer ads, early access, access to a show’s archive” and more. Multiple tiers can be created and pricing is customizable. 

Shows launching membership programs today include The Adam Friedland Show, Making Sense with Sam Harris, The Shawn Ryan Show, The Sculpt Society, Two Hot Takes, and 12 shows across the YMH Studios network.

	

Creators keep 90% of the revenue generated by memberships.

Spotify podcast memberships are available in Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hong Kong, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Singapore, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, the UK, and the US to start.

title: Spotify Launches Paid Fan Memberships for Podcast Creators
snippet: Early adopters are charging $5 per month for premium content, but pricing is up to them.
fullText:
The Spotify podcasting world is evolving. The audio-streaming platform announced a new Memberships program on Tuesday that allows creators to offer monthly subscription plans to their fans. The program is rolling out immediately in the US, UK, Canada and dozens of other markets.

Podcasters have total leeway in how much they charge and what content they offer behind the paywall, such as “exclusive audio or video, bonus episodes, fewer ads,” Spotify said. Creators can also charge a simple monthly fee or offer tiered pricing that grants access to different types of content. It’s their call. Spotify said creators will keep 90% of membership revenue.

Creators can also choose not to offer a monthly paid subscription.

			

More from CNET

Until now, podcasters have monetized their content primarily through ad revenue in the Spotify Partner Program, brand sponsorships and video stream revenue from Spotify Premium subscribers. Creators have also offered paid subscriptions, which may include bonus shows and ad-free content.

But the new Memberships program doesn’t mean fans will have to pony up monthly to listen to podcasts. Creators can offer a mix of free and membership content, but it’s their choice what that mix will look like.

Spotify listed several creators who are pioneering the Memberships program. That group includes The Adam Friedland Show, Making Sense with Sam Harris, The Shawn Ryan Show, Two Hot Takes, The Sculpt Society and YMH Studios.

How fans become members

To become a member of a certain podcast, visit its main page on Spotify. Near the top of the page, you should see an option to join.

The creators I looked at were charging $5 per month for memberships, but membership prices could vary as other podcasters join the program with different offerings.

Listeners can now support and connect with their favorite podcasts through custom memberships.Spotify

Creators must be eligible

To join the Memberships program, shows must be hosted on Spotify for Creators or its high-volume platform Megaphone with these stipulations: three published episodes, 100 listeners or viewers, and 100 consumption hours on Spotify in the previous 30 days.

title: Moto Tag 2 is no longer $19.99 as the UWB tracker gears up for Pixel Tag competition
snippet: The Moto Tag 2 was always supposed to be $30, but a long-running introductory discount left the Find Hub tracker cheaper. Now, that deal has ended. more…
fullText:
The Moto Tag 2 was always supposed to be $30, but a long-running introductory discount left the Find Hub tracker cheaper. Now, that deal has ended.

Moto Tag 2 is inarguably the most capable tracker for Android’s Find Hub network thanks in no small part to its inclusion of UWB. On top of Bluetooth pings for general location, the tracker also lets you pinpoint its exact location when you get up close.

That’s why its $20 introductory price was so attractive.

The discount brought its price below virtually every other Android Find Hub tracker on the market despite the added hardware. But that price has now vanished from both Motorola’s website and from Amazon, where Moto Tag 2 is now sold for $29.99. A 4-pack costs $100, but Amazon is still selling it for less.

	

Moto Tag 2 at Motorola.com

Moto Tag 2 at Amazon

Moto Tag 2 (4-pack) at Amazon

It’s still a good value at that price – especially the 4-pack deal at Amazon – but the $10 hike certainly stings for anyone who waiting too long to score the initial price point. Even at $30, though, Moto Tag 2 remains a great value. Comparable trackers from Pebblebee and Chipolo are sold for $35 or even $40, and those don’t even have UWB. You will still need some sort of add-on if you want to mount the Moto Tag 2 to a keychain or backpack, though, as the AirTag-like form factor lacks any built-in mounting points.

Meanwhile, there’s finally another UWB tracker on the horizon in Google’s Pixel Tag. The oblong tracker was announced back in August and is set to go on sale for the same $29.99 as the Moto Tag 2 was always supposed to sell for. It’s entirely possible that Motorola will drop that price again by the time Google launches its option, but these two are currently set to battle at the same price point.
